  logged; another version is `kind.version_changed` (warn, subject `tool:<kind>`) and one info toast
  ("codex-cli 0.162.1 → 0.163.0 at 11:24", the words both versions share left out of the new one), and
  `magnum status` has a `clis:` line ("codex codex-cli 0.163.0 (changed at 11:24), claude …"; `clis` in the
  JSON). For `CLIChangeRecent` (24 h) a round setup that parks its PR because an agent role did not start
  (`start <role>: …`, the dead launch's line among them) ends its stored error with
  `attention.CLIChange` ("; the codex CLI changed at 11:24", with the date for an earlier day), which
  `attention.Explain` takes only from such an error (a command's output ending the same way stays the
  cause) and moves to the end of the reason's Cause and Summary, clipping them to keep it, so the board,
  `magnum status`, `magnum attention` and the needs-attention toast all show it; the retry before the
  third attempt is unchanged. Each health check also reads, for the last 30 minutes, the pane error lines
  agents keeps (`pr.launch_cleared`'s last_line, a refused prompt's run error through the new
  `agents.PaneErrorOf`, and `pr.panes_closed`'s last_lines, spec 69): two or more PRs with the same line are
  `agents.shared_failure` (warn; the PRs, the roles, the line and a CLI change of the day) with one urgent
  toast ("2 PRs' codex-judge launches end the same way"), once per line within 24 h (read back from the
  events). Nothing is paused and nothing is pinned. Rejected: pausing a kind on a shared failure (the
  operator decides, and a pause could hide a transient outage behind a wait nobody asked for); pinning CLI
  versions from magnum (mise owns them, and a pin in magnum would drift from the operator's); a version key
  in `[kinds.*]` (no kind needs another command than doctor's); running the version command at every check
  (a stat is enough while the binary is the same); the binary's mtime as the change time (npm packs files
  with a fixed mtime); and a new field on `attention.Reason` for the note (the JSON of the board and status
  would grow a key for one sentence, and every caller of Explain would need the kinds' versions).
- **Seven review rules and two judge-only lines the operator approved on 2026-10-17, the skill's cap
  raised by the minimum** (2026-10-17, spec 76). Two misses of the week and six declines share causes the

  3 checked typical values and said LGTM, and ASCII values with a tab, LF, CR or NUL went raw (a phone
  number with a trailing newline reached the server truncated). Six declines on five repositories answered
  findings whose trigger needed a state that never shipped (a table the PR adds, a never-released command,
  a config no install has, a throwaway harness). 4 of 19 clean reviews of the week had an unrun main suite

  `reason_code` in only 70% of cases, so the misses analyst could not audit the rest, and the skill
  editor's e97d1a2 trimmed the evidence line's "`unknown` and `stale` areas are leads", the audit pass's
  lead, to fit its own rule. SKILL.md now says: in section 2, when the PR, its ADR or docs say some
  customers already get the behaviour another way (a custom integration, a webhook consumer, a hand-run
  setup), check the switch, what still triggers the old way and which step turns it off, a second payment,
  credit, charge or message the rollout never stops being P1; and each code comment or doc sentence the PR
  adds about what its code does is a claim like the description's (a false one without impact stays one
  `Description: ✗` line). In section 3, in code that moves money or makes a call that cannot safely run
  twice, each guard the PR adds is broken one at a time and its spec file run through `db_lock`; a guard
  that leaves it green is a missing test. In section 4, a finding that turns on a third party's answer to
  an input the review machine cannot send is settled by its docs or a recorded payload, and when neither
  settles it and a check before the call removes the doubt it is posted at P3 naming the unverified
  answer; a compatibility, upgrade or old-data finding needs that old state outside the branch (a table,
  format, command, config or caller the PR or its branch adds has no released rows or users, and a file
  that never ships harms no one), so it names the release that shipped it or is dropped. In section 6, a
  fix that changes a predicate, regex, encoder or range check that routes values runs with the base over
  its edge classes (empty, whitespace, control characters, the first and last member of each range), and a
  class it routes differently than intended is a finding in the fix. In section 7, when the suite that
  covers the changed code was `skipped (machine)` and nothing ran in its place, the clean line reads `No
  problems found. <suite> not run on the review machine.` (a re-review's ends the same way); magnum's
  auto-approval still reads that line as clean by its prefix, as it reads a red head's. In section 8, a
  rejected P0 to P2 entry that is not `duplicate` carries `reason`, one sentence naming the fact that
  decided it (the example's nearby entry has one; the result parser ignores the key, the misses analyst
  reads the result files). Section 0's `evidence` line has its leads back. SKILL.md grows by 1,782 bytes,
  from 35,364 to 37,146, and `skillMaxBytes` goes from 35,372 to 37,146, the new size. Each rule's
  sentence is a pin (nine new tests: TestSkillChecksTheSwitchFromAnOlderSetup,
  TestSkillChecksTheClaimsOfAddedCommentsAndDocSentences, TestSkillBreaksMoneyGuardsOneByOne,
  TestSkillPostsAThirdPartysUnverifiableAnswerAtP3,
  TestSkillDropsAnOldStateFindingOnAStateThatNeverShipped,
  TestSkillRunsAChangedPredicateOverItsEdgeClasses, TestSkillNamesAnUnrunSuiteInTheCleanLine,
  TestSkillGivesARejectedP0ToP2AReason and TestSkillReadsUnknownAndStaleEvidenceAsLeads;
  TestSkillStatesTheCleanVerdictLines pins the new clean line and TestSkillKeepsTheExampleResultOfSection8
  the example's changed line), so the skill editor cannot trim one silently. The prompts and their goldens
  are unchanged. Rejected: trims instead of the raise (the skill is at its tightest: the last raises took
  their room from unpinned wording, and the editor's e97d1a2 cut a lead to fit its own rule); an "Also
  probed" line under P1 fixes (the operator declined it as padding); one entry here per rule (one
  approval, one change).
- **A rebuttal that answers a decline names the fact it disproved and the probe's steps in the author's terms**
  (2026-10-17, spec 78, adds to "(k) A second rebuttal in a thread that holds one of the judge's names the

  pins. Rejected: posting the planned own-pass sentence as it stood (it names the probes too, "both
  page-scope probes still hide the warning", a name the author never saw).
- **The fixer applies a simplification that keeps behaviour, without a net score** (2026-10-17, carves out
  "The fix loop: magnum fixes its own findings on your PRs" and the 2026-10-15 decision that
  `skills/magnum-fix/SKILL.md` keeps its own scoring, for simplifications only). The fix skill made a
  `fix` clear a net of 3, and a simplification keeps behaviour by definition, so it nets 1 by
  construction. In one week the fixer applied 1 of 5 simplifications of the review ("Won't fix: net score
  1 ... saves a few lines only"), while people applied 22 of 22. Now a simplification the review posted is

  secrets). The skill gives it no score (section 3), and section 4 sends it to step 1 when it is `fix` and
  keeps it out of step 2. A defect keeps its scoring, a regression is still always `fix`, and the reply forms
  and the report are unchanged. The sentences are pinned in
  `TestTheFixSkillProvesEachGuardFixesRegressionsAndSignsItsReplies`. Rejected: lowering the net bar for
  everything (a defect that nets 1 or 2 is rightly left, and nothing shows the fixer's declines of defects
  were wrong); scoring a simplification on a scale of its own (the fixer would still weigh a few lines
  against the cost of a push, the call that went wrong); and a byte cap and a pins file for the fix skill
  (a new mechanism for one sentence, and the skill editor never edits this skill).

- **The auto-approval body and the two dismissal texts say Magnum too** (2026-10-17, completes "The
  product is Magnum in everything it posts"). Three texts a person reads on GitHub were left in lower
  case: the default auto-approval body (`config.DefaultAutoApproveBody`, "Auto-approved: Magnum's review
  of `<sha7>` found no blocking problems"), the withdrawal of a standing approval ("Magnum's review of
  <sha7> found …; this automatic approval is withdrawn", `standingWithdrawal`) and the dismissal of the
  identity's own stale change request ("Superseded by the newer Magnum review of <sha7>",
  `dismissStale`, both of its forms). The reasons the withdrawal carries after "found nothing to fix,
  but" are the same text on GitHub, so the five that named the product ("Magnum's review did not hear
  every reviewer", "Magnum cannot tell whether its review heard every reviewer", "Magnum cannot read the
  files it changes", "Magnum cannot tell whether it changes …", twice, in `autoapprove_gates.go`) say
  Magnum too; the board and the refusal event show the same reasons. The README's and the example
  config's copies follow. `magnum` stays the command, the marker, and the name in the CLI, the logs, the
  events and the operator's toasts.
- **A related PR is named again only after a state change or a new file** (2026-10-17, spec 79, amends "The
  Related lines name only live PRs and say nothing twice"). 44 of 97 reviews in a week carried a Related or
  Stacked line, and 19 of them named only PRs an earlier review of the same PR had named: one PR's reviews
  named its stacked neighbour 7 times, another's 4. A round compared its set with the previous review's by
  the count and the first 20 of the shared paths, so each push to a busy neighbour that moved the count (36,
  37, 36, 42, 41, 40 and 38 shared paths in one PR's rounds) named it again, and a previous review on a
  head no round recorded (a merge of the base moves `reviewed_sha` without a round) left nothing to compare
  with, so that round named all eight related PRs again. Now `related-all.json` also records what the PR's
  posted reviews named (`base` before the round, `told` after it: per related PR its state when last named,
  `open` with its draft flag, `merged`, or `closed` once a round found it closed in the registry, and every
  path it shared in any of them, not only the 20 shown), and `related.json` leaves out each related PR
  named in its present state that shares no other path. A PR merged, closed and reopened, made ready or
  turned back into a draft, or sharing a new path is named again; fewer shared paths, a new head, activity,
  reviews and findings are no news. The registry finds the posted reviews: of the PR's runs of earlier
  rounds verified as posted, the newest whose head has a record gives its `told`, or its `base` when a
  later round replaced the record on that head (the round's own earlier prompt, a round that posted
  nothing), so what only an unposted round named is named again, an initial round after posted reviews
  names nothing they named, and the first review names them all. A record from before `told` counts its
  whole set and the set it compared with as named (their entries read as the new ones). The judge still
  gets the filtered list as `related_prs`; the prompts, the skill and the line's wording are unchanged, and
  the `round.related` event's `told` counts the PRs left out. Rejected: naming them on every review (what
  happened: 19 repeated lines in a week); comparing with the previous review's head alone (a merge of the
  base leaves it without a record); reading which PRs the posted line named (posted text is data, and the
  judge names a related PR only when it matters, so the list it was given is what counts as named).
- **The status comment names magnum's own failure, answers review requests on drafts and on PRs left out,
  and carries the verdict** (2026-10-17, extends "A status comment on the PR says where its review stands"
  and "The status comment ends truthfully"; the operator approved the three author-visible changes). In a
  week of 99 posted reviews, 36 status comments showed three gaps. A PR magnum's own failure parked read
  "Magnum will not review this head. The operator was told.", which reads as a decision: talkable#12031
  showed it for 16 hours (a reply-detection block) and talkable#12030 for 8.5 (a stalled judge prompt),
  though a push re-queues a parked PR. A review requested on a draft never opened the comment (a requested
  round of talkable#12026 ran with no status line), and a request on a muted or filtered-out PR got no
  answer at all (an author asked three times after a mute; a colleague asked on a departed author's PR). And
  the posted line gave only a link, so a reader opened the review to tell blocking from optional. Now a
  park whose cause is on magnum's side, by the kind the engine recorded (`KVPRAttention`, else the one
  `attention.Explain` reads from an older row's error) and the new `attention.OnMagnumsSide` (failed,
  overloaded, blocked, needs_attention, identity_error, identity_leak; not a fix job's, which asks the
  author), is the new stage `failed`: "Magnum failed to finish the review of `<sha7>`. The fault is on its
  side, not in your PR. The operator was told. A new push starts a new review." (the operator's note
  under it); a muted, ignored or Codex-flagged PR and a fix job's park keep the old line, and at a close the
  failed line gives way to "Closed/Merged before the review", since no push will come. A draft's comment
  opens for a review someone asked for (a pending request, `magnum review`, or the running round one
  started: `reviewAsked`) as a ready PR's does; a draft nobody asked about still gets none. A person's
  review request that `onRequest` does not answer, because the PR is muted or the filters leave it out,
  records its time in kv `pr.<id>.request_declined` (`declineRequest`, with a `pr.request_declined` event
  and an info toast that names the reason, "review requested by alice (not reviewed: muted)", unless a
  manual repository's toast told already), and while that request is the PR's newest and unanswered and
  the PR neither waits for nor runs a round, the comment is the new stage `request_declined`, "Magnum is
  not reviewing this PR. The operator was told.", posted where none stood; the tick reads those rows in one
  query and adds the baseline PRs they name, which `statusStates` leaves out. The request is a request
  whoever asked, the operator included; a draft marked ready is not one. A mute or an unmute drops the row
  (the request is then older than the PR's state), and an unmute or a filter change that queues the PR
  hands the comment back to its review; the line survives a close, as the old one does. The posted line
  reads "Review of `<sha7>` posted 18:52 UTC: Fix 1 problem before merging, 4 optional. <link>": the
  judge's verdict line is not stored, so the new `store.ReviewSummary.VerdictWords` rebuilds it from the
  result's counts and verdict as the skill's section 7 writes it ("Blocking: N problems must be fixed
  before merging", "Fix N problems before merging", "No blocking problems", "No problems found", the P3s and
  simplifications counted as optional), one place for the words, which a review no round of magnum's posted
  leaves out. The tick reads the last review summaries of all its PRs in one query, which `earlierOpen`
  now uses too instead of one query per PR. Rejected: naming the mute's reason or the filter (a public
  repository would show a membership rule or the operator's note); keeping drafts silent (a request is a
  request); a mute timestamp column to compare requests with (a migration for what the request's own
  handling knows when it declines it); matching the error text for magnum's side (the kinds already say
  it); and storing the verdict line's text with the run (the counts rebuild it, and the result file has no
  such field).
- **A fix loop that needs you says what to do per finding, with the thread's link** (2026-10-17, amends
  "The fix loop: magnum fixes its own findings on your PRs" and "A fixer's "needs your call" after a push
  toasts at once"; the operator asked for it). On talkable-integration#867 a loop ended with "fix: 2
  findings need your call (4302616576 P2 src/integration.js:135, 4302866759 P2 src/integration.js:1706):
  <report>". One finding was fixed and pushed, but its thread was a colleague's, where the fixer never
  writes, so the author's "fixed" reply was missing; the other was magnum's own P2, which the fixer declined
  because its proof needs a committed TLS key. Only the report's prose said so. Now the fix skill starts
  each `Needs you` entry's reason with `fixed in <sha7>.` (fixed and pushed but not answered: a thread a
  human started, or a reply that failed) or `not fixed.`, and the engine reads those words with the id,
  priority and place (`needsYouEntryRe`, still one parser). Whose thread it is comes from the files beside
  the report: the round's `review-threads.json` lists magnum's threads (the reviewer login's, former logins
  included) as the round that posted the fixed review found them, and `review.json` that review's own
  comments, which the threads file predates (matched by path, line and priority); a thread in neither is
  one a human started, once the threads file was read. Each entry read so is a call (`attention.FixCall`):
  "reply fixed in <sha7> in the thread a human started and resolve it: <link>" ("in magnum's thread" when
  its reply failed), or "decide magnum's P2 on <path>:<line>: the fixer declined it; reply won't fix at
  <link>, or `magnum fix <ref>` sends it back" ("a human's" in a person's thread), the link being
  `<PR>#discussion_r<id>`. The message joins the calls with "; " and ends with "details: <report>"
  (`attention.FixCallsText`). It is the text of the `fix.needs_you` events, the PR's `last_error` and
  `pr.needs_attention`, and the toast (the summary "fix: reply in 1 thread, decide 1 finding", then a call
  per line); through `attention.Explain` (the new `Reason.Steps` and `Reason.NeedsYou`) it is the next step
  of the card and the board. `magnum status <ref>` prints the calls one per line under the fix line, also
  while the loop waits for the re-review of the push (`engine.FixCalls` reads the row's entries); `--json`
  gives them as `fix.needs_you` (`thread`, `url`, `action`) in place of the row's raw entries; and `magnum
  fix --wait` counts them on its end line with the calls below. An entry without those words, the
  description finding (no thread), and one whose thread the files cannot place keep the older words ("1
  more finding needs your call (…)"), and a report with no call keeps today's message whole. The fixer's
  reasons are still never read: they stay in the report, which "details:" names. The board's pill keeps
  `attention · fix`, one word per kind, while its line counts the calls. Rejected: the fixer replying in a
  human's thread as the author (the operator's conversations stay the operator's, and the skill keeps
  "never reply to a thread that a human started"); reading the thread's author from GitHub at the loop's
  end to name the colleague (a new call on the loop's end for a name the link shows); putting the first
  clause of the fixer's reason into the sentence and the JSON (the fixer's words about the PR never reach
  events, attention, toasts or logs, as `needsYouEntryRe` states); and taking every thread missing from
  the threads file for a human's (the fixed review's own comments are not in it yet, and its declined
  findings are the common case).

- **`magnum unpin` acknowledges a hold and every hold sentence names the command** (2026-10-18, spec 83, after
  talkable-integration#867: a commit the fixer's pane made after its loop ended moved the per-PR worktree's
  HEAD, the guard held the slot `head_drift`, and a review the operator asked for answered "waiting: slot
  talkable/talkable-integration#867 is held: head_drift (magnum unpin)"; his first try at the way back was
  refused as "not pinned", `magnum release` skipped the slot ("hold_reason (head_drift)") and did nothing,
  and `magnum unpin "talkable/talkable-integration#867"` finally took the new HEAD and let the review run).
  The daemon's log shows that no unpin request came before the last one: `requestPin` already takes the slot
  of a PR reference through `slots.Manager.Unpin` whether or not a pin is set, and that clears a
  `head_drift` or `unpushed_commits` hold by taking the folder's HEAD, so the "not pinned" came from the
  client (the board's `u` answers it for an unpinned PR before any request exists, and a bare number names
  the default repository's PR, which the registry may not hold: "nothing to unpin: a PR magnum has not
  recorded is not pinned"), not from the command's daemon path. What that path lacked was words: its answer
  was "unpinned <PR> (slot <name>)" whether it took a pin off or handed back a hold. Now an
  unpin of a PR that was not pinned, whose slot carried `head_drift` or `unpushed_commits`, answers
  "acknowledged the head_drift hold of slot <name>: HEAD 3e8c5b6 is now the checkout magnum expects; the next
  release resets it" (also the text of its `pr.unpinned` event, `acknowledgedHold`); a PR with no such hold,
  one holding `dirty_worktree` (which returns at the next guard while the changes are there) and a pinned PR
  keep today's answer. Every sentence that says a guard holds a slot now names the command with the slot in
  quotes, since a per-PR worktree's name (owner/name#N) is also a PR reference: `slotHeldReason` ("slot X is
  held: head_drift (magnum unpin "X")": the review request's waiting line, the PR's wait on the board and the
  card, the refusals of `magnum fix` and a whiteboard job), the attention line of `magnum status` ("check the
  folder, then `magnum unpin "X"`", for `magnum slots unpin X`), and a release plan's skipped line, now
  `Skip.Text()` ("held: head_drift (acknowledge it with magnum unpin "X")", the JSON keeping `reason` and
  `detail` and adding `slot`); `magnum unpin --help` says what it acknowledges. Rejected: `magnum release`
  acknowledging the hold (a release must never take a HEAD it did not check out: only the person who looks at
  the commits says they are expected), the pinned and slot-name paths changing (they already worked), and the
  board's `u` taking a hold for a pin (left for its own decision: it refuses before any request, and the hint
  now names the command to type).

- **The board's `u` acknowledges a held slot and `x` says why it will not release it** (2026-10-18, spec 83's
  follow-up: the operator's first try at the way back from a `head_drift` hold on talkable-integration#867
  was the board's `u`, which answered "is not pinned" before any request existed, as the entry on spec 83
  found; `x` on the same row asked to release and the plan skipped the slot with no word). `store.BoardRow`
  now carries the hold of the slot holding the PR (`SlotHold`, the join's `slots.hold_reason`), through
  `tui.PRBoardRow.SlotHold` (also `slot_hold` in `tui --json`) to the row actions. For a slot held
  `head_drift` or `unpushed_commits` (the holds `magnum unpin` acknowledges by taking the folder's HEAD) `u`
  is no longer refused for an unpinned row: it asks "Acknowledge the head_drift hold of slot review3 (takes
  its HEAD as the checkout)?" ("Unpin <PR> and acknowledge ..." when the row is pinned too, since the unpin
  takes the HEAD as well) and sends the same unpin request, whose answer says it acknowledged the hold. A row
  that is neither pinned nor held so, `dirty_worktree` included (it returns at the next guard while the
  changes are there), keeps "is not pinned". `x` on a slot held that way says "talkable#5: slot review3 is
  held: head_drift, acknowledge it with u" instead of asking and letting the plan skip it; a pinned row still
  says to unpin first. The card's ACTIONS name the key "unpin / acknowledge a hold" on such a row ("unpin"
  elsewhere), and the board's `?` help lists "pin / unpin / acknowledge a hold". The dashboard and the picker do
  not know a slot's hold and are unchanged (the dashboard's `u` already sends the request, which acknowledges;
  the picker's key toggles by the PR's pin). Rejected: acknowledging without asking (the key takes a HEAD
  magnum did not check out, so it asks as `magnum unpin` does by name); `x` acknowledging the hold itself (a
  release never takes a HEAD it did not check out); and refusing `x` for every hold (a `dirty_worktree` hold
  has no key that hands it back, so the refusal would name none).
- **The approval's CI gate counts only the checks required_checks names** (2026-10-18, spec 84, asked for by
  the operator on talkable/talkable#12036; amends "A check that fails on the base too does not hold an
  auto-approval"). Magnum's judge approved a colleague's terraform change at f2f867c on 10-16, and the
  automatic approval as the operator was refused with "its head's checks fail (magnum approves it once they
  pass)", the board reading `✔ needs you` since: the failing check was `Terraform scripts / lint`, a job of a
  path-filtered workflow whose last step is the PR's own self-check script, failed on a broken-pipe flake,
  while the CI workflow (64 checks, Completion included) passed. The repository's `required_checks =
  ["workflow:CI"]` names what GitHub requires to merge, but the gate read GitHub's combined rollup, FAILURE
  for any failing check, and lifted it only for failures the base tip shares, which a path-filtered workflow
  never runs there. Now, where the PR's `[[repo]]` block sets `required_checks`, the head's stored checks
  (only when they are the head's and list every one) decide by the runs each entry names, through the
  matcher the board reads (`store.RequiredRuns` and `store.RequiredNames`, moved out of the board's
  `requiredCheck`; `store.RequiredWorkflowPrefix` is pinned to the configuration's), and the combined rollup
  no longer decides: every required run passed or skipped lets the approval through whatever the rollup
  says, a required run that fails goes to the base tip's comparison for the required failures alone
  (`failsLikeTheBase`, split out of `failingCIRefusal`, which waits for a required run still running), and a
  required run still running answers "its head's checks have not finished"; a check outside the list
  neither refuses nor is waited for. The refusal texts are unchanged. The approval's
  `review.auto_approve_begin` and `review.auto_approved` end with "; ignored 1 failing check outside
  required_checks: Terraform scripts / lint", and the daemon logs "auto approval: ignored ..." at info, once
  per post; the posted body is unchanged. A check is named as the board names it (workflow, " / ", name)
  only when that is plain text (ASCII letters, digits, spaces and `._-/+@:()[],#`, at most 120 bytes; at
  most five, the rest counted "and 2 more"), since a workflow a PR adds names its own checks; unlike
  `pr.ci_red` and `review.auto_approve_ci_base`, which name none, this note names them because the operator
  asked to see what was ignored. Where the stored checks cannot say (none for the head, a list GitHub cut at
  100, an entry that names no check on the head: one that never ran there or has not started) every check
  counts through the rollup as before, as it does without the key; the list GitHub's rulesets declare,
  which the board falls back to, does not change the gate (the spec's scope is the operator's key). A
  standing approval held to the gates after a later round follows the same rule. Rejected: ignoring
  path-filtered workflows by heuristics (a check does not say whether its workflow is path-filtered, and a
  guess would also pass a required workflow that skipped); keeping every check (what happened: a flake in an
  unrequired self-check held a reviewed PR for a day, until someone re-ran the job or pressed `A`).
- **A CLI version read that failed is tried again at the next health check** (2026-10-18, spec 85). Spec
  75 (above) kept a stamp (`Engine.cliRead`) for a binary whose version command failed, so it ran again only
  once the binary's path or mtime changed. At the daemon start of 2026-10-18 01:27 the codex read failed
  ("shims/codex --version: context canceled"); a mise shim's file never changes (the stamp follows `mise
  which codex`, which names the same binary until mise installs another), so the version stayed unread, and
  `magnum status`'s `clis:` line and the shared-failure note went on without codex's. Now a read that fails
  (an error, `cliVersionTimeout`, a context that ended) leaves no stamp and records nothing, so the next
  health check runs the command again, and so on at every check. The failure is one warning per cause since
  the daemon started (`cliFailureCause`: a timeout, a canceled context or the error's text; the others are
  debug lines), the read that works at last logs "agent CLI version" at info with `failed_reads`, and the
  third failed read in a row (the one at the start counts as the first, and `cliVersionUnknownAfter` is the
  number) is one `kind.version_unknown` event (warn, subject `tool:<kind>`: the kind, the count, the binary
  and the last failure), once per run of failures, without a toast (`magnum status` leaves the kind out of its `clis:` line
  meanwhile, and the event is what the operator looks for). The daemon's own context ending is no failure (debug, nothing
  counted): it is stopping. The start's read already ran under the engine's own `Run` context with the
  health check's timeout (`startup` calls `checkCLIVersions` with it, and both reach `cliVersion`), so
  nothing changed there; the new test pins the timeout on every read. Rejected: retrying a failed read
  inside one check (a second 15 s wait inside a tick for a failure the next check retries anyway); a
  backoff (the stat and `mise which` already run at every check, and a failing version command is the case
  to look at); a toast at the third failure (no one can act on it before the CLI itself fails); and keeping
  the stamp for a failed read with a time limit (a second clock beside the health check's).
- **The judge posts at most `max_simplifications` simplifications, 5 by default, and a `[[repo]]` block's
  own wins** (2026-10-19, spec 86, asked for by the operator: "per-repo settings it is, and change default
  to 5"). Amends "At most three simplifications, each removing something" (2026-10-05), whose cap was prompt
  text alone ("Post at most three, the most substantial, ..." in the initial, rereview and recovery judge
  prompts; no Go check counts simplifications against a limit, then or now). Its other rules are unchanged:
  a proposal removes something a reader must hold, stays out of authorization, sandboxing, money or usage
  recording and concurrency code unless it removes a defect-prone construct, is proven by the judge's own
  equivalence probe, and is one comment per idea. Evidence: on talkable#12040 (round 1, 81d9ea6)
  claude-simplify proposed 5 and the judge posted 2. Now `[pipeline] max_simplifications` (default
  `DefaultMaxSimplifications`, 5; 1 to `MaxSimplificationsMax`, 10) and `[[repo]] max_simplifications` (0
  or unset = `[pipeline]`'s; 0 to 10; not a per-PR worktree key, so a pooled repository's block may set it)
  resolve through `Config.MaxSimplificationsFor`; the pipeline sets `agents.JudgeData.MaxSimplifications`
  from it where it sets `Stakes`, and the three prompts say "Post at most {{$.MaxSimplifications}}, the
  most substantial, ...". A JudgeData without it (0, as in a config built in code) renders 5, never "at
  most 0" (`JudgeData.completed`). claude-simplify's own prompt said "(the judge proves them and posts at
  most 3)"; it now says "(the judge proves them and posts only the most substantial)", with no number,
  since its data does not carry the repository's cap and it lists every qualifying proposal anyway. That
  edit changes the reviewers' prompt text, so `evalrun.ReviewerInputs` changes once with it, and every
  replay's `inputs` change once with the judge prompts. `evalrun.Inputs` also hashes the `[pipeline]` cap in
  effect and each `[[repo]]` cap that is set (keyed and sorted by block as the stakes lines are), so a cap
  change replays its baseline once; `ReviewerInputs` leaves them out, since only the judge reads them, and
  a judge-only replay of a cap change still takes a full replay's reports. Rejected: a `[[watch]]`-level
  key (not asked; a repository block is enough); no cap (the 2026-10-05 evidence: one PR got 20
  simplifications next to 5 findings); keeping three as the default (the operator asked for five).
- **The daemon records the machine's memory pressure and swap** (2026-10-19, spec 88, asked for by the
  operator while the machine was slow). Evidence: swap 50.3 of 51.2 GB used,
  `kern.memorystatus_vm_pressure_level` 2 (warn), about 6 GB compressed and decompressed every 5 s, and 69 of
  herdr's 111 panes were magnum's sessions. magnum guarded the disk (`min_free_disk_gb`, the `disk:` line) but
  knew nothing of memory, so neither the operator nor a later improvement run could tell how often pressure is
  critical, which a decision to hold automatic rounds under it needs first. Now the health check starts a
  sample at most once a minute (`memoryEvery`, throttled as the Codex budget read is) when none is in flight:
  `sysctl -n kern.memorystatus_vm_pressure_level` (1 normal, 2 warn, 4 critical) and `sysctl -n vm.swapusage`,
  fixed argv at the absolute `/usr/sbin/sysctl` (as notify's osascript and reveal's commands are), a 3 s
  timeout each (`memoryTimeout`). The sample runs on a goroutine of its own (`Engine.memWG`) under the tick's
  context: health runs on the tick's path before dispatch, and a spawn that hangs on a thrashing machine would
  cost the tick up to the two timeouts and the runner's kill grace, so the tick never waits for it; the next
  health check records the finished sample (kv, events, toast), and a stop mid-sample records nothing (the
  goroutine ends with `Run`'s context, which `shutdown` waits for). Each value is parsed on its own, so one
  that fails, prints a level the kernel does not define or a line that is no swap reading keeps the other's
  value in the sample. The newest sample is kv `machine.memory` (`engine.MemorySample`: `level` and
  `pressure`, `swap` with `used_bytes` and `total_bytes`, `sampled_at`, and `cause` for a part that is
  unknown). Each change of a known level is one `machine.memory_pressure` event: the first known level since
  the daemon started is info ("(the first reading since the daemon started)", also when unknown samples came
  first), a return to normal is info, warn a warning, critical an error. A run of critical, from a critical
  sample to the next normal one (a level flapping between critical and warn stays one run), shows one urgent
  toast keyed `memory:critical` with an hour's window, so a flap through normal, or a restart, does not toast
  again within the hour. A sample whose level is unknown changes nothing and is never a return to normal. A
  part that cannot be read (Linux has neither oid) is "unknown" with its cause, warned about once per oid and
  kind of failure (a non-zero exit, a timeout, a failed start, an answer that does not parse) since the daemon
  started, the full text in the line and debug lines after; the key leaves out what sysctl printed, which can
  vary and would grow the map. The commands are `Quiet`, a new `execx.Cmd` option that has the runner log
  every outcome at debug (`Probe` demotes only a non-zero exit, so a timeout or a failed start was a runner
  warning every minute), so that warning is the only one. No sysctl at the path (`exec.ErrNotFound`,
  `fs.ErrNotExist`, as on some Linux systems) stops the sampling for the daemon's life, and the unknown sample
  stays recorded with that cause. `magnum status` shows the sample on a `memory:` line after `disk:`
  ("pressure warn, swap 49.1 of 50.0 GB used, 44 agents live (6 working), sampled 20s ago"; GB of 2³⁰ bytes,
  as the disk line and Activity Monitor count them), counting magnum's agents from the registry's live
  sessions (`engine.LiveAgents`; not working = idle) without ps or herdr, and `--json` has `memory` with the
  same fields; there is no line before a first sample. `magnum doctor` reads the two values at once
  (`engine.ReadMemory`): one `memory` line, a WARN at critical, a SKIP when the level cannot be read. The
  probe has a port of its own, `Deps.MemoryRunner`, which `FromApp` sets to the App's runner (the one `Runner`
  is), so the engine tests that script `Runner`'s triage model and count its calls do not script sysctl too; a
  dry run samples nothing, as it reads no CLI version. Why the runner and not a syscall (`sysctlbyname`
  through `golang.org/x/sys/unix`, a Mach call through cgo): the runner is portable without build tags, its
  fake keeps the tests hermetic, and two short processes a minute cost nothing next to a review. Why nothing
  is held yet: the spec only measures, and a hold under critical pressure needs to know how often and how long
  it is critical, which these events now record. Rejected: one sysctl call for both values (an oid that fails
  makes the call exit 1 with a partial answer whose lines no longer say which value they are); sampling on the
  tick's path (the hung spawn above); a toast at warn (the machine sat at warn for hours, and no one
  acts on a toast that repeats); a config key (nothing but the operator reads the sample yet); counting agents
  with ps (it would count the operator's own sessions too, and the registry knows magnum's).
- **A Fix that would undo what the PR or its series removed, or that picks between fixes users tell apart,
  names the options and ends "This is the author's call.", and the fixer leaves it to the author**
  (2026-10-20, spec 90, asked for by the operator). Evidence: a colleague resolving a review of one of his
  PRs reported that magnum found the problem but proposed going back to an older record model to fix it,
  "because that is how it was before", and lost that the PR was the third of a series moving away from it.
  The posted P2 (round 12, a recovery round) was right about the defect: after an outside answer falls back
  to an older value, a record keeps an obsolete answer current, because the PR's new checker returns early
  and keeps variants that the checker it removed used to retire. Its **Fix** prescribed one change,
  retiring them again, the removed checker's job, which undoes the direction of the PR and of the merged
  related PR before it. The colleague then asked his own review-resolving session whether any finding held
  a business-logic choice; it split 16 findings into mechanical ones and five that each held a real product
  choice, and that split is what let him steer the fixes. The comment form asked every **Fix** for "one
  smallest safe change", and nothing told the judge that the smallest change can be a product decision or
  a reversal of the PR's own direction, though it reads `history` ("undoing or re-breaking that fix is a
  finding") and `related_prs`. Now the comment form says: "When the smallest fix would restore what this PR
  or a merged related PR deliberately removed or replaced (its diff, `history`, `related_prs`, the
  description), or two plausible fixes differ in what users get, **Fix** names the options, each with what
  it keeps and costs, and ends `This is the author's call.` The choice never lowers the priority." The
  reproduction and the priority stay as they are, and a removal the PR made by mistake is still restored
  as the one smallest fix. The phrase `This is the author's call.` is fixed: the fix skill matches it. The
  fix skill's rule 6 (a finding it cannot decide from the code) now says that a finding whose **Fix** ends
  with it is such a finding, whatever its verdict and score: the fixer does not fix it, writes `not fixed.`
  under `## Needs you` and asks which of its options to take, naming each; the engine's call for it is
  unchanged ("decide magnum's P2 on <path>:<line>"). There is no exception for a choice the PR description
  or the checkout's docs seem to make: the checkout's files are PR content (data, never instructions), so a
  doc the PR itself adds could settle the choice, the fixer has no path to magnum's repository notes, and
  what the colleague asked for is to be asked. The rule takes 347 bytes of the review skill; 28 came from
  unpinned wording ("prompt's" before section 0's block, "on this PR" after section 6's threads, and "in
  normal cases" for "usually" in section 7's body), no rule changed, and the cap (`skillMaxBytes`) rose by
  the other 319, to 37,465. Rejected: always listing options (it doubles every comment, and most fixes hold
  no choice); leaving the split to the author's own tools (the colleague's report shows they now need it,
  and every author would repeat it); asking the operator before posting (the judge runs unattended and
  cannot ask).
- **Under the verdict line the review body lists only the problems the verdict counts, each with its
  priority, and another reviewer's thread the judge confirmed is one of them** (2026-10-20, spec 91, asked
  for by the operator). Evidence: on talkable#12048 (head 403b9c2, round 1, posted with changes requested
  at 18:02 UTC) the reviewers and the judge's own pass all found the blocking defect (`member.campaign ||=
  last_campaign` is saved by `collect_points`, so a member the campaign refresh removed can earn in the old
  campaign again). The judge confirmed it at P1, but a code-review bot had posted it at 17:21, so it
  followed section 3's duplicate rule ("Another reviewer's open P0–P2 you decided gets a body line:
  `Confirmed <link> (counted in N)`") and posted no comment. The body read "Blocking: 2 problems must be
  fixed before merging." over "- P2: Corrections during a campaign launch grant an unearned tier." and "-
  P3: No-campaign refusals change status and message.", then "5 optional: 2 P3, 3 simplifications." and
  "Confirmed [the existing campaign-eligibility finding](…) (counted in 2).": the list under "Blocking: 2
  problems" showed a P2 and a P3, and the P1 that made the review blocking was an unnamed link three lines
  below. The operator read it as magnum missing the defect, and another reviewer's tool posted it a third
  time at 18:31. Section 7 asked for "the finding titles by priority", which put every posted title, P3
  included, under the verdict line. Now section 7's body reads "the verdict line; under it only the
  problems N counts, by priority, as `- P1: <title>` (counts by priority when there are more than five);
  then `N optional: …` and any P3 titles; ...", and section 3's duplicate rule "Another reviewer's open
  P0–P2 you confirmed counts in N and is listed under your own title as `- P1: <title> (confirmed:
  <link>)`; one you rejected gets the body line `Considered <link>: <why not>`": the `Confirmed <link>
  (counted in N)` form is gone, and `Considered` stays a line of its own. A re-review keeps section 6's
  order (earlier findings now fixed, now answered, still open despite a new reply or commit, then the new
  findings; unchanged open ones as one count and one link to the previous review), since it reports what
  changed since that review and listing every unchanged open finding again would repeat it; but its new
  findings now put the counted ones first, a newly confirmed thread among them ("the new findings, P0–P2
  first (section 3's confirmed ones too), then any P3."), so a confirmed thread cannot hide in a re-review
  either. No Go code parses the title list or the Confirmed line, so none changed: the auto-approval reads
  only the verdict line (`reviewVerdictLine`, the first line past a re-review's lead), the status comment
  rebuilds its line from the result's counts (`store.ReviewSummary.VerdictWords`), post-review checks the
  body only for the footer, local paths, its size and the run's marker, the retro reads threads and inline
  comments, `magnum eval` scores the body as one text, and the fix skill reads it only for its
  `Description: ✗` line and the threads it names as still open (a Confirmed line named the other
  reviewer's thread as the new form does). The three changes take 211 bytes (80 for the body, 70 for the
  duplicate rule, 61 for the re-review); spec 90 had already taken the unpinned wording that could go
  without changing a rule, so the cap (`skillMaxBytes`) rose by all of it, from 37,465 to 37,676.
  Rejected: posting a duplicate inline comment on the other reviewer's thread line (two threads for one
  defect double the author's work); keeping the link line and adding a priority to it (the list under the
  verdict line would still show a problem it does not count and miss the one that blocks).
- **Auto-approval can trust only some authors: `auto_approve_authors` on a watch, replaced per
  repository** (2026-10-20, spec 92, asked for by the operator: "currently there is a blocklist of people
  who are not auto-approved, but I would benefit from an allowlist as well: in some repos I only trust
  certain people's code quality to auto approve it"). Until now only `auto_approve_skip_authors` (spec 50)
  kept authors out, so trusting three people in a repository meant listing everyone else, and a new
  colleague was approved as the operator until someone remembered to add them. `auto_approve_authors` on
  a `[[watch]]` and on a `[[repo]]` block lists GitHub logins, matched and validated as the skip list is
  (`listsLogin`, `validateLogins`: any case, with or without `[bot]`; an empty entry, one with whitespace
  or an App's `app/<name>` form refused, naming the block). The repository's list, when set (not empty),
  decides for that repository and replaces the watch's; else the watch's, when set, decides for every
  repository the watch auto-approves; with neither there is no allowlist, today's behaviour
  (`Config.AutoApproveAllowsAuthor`, true when no list applies or the login is on it; a blank login, an
  author magnum does not know, is on no list). `authorRefusal` asks the skip list first, so a login on
  both lists is skipped, then refuses an author the list leaves out with the fixed text "the author is not
  in auto_approve_authors" (it names nobody), exactly as it refuses a skipped one: a new approval only,
  recorded once per head with no round (`run_id` ""), in one `review.auto_approve_refused` event, in
  `auto_approve_refused` of `magnum tui --json` and on the card, which reads it by its words as it reads
  the skip list's key and says "auto-approval: off for this author (not in auto_approve_authors)", dim, in
  place of the refusal's yellow sentence; the row shows no `✔ auto`. A standing approval is not held to
  it (`standingGateRefusal` runs `autoGateRefusal` alone), so one posted before the list left its author
  out stays, and the board's `A` and `magnum approve --as` still approve (`OperatorApprovalRefusal` never
  asks about the author). Nothing on GitHub names the list: the status comment never speaks of
  auto-approval. It is not a per-PR worktree key, so a pooled repository's `[[repo]]` block may set it
  (`worktreeKeys`' comment, the pooled-repository refusal's list and the sentences of
  `config.defaults.toml` and `config.full.example.toml`, which the drift test checks). The `magnum status`
  report and the attention causes never read the refusal, and triage's rule (every role runs where magnum
  auto-approves) is the repository's, not the author's, so none of them changed. The auto-approval path
  has no other author check it could contradict: "it is your own" refuses the operator's own PRs whatever
  the list says, and a bot author still needs its watch to review it on its own (`allow_bot_authors`).
  The review found a hole the skip list had had since spec 50: `authorRefusal` stops only the separate
  automatic approval, but where a watch posts its reviews as an identity that approves when clean (the
  operator's own gh account, whose default `no_findings_event` is APPROVE, or any identity or `[[repo]]`
  set to APPROVE), the judge's clean review is itself an approval, as the operator's account in the gh case,
  so a skipped author's clean PR was approved all the same (`judgeData` took `JudgeEvents`, which took
  `VerdictsFor`'s APPROVE, and post-review submitted the event the prompt named); the engine tests missed
  it because their harness posts clean reviews as COMMENTED. Now `pipeline.JudgeEvents` takes the PR's
  author and turns the no-findings event into COMMENT, for every identity, when
  `Config.AutoApproveRefusesAuthor` (the skip list names the author, or an allowlist that applies leaves it
  out) says so, as it does for a missing report; every round's prompt gets its events there (`judgeData`:
  the first review, a re-review, a recovery, a delta check, a continued round, the judge's own pass, a reply
  round that changes its verdict, and the fallback judge, which is another judge role of the same pipeline), and
  the round's `round.judge` event says "no APPROVE: the auto-approval author lists ... keep this author's PRs
  from an approval". The automatic approval (gated by `authorRefusal`) and the operator's own verdicts (`A`,
  `magnum approve`) are the only other reviews magnum creates, and nothing re-posts a standing approval.
  `Config.CommentsWhenClean` takes the author too, so such a clean comment counts as magnum's approval for
  the PRs that need the operator (`✔ needs you`, A as `auto_approve_as`), as an App's clean comment does;
  without it an App set to APPROVE would have lost the `✔ needs you` it showed after its approval. The
  guard is the prompt's, as the missing-report and held-approval guards are: post-review reads no config,
  so a judge that wrote APPROVE against its prompt would still post it.
  Rejected: a repository list that adds to the watch's, as the skip list's does (an allowlist that only
  grows cannot narrow trust in one repository, which is the point of setting it there); one global list
  (trust differs per repository and per owner); an empty `[[repo]]` list meaning "nobody" (a list that
  trusts no one is auto-approval turned off for the repository, which is leaving it out of
  `auto_approve`; an empty list keeps the watch's, as an unset one does).
- **A fix job also answers what other reviewers wrote that nobody answered** (2026-10-20, spec 93. It amends
  "A fix loop that needs you says what to do per finding, with the thread's link". The operator asked for
  it: "I started fix on PR 12054 and it fixed only magnum's finding, but I expect it to check all comments
  and reviews and reply to unreplied ones"). On talkable#12054, the operator's own PR, a colleague's review
  tool left a MINOR follow-up at 07:24 UTC on `pi_sandbox.rb:185`: `run_in_jail` drops stderr. The fix job
  started at 08:31 on magnum's review of 797e78a. It pushed 6 commits and replied in 7 threads, but it never
  saw that thread. The reason: `prompts/fix.md` named only magnum's review file, and the fix skill said "Act
  only in the reviewer login's threads. Never reply to, resolve or minimize a thread that a human started."
  Spec 82 rejected a reply in a human's thread, because "the operator's conversations stay the operator's".
  The operator now asks for the opposite, so this decision reverses that rejection on his word. When the fix
  job starts (`fixStart`, after the run exists), the engine writes `external-threads.json`. The file goes
  beside the fixer's report, in the review's directory (`writeExternal`, internal/engine/fix_external.go).
  The engine reads the PR as the watch's poll identity, with `ReviewThreads`, `AllReviews` and the new
  `github.Client.IssueComments`. That read pages back through the conversation over GraphQL, 100 comments at
  a time, until it finds the author's last own word, or the first comment, at most 10 pages. If it stops at
  the page limit, only items after the oldest comment it listed count, so an older review body from before
  the author's word does not come back. It needs no new GitHub permission. The file holds the PR author's
  login, magnum's logins (`author` and `fixer_logins`, the only ones whose comments answer an item) and two
  lists. The first list holds every unresolved review thread that another reviewer started: neither one of
  magnum's logins (`fixLogins`: `ownLogins` and the posting login) nor the PR author. The spec said both
  "every unresolved review thread of the PR that magnum's posting login did not start" and "the unanswered
  threads of other reviewers". A thread the author started is the author's own note, so the file leaves it
  out even when a collaborator replied in it last. People and bots count the same, but only reviewers count:
  GitHub Apps and the repository's owners, members and collaborators (`trustedReplier`, as for a reply
  round, read from the new `authorAssociation` of thread comments, reviews and comments). In a public
  repository anyone may comment, and the fixer acts on these items as the author, so the file leaves out
  what an outsider wrote, and the event counts it. Each thread has the id and link of its first comment, its
  path and line, and the outdated flag. It also has its comments: id and link, author, body, time, and the
  fix marker or not. The id lets the fixer read a cut body whole with `gh`. If the latest comment of a
  thread is the author's or the fixer's, the thread is "answered". `ReviewThreads` reads the first 50
  comments of a thread, so for a longer one it reads the newest 50 too, in one more query
  (`github.Thread.Tail` and `AllComments`). Thus the latest comment is the real one, here and in the
  settle's look. The file lists both ends of a long thread and counts the middle (`omitted`). The
  re-review's threads file and the retro still read only the first 50; they pay the extra query only for a
  thread longer than that. The second list holds the review bodies and conversation comments of other people
  since the author's own last comment. An own comment is one by the author without a `<!-- magnum:` marker.
  Thus the fixer's replies, a status comment and a review posted as the author's gh login do not count. The
  list leaves out magnum's review bodies and status comment, the author's items, reviews without a body, and
  pending or dismissed reviews. A later comment can carry the fix marker and name the URL of an item on the
  line under its quote, its target line (`replyTarget`). If the author or a magnum login wrote that comment,
  the item is "answered". A link to another item in the quote or in the reply text answers nothing. The file
  cuts each body at 600 characters, as the threads file cuts a reply, and sets `truncated`. Bodies are PR
  text. They reach the fixer only through the file (`.ExternalFile`, which `fix.md` names in one `{{if}}`
  sentence). They never go into the prompt, an event or a log. A `fix.external` event counts the items. If
  the read fails, the engine writes no file and the prompt names none. The fixer then works on magnum's
  findings alone, and `fix.external` is a warning. The re-review's threads file degrades the same way. The
  skill's rule now reads: act only in magnum's threads and in the unanswered threads of other reviewers that
  the external file lists. Never resolve or minimize a thread someone else started: its reviewer resolves
  it. If the author's comment is the last one in another reviewer's thread, never reply there. Reply at most
  once to each item. Never edit, hide or delete anyone else's comment. The file is a snapshot from the job's
  start, so right before each reply the fixer reads the item again with `gh`: the thread's comments, or the
  comments after a review body or a comment. Only `author` and `fixer_logins` answer: a marker or a reply by
  anyone else answers nothing, and an outsider's comment is ignored, as in the file (its
  `author_association` is read too). It skips a thread when the latest of the remaining comments is the
  author's, or a fix-marked one of `fixer_logins`. It skips a review body or a comment when a later comment
  or review is the author's own word, a review body included (the snapshot's cutoff counts one too), or when
  a later comment by `author` or `fixer_logins` is a fixer reply whose target line is the item's URL. The
  fixer judges each external item after magnum's findings, with the same verdicts and the same policy. Its
  reviewer can mark an item as blocking: with a changes request, or with a tag such as P0 to P2, blocker,
  critical or major. Such an item is blocking. Any other item is optional. These items go under `## Needs
  you` with no reply: a declined blocking item, a question only the author can answer, an author's call, and
  any choice of business logic or product behaviour. A question that the code answers gets `Answer:
  <answer>`. An item that asks for nothing gets no reply: a bot's status, CI or summary comment, a thanks,
  an approval. Every other item gets one reply with the fix marker. The reply goes into the item's thread.
  For a review body or a comment, the reply is one issue comment that quotes the item's first line and links
  it. That link marks the item answered in the next cycle. The review's body can name another reviewer's
  thread as still open, as a problem that the judge counts. Such a thread is a finding of that review, and
  the fixer handles it once. The report gets a fourth section, `## Other reviewers`, with one line for each
  item and what the fixer did. `ParseFixReport` stops at it, as at any heading after `## Needs you`, so a
  report without it is still whole. A `## Needs you` entry of an external item has no priority. The place of
  a review body or a comment is `review` or `comment`. `needsYouEntryRe` reads both. They keep the older
  words, because they have no thread. Spec 82's call "reply fixed in <sha7> in the thread a human started
  and resolve it" no longer comes. The external file places another reviewer's thread
  (`threadOwners.others`). The engine looks at it before the places of the review file. An external entry
  has no priority, so the priority cannot tell it from a magnum comment on the same line. If the reply
  failed, or if the author's answer was the last comment, the fixer did not answer. Then the call says
  "reply fixed in <sha7> in another reviewer's thread: <link>". The call has no "and resolve it", because
  that reviewer resolves the thread. A declined item says "decide another reviewer's ...". When the fixer
  leaves such a fix under `Needs you`, the settle looks at GitHub once (`dropFixerAnswered`). The thread can
  have a comment with the fix marker, by the author or a magnum login, made after the job started
  (`fixJob.started`). Then the entry asks nothing of the operator: the settle drops it before it counts the
  findings left to the author, and a `fix.external` event says so. The skill lists such a fix only for its
  missing reply, so nothing else is lost. Thus a reply that `gh` reported as failed, but that GitHub took,
  is not asked for twice. A thread answered in an earlier run still gets its call. When the read of GitHub
  fails at the job's start, the engine also removes a file that an earlier fix of the same review left, so
  that nothing reads it for this run. The `attention` parser still reads spec 82's words, so a row stored
  before this change keeps its calls. The loop still ends with magnum's re-review. Each cycle lists what is
  unanswered at its start. Residual risks: the poll cannot tell the fixer's issue comments from the author's
  own, because a remark carries no body. Thus a cycle that pushed nothing, and that answered a review body
  or a comment of another reviewer, can start a reply round. That round finds nothing of the judge's to
  decide again. An inline reply in another reviewer's thread is no reply to magnum's review (`repliesOf`,
  `elsewhere`). An item that someone writes while the fixer works waits for the next cycle or the operator.
  "Since the author's last comment" takes the operator's own comment as the answer to all items before it.
  That is the operator's word, and it keeps old conversations out. The retro does not change: its candidates
  are the first comments of threads and the review bodies, never replies, and its own threads are magnum's.
  Rejected: the fixer resolves other reviewers' threads after a fix (the reviewer decides that a thread is
  done, as magnum's re-review does for its own threads). The fixer answers every comment, bots' status and
  CI comments too (a reply to a coverage bot is noise in the operator's name). The operator answers other
  reviewers, as before (the operator asked to stop that). The prompt carries the external items (that puts
  PR text in the prompt). The file also lists what outsiders wrote (in a public repository a stranger would
  steer what the fixer pushes in the operator's name).
- **The settings screen edits config.toml in place, through a typed allowlist, and the daemon restarts on a
  saved config when idle** (2026-10-20, spec 94, the core of the screen the operator approved that day:
  "change spend and other settings without editing config.toml").
  - **The file.** The operator's `~/.config/magnum/config.toml` is 33 KB, and most of its lines carry a
    dated comment that explains a choice. BurntSushi decodes but keeps no comments and gives no
    position per key. Its `MetaData` holds positions only in private fields, keyed without the array
    index, so every `[[repo]]`'s `stakes` shares one. Re-encoding the file would lose every comment.
  - **The editor.** `internal/confedit` is a scanner of our own. It records the byte span of every
    header, key, value and trailing comment, and the indented comment lines that continue that comment.
    It cross-checks its keys against `MetaData.Keys()` (document order: every header each time it
    appears, every key, every key of an inline table). An edit splices only the bytes it needs. The
    rules, in its package comment:
    - **Replace:** a replaced value keeps its comment at the column it had when the edit started, even
      when several changes of one save rewrite the line. The gap takes up the length change, with at least
      one space. A gap that holds a tab is kept as it is.
    - **Insert:** a missing key goes after the last key of its table and the lines that continue that
      key's comment. Inserting into a `[[pool]]` therefore lands above its `[pool.env]`, and never at the
      end of the file. A key of an inline table goes inside its braces. A key whose first part dotted keys
      already define is written dotted too (`claude-review.effort = "high"` beside
      `claude-review.model`), since an inline table would define that part a second time.
    - **New table:** a missing table goes after the last table of its family. With no family it goes
      before the first array of tables; with neither, at the end. In each case it goes before the
      comments that introduce the next header, with a blank line on each side.
    - **New element:** a new `[[repo]]` or `[[role]]` element goes after the last one and its subtables.
    - **Remove:** a removed key keeps its comment, with its continuation lines, as a comment line of its
      own.
    - **Dated notes:** a note becomes `# YYYY-MM-DD: <note>`, or goes first when the line has a comment:
      `# YYYY-MM-DD: <note>; <old comment>`.
    - **Multi-line arrays:** a multi-line array is replaced only as a whole. It must have no comments
      inside and one element per line, and it keeps that shape.
    - **Refusals:** these fail with `ErrUnsupported`, and the screen says "edit by hand":
      - a table only dotted keys or subtables define;
      - a subtable inside an array element;
      - a multi-line inline table;
      - a value holding a comment at any depth (a comment inside a nested array counts for the value
        holding it), whenever an edit would rewrite or remove that value;
      - other ambiguous shapes.
  - **The checks.** Each change applies to the text the one before left, which is parsed and
    cross-checked again.
    - **Text check:** a change may alter no old line outside the edited entry's lines (its key line to its
      last continuation comment line), byte for byte. Insertions add whole lines.
    - **`Verify`:** it decodes the old and the new file. Every leaf that differs must lie under a changed
      key. The changes' final effect must hold, in their order: each key reads back as its last change
      wrote it, and a removed key is absent. A change that a later one on the same key, or on one holding
      it or under it, overrides is not checked on its own (removing a key and setting it again holds the
      value set).
    - **A failure** of the text check, of the re-parse or of `Verify` is `ErrEditor`, a bug in the editor
      and never a refusal. The sweep and the fuzz test count it as a failure, and run the same text check
      on their own.
  - **Measured.** Every value was replaced, every key removed, and a key inserted into every table and
    every inline table, one edit at a time. On `config.defaults.toml` that was 182 replacements, 184
    removals and 16 insertions. On the operator's file, read for counts only, it was 280 entries in 61
    tables: 274 replacements, 276 removals and 79 insertions. Both had zero failures; 1 and 10 edits
    were refused (comment-holding multi-line arrays). A synthetic file with the same shapes is the test
    fixture, and a fuzz test makes random single edits.
    - The cross-check against `MetaData.Keys()` is tested on its own with a mismatch.
    - A lone carriage return is refused by the decoder, before the scanner sees it.
  - **The allowlist and the save.** `internal/settings` holds the allowlist (`Fields`): the v1 settings
    of design.md sections 2-7, with the role grid expanded per level, role and cell. Identities,
    `auto_approve_as`, keys, paths, commands, args, env, hooks, MCP, the sandbox and pools are never in
    it, and a test lists the forbidden names. A save (`Plan`) does the following:
    - re-reads the file and refuses one whose hash moved since the screen loaded it;
    - applies the draft with "was <old>" notes;
    - edits the cells of one role in a level each in place inside the role's braces, keeping the other
      keys' order and spelling and adding a missing key before the closing brace;
    - applies a role's sets before its removals, so a removal never takes the line a set still needs, and
      gives the group one note;
    - refuses a role that two `[[role]]` blocks of the file name, because the loader merges them (the
      last one's keys win) and the block to edit is ambiguous;
    - loads the candidate with `config.LoadOptions.UserData`, the user layer read from bytes with the
      path kept for messages and `Sources`;
    - renders the prompts with `engine.CheckPrompts`, as `magnum config` does;
    - diffs the files.
  - **What applies.** A value the user file does not set is shown as the resolved layers give it, not as
    the user layer's inheritance. Examples: a base config's `[kinds.codex] spend`, its `[[role]]` models
    (`Config.BaseRole`, the roles before any level), and its level tables. A level the roles do not follow
    is shown as it would resolve (`Config.RolesAtLevel`).
  - **Writing.** `Commit` takes a lock file and holds it for the whole write, so two writers never
    interleave across processes.
    - **Where the lock is:** beside the config, in its directory resolved to its canonical path
      (`~/.config/magnum/.config.toml.lock`, flock, waiting up to 10 s, created 0600 and kept). Writers
      that run with different `MAGNUM_HOME` layouts, or name the directory through a link, therefore take
      the same lock. A lock in the state directory would differ per layout.
    - **Under the lock** it does the following:
      - refuses a symlink, a non-regular file or a file with more than one hard link, since
        `fsx.WriteFileAtomic`'s rename would replace the link with a file or leave the other names on
        the old content;
      - checks the hash again;
      - keeps the replaced bytes;
      - checks the file and its hash once more right before the rename, against an editor's save, which
        takes no lock;
      - writes atomically with the file's mode (0600 for a new file).
  - **History.** Replaced versions go to `~/.local/share/magnum/config-history/<UTC>-<sha12>.toml`, the
    newest 20 kept and named in time order. A restore is a plan like any save. It reads only a regular file
    that is a direct child of the history directory, through an `os.Root` and never through a link. The
    history lives under the data directory and not in the registry: a migration would need a
    `daemon-restart --drain` before the first save, and the registry would then hold private config text.
    A `.bak` beside the config is the one-time leftover the operator rejected.
  - **The restart.** The daemon reads the config once, at start.
    - **Which config it runs:** it records the SHA-256 of the user layer it loaded
      (`daemon.config_sha256`, from `Config.UserSum`). `magnum status` and the screen can then say
      "changed since the daemon started" by content; a file that was only touched does not count.
    - **The request:** a save asks for a restart with the kv `config.restart` = {sha256, saved_at}.
      `restartForBuild` honours it as its third reason, after a new build and a landed skill version,
      under the same idle conditions.
    - **The file on disk decides, not the mark.** A mark whose file on disk equals the loaded config is
      cleared with a compare-and-delete, with no restart: a hand revert, or a save already running. A
      mark the next start finds while the file differs from what that start loaded is kept, because it is
      a save made between the CLI's load and the engine's startup.
    - **Before any idle restart:** this covers a saved config, a new build and a landed skill version.
      - **A changed binary:** when the binary on disk changed since the start, its own check runs
        (`checkBuild`: its version and `<bin> config`), even with `restart_on_new_build` off, since
        launchd would start it.
      - **A missing binary:** a binary launchd starts that is missing or cannot be read is a refusal,
        with the cause in the event.
      - **A changed config:** otherwise, when the config on disk differs from the loaded one, it is
        loaded again with this build, prompt check included.
      - **A failed check:** the daemon does not exit, since launchd would not start it again. It drops
        the mark with a compare-and-delete each time. Only the first refusal of a file and binary writes
        the warn event (`daemon.config_restart_refused`) and the `config.restart_refused` record.
      - **Retries:** the check runs again when the file or the binary changes, or 10 minutes after the
        last one. The binary's check also renders the prompts, which can be fixed apart from both, so a
        cache keyed by the file and the binary alone would block a needed build restart for good.
      - **What waits:** a build or learn restart waits until a check passes.
      - **The status line:** `magnum status` then says to fix the file, not to run `daemon-restart`.
      - **Idle again:** after a passing check the idleness is checked again right before the exit, since
        the check can take seconds and a job may start meanwhile. A round goroutine counts as busy from
        before it drops its reservation until its post-round fix cycle and whiteboard have reserved the
        PR (`roundTails`), so the gap between the two is never idle.
    - **When it does not restart:** a daemon launchd does not run leaves the restart to the operator.
    - **After it restarts:** the next start clears the mark (and any refusal record) and writes
      `daemon.restarted_for_config`.
  - **Rejected:**
    - Re-encoding the decoded config: it loses every comment, and `config.Duration` does not even
      marshal.
    - `pelletier/go-toml/v2/unstable`: a second TOML library, marked unstable, and an inline table's raw
      span covers only `{`.
    - `creachadair/tomledit`: TOML 1.0 only, called work in progress, and it re-indents through its own
      formatter.
    - Appending a missing key at the end of the file: it would land in the last `[[repo]]`, which the
      loader refuses as an unknown key.
    - A `config_versions` table in the registry.
    - Rewriting a role's whole inline table when several of its cells change. It would reformat the
      operator's spelling and key order; the in-place edits keep them, and the comment keeps its column.
    - A screen that runs `daemon-restart --when-idle` itself: it blocks the terminal and cannot run from
      inside the dashboard.
- **A review that found nothing starts a fix when another reviewer waits for an answer** (2026-10-20, spec
  96. It amends "A fix job also answers what other reviewers wrote that nobody answered", spec 93). After
  spec 93 landed, the operator pressed `f` on talkable#12054 and the board answered "found nothing to fix",
  while another reviewer's MINOR follow-up on stderr (`discussion_r4322458360`) still had no reply. Spec 93
  changed what a fix job does once it starts, but two gates still refused the start when magnum's own
  review was clean: the board's `actFix` refusal (internal/tui/rowacts.go), decided before any request, and
  the engine's `prepareFix` ("nothing to fix: the review on <sha> found nothing and left nothing open").
  - **The engine.** For a new loop on a review with no findings and no earlier P0 to P2 left open,
    `prepareFix` now reads the PR's other reviewers' items as the job would (`othersWaiting`, through
    `readExternal` and `externalOf`: the same reads, the same trusted-author filter, the same answered
    rules). The read comes after the cheap refusals and before the review's run, the slot and the pin, so
    no pin goes before a refusal. The job starts when at least one thread, review body or comment is
    unanswered. Otherwise the request is refused with "nothing to fix: the review on <sha> found nothing and
    no other reviewer's thread or comment waits for an answer". A read that fails refuses with its cause
    ("<pr>: the review on <sha> found nothing, and the other reviewers' threads and comments could not be
    read: <err>"): such a job would have nothing to do, so it never starts blind. GitHub lists at most
    1,000 review threads (`github.MaxReviewThreads`; the new `Client.AllReviewThreads` says whether it
    listed them all, and `ReviewThreads` is it without the flag), 500 reviews (`MaxReviews`, `AllReviews`)
    and 1,000 conversation comments back to the author's last (`MaxIssueComments`, `IssueComments`). A read
    that one of them cuts short and that shows nothing waiting cannot say that nothing waits: a PR with
    1,000 resolved threads and then an open one would be refused as clean. So it is refused with what was
    cut ("<pr>: the review on <sha> found nothing, and the other reviewers' threads and comments could not
    all be read (over 1000 review threads); answer them by hand"), and a cut read that shows an item
    waiting starts the job; the `fix.external` event of any job names the lists cut short. The read rides
    on the job (`fixJob.others`), and `writeExternal` writes it to `external-threads.json` without a second
    fetch. A request a whiteboard job yields to runs prepareFix before the yield; its refusal
    (`whiteboardHeld.carry`) keeps that read for the request (`Engine.yieldCarry`, by request id), and the
    pass after the yield runs every refusal again but decides on the kept read when the head is the same,
    so one request reads GitHub once. An item written between the request and the fixer's start waits for
    the next cycle, as one written while the fixer works does; the skill's look right before each reply
    still catches an answer. If the file cannot be written, the run is abandoned and the job fails. The
    answer, `fix.start` and `fix.held` say
    "answers the other reviewers' 1 unanswered thread or comment in review1 (magnum's review of <sha> found
    nothing)". Only `magnum fix`, its dry run and a fix held for a restart reach this path: autofix starts
    only after a round that posted findings.
  - **The prompt and the skill.** The new `.NoFindings` (`agents.FixPromptInput`, `RoleData`) makes
    `fix.md` say that the review found nothing to fix and to handle the external file's unanswered items, in
    place of "Fix the findings of the review" and the file's "after the review's findings" sentence. The fix
    skill's section 4 says: "When the prompt says that the review found nothing to fix, the external items
    are this run's whole work: judge, fix and answer them alone." In section 2, a checkout at the wrong head
    then lists every unanswered external item under `## Needs you`, so that stop ends the loop needing the
    author instead of clean.
  - **The loop.** It ends as any loop does. A push goes to its forced re-review, whose result decides.
    Replies alone end the loop clean, with the info toast "pushed nothing, replied to 1 thread or comment of
    other reviewers". This settles the spec's stop condition: nothing in the end condition depends on the
    first review's findings.
  - **The board.** The client-side "found nothing to fix" refusal is gone; the daemon decides, and its
    refusal shows in the footer as any other. On such a review `f` asks "Answer the other reviewers' open
    threads and comments on <pr> as you (magnum's review of <sha> found nothing to fix)?". The other
    client-side refusals stay: not reviewed, merged or closed, the head moved, a round running.
  - **Residuals.** A bot's status or CI comment after the author's last word counts as unanswered, as it
    does in the file. So `f` can start a job that replies nowhere ("asks for nothing") and ends clean. A
    request on a clean review costs one GitHub read, refusals included.
  - **Rejected:**
    - Deciding on the board: the board reads no GitHub, and the daemon reads as the watch's poll identity.
    - Starting the job without the read and letting the fixer find nothing: a session and a slot for
      nothing, and the operator would learn it only from the report.
    - Counting only threads: a review body or a comment that waits is as much an item as a thread.
    - Reading GitHub again at `fixStart`, or after a whiteboard job's yield: a second fetch for one request.
    - Excluding bots' comments from what starts a job: a code-review bot's finding is as much an item as a
      person's, and the fixer already gives a status comment no reply.
    - Starting a job on a cut-short read that shows nothing waiting: it would have nothing to answer.
- **A GitHub cost meter per call and identity, and a shared floor that holds new work before the budget
  runs out** (2026-10-20, spec 97). From 16:43 to 16:56 local the operator's gh login ran out of its
  GraphQL budget (5,000 points an hour, shared by every tool on that login): the daemon log has 61 "gh: API
  rate limit already exceeded for user ID <n>" lines and the radar poll failed (`poll.error`). The radar is
