  cheap by design (scalars only, about one point per owner), so the spend was elsewhere: about 20 call sites
  read as the watch's poll identity (a round's setup and settle, triage, delta checks, the full pass, the
  post-merge base, the push's delta, reruns, the fix job's settle and its read of the other reviewers, the
  retro, auto-approval's base checks, whiteboards), plus whatever else the operator runs. Magnum kept only
  the last radar's rate limit and could not say who spent it, and only the poll held back below a floor
  (`rateFloor`, 50), so rounds and jobs spent the budget to zero and the poll then failed.
  - **The meter.** `github.Client.Meter` hears every `gh api` command right after it returns: a GraphQL call
    with the rate limit its answer carried (its cost; beside a partial error too; zero when gh failed before
    GraphQL answered), a REST call as one request against the core budget, a retry after a 401 as a second
    call. Every GraphQL query already asked for `rateLimit`; a test scans the package's query declarations
    and its `c.graphql` calls, so a new query cannot leave it out. The caller labels what it reads GitHub
    for with `github.WithOp` in the call's context (the innermost label wins); a call without one counts
    under its own kind, read from the start of its error label (`callKinds`; a test scans every label the
    package builds). FromApp sets the Meter of each identity's client. The hook takes one lock, adds and
    returns: it never touches the store, and a Meter that panics fails no call.
  - **What it keeps.** Per identity, per op and per clock hour, the last 24 hours, and each identity's latest
    rate limit (a later reset window, or the same window with no more left: calls in flight return in any
    order), which the radar's own reading feeds too. A call counts in the clock hour it returned in, so a
    clock that stepped back adds to an earlier hour, made in its place when missing. The tick writes
    `github.cost.<identity>` at most once a minute and the stop writes the last calls; every flush first drops
    every record's hours older than the last 24, an idle identity's too, and a write that fails (a store
    error, the stop's cancelled context) leaves its record to be written by the next flush. The start reads
    the records back.
    The ops: `round` (the pipeline's threads file, posting and verification), `round.setup`,
    `round.settle`, `round.triage`, `round.delta_check`, `round.full_pass`, `round.post_merge`,
    `round.rerun`, `poll.delta`, `poll.since_review`, `auto_approve`, `approval`, `status_comment`, `fix`,
    `fix.external`, `fix.settle`, `whiteboard`, `retro` and `verdict`; `GitHubOpWords` gives each its plain
    words. One comparison serves a tick (`compareMemo`), so it counts as its first caller's.
  - **Status.** `magnum status` shows one line per metered identity: "github:   zhuravel 4692/5000, resets
    17:13 · since 16:00 1,470 points: round setup 620, settle 300, radar 180, …". The window is the current
    clock hour, or reaches back to the hour before while the current one is under 30 minutes old. A run of
    low budget adds "below the floor of 500: new work waits until 17:13" and a `github:<identity>` pause.
    `--json` carries the window by op and the 24 hours (`github.identities`). Without a record the radar's
    old line stays.
  - **The floor.** `[github] budget_floor` (default 500 points, 0 = off, at most 5000) is checked only where
    work starts, never on a read:
    - **A round:** dispatch holds it while its watch's poll identity or its posting identity is below the
      floor (`WaitGitHub`: "github budget: zhuravel at 312 points until 17:13", `review · github budget →
      17:13` on the board, not overridable). A paused round's continuation passes: it finishes a round that
      ran. `magnum review` still forces the round, which waits too, and its answer says why.
    - **A fix cycle:** `prepareFix` looks at the floor before anything it reads from GitHub: below it,
      a review that found nothing does not read the other reviewers' threads, reviews and comments (spec
      96's read: it would spend the very budget the floor keeps, and a read GitHub refuses at exhaustion
      would drop the request), and a `magnum fix` takes no pin off; the job carries the low budget, and
      `startFix` refuses with `githubBudgetError`, which keeps the job it prepared. `magnum fix` and autofix
      become held fixes (`KVPRFixHeld` with why `github_budget`, as a drain holds them; the answer says it
      starts once the budget recovers), and a loop's next cycle is held in phase reviewing (`fix.waiting`).
      The tick that finds the poll identity's budget recovered goes on with them (`continueBudgetHeld`)
      before dispatch, so a round queued meanwhile for the same PR (a reply round, a forced review) waits
      for the fixer instead of taking the PR and having the held fix dropped as a round in flight; the
      restart's recovery does the same, and holds them again while the budget is still low. A held start
      whose read GitHub refuses for its rate limit stays held. A held autofix runs autofix's own checks
      again before it starts (`autofixGone`: the watch still asks for it, the PR is the operator's, no
      `magnum fix --off`, a fix role) and is dropped otherwise.
    - **A whiteboard:** a posted review's whiteboard is remembered as pending, as a drain's skip is, under
      the identity its job reads as, and made once that identity recovered: a pass of the pending
      whiteboards leaves pending those whose own identity is still low. `magnum whiteboard` is refused
      with the budget and its reset.
    - **The retro and a notes curation:** the day's retro waits, and `magnum retro` and a requested curation
      are queued ("starts when the GitHub budget of zhuravel recovers"; `QueuedGitHub`). The curation reads
      nothing through the daemon's clients; it waits because its agent's pane runs with the operator's own
      environment, whose gh login is this budget, and a learn job is the easiest work to put off.
    - **What goes on:** a running round finishes (its settle and posting reads are the round's), a fix job
      or a whiteboard that started runs to its end, and the poll keeps `rateFloor`, so new pushes and
      requests are still seen.
    - **Announced once per run:** the first tick of a run below the floor writes `github.budget_low` (warn)
      and toasts once ("GitHub budget of zhuravel at 312 points: new rounds wait until 17:13"). The run is
      written at once in a row of its own (`github.low.<identity>`, with its budget), apart from the cost
      records, which stay at once a minute; the start reads it back, its budget included, so a restart
      neither announces the run twice nor forgets the low budget a minute's flush had not written yet. The
      tick that finds the budget recovered (above the floor, or past its reset) removes it with
      `github.budget_recovered` and lets the next run toast again.
  - **Residuals.** The ops count the daemon's calls only: agents' `gh` calls in their panes (the reviewers,
    the judge's post-review, the fixer, the whiteboard writer) spend the same budget unseen, as does every
    other tool on the login; the remaining the line shows is GitHub's, so their spend is in it. An
    identity's budget is known only from the daemon's last call as it, so after the reset nothing is held
    until a call shows the new window. A held fix whose PR moved on is dropped as after a drain
    (`fix.dropped`; an autofix's without a toast).
  - **Rejected:**
    - Webhooks first: they would replace the radar's polling, not the per-round reads that spend.
    - Moving the reads to the App's token: a later step, once the meter shows which reads dominate.
    - A floor only on the poll: today's state, which let rounds and jobs spend the budget to zero.
    - Checking the floor on each read: a half-read round would fail where it should finish.
    - Writing the store on each call: the hook runs on every read path, rounds' goroutines included.

- **Webhooks reach magnum through a relay of its own, `magnum-relay`** (2026-10-20, spec 98). The poll
  identity ran out of its GraphQL hour twice that day. The operator then decided to receive the App's
  webhooks instead of polling, through a Go relay self-hosted on his own server. The daemon's consumer is spec 99,
  and the deploy guide is `deploy/relay/README.md`.
  - **Why a relay.**
    - GitHub posts a delivery once ("GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed deliveries") and wants
      a 2xx within 10 s.
    - The daemon runs on a Mac that sleeps behind NAT. Something always on must receive the deliveries and
      keep them until the daemon asks.
    - GitHub's 3-day deliveries log is the backstop for what the relay misses.
  - **Why Go, on the operator's server.**
    - PocketBase: a pre-1.0 framework, with a public admin UI to lock down and to upgrade, for one table
      and two endpoints.
    - Appwrite: 17 containers and the Docker socket for one HTTP function.
    - A Cloudflare Worker with D1 (the research's first choice): nothing to host, but the events' metadata
      would rest at Cloudflare, and the code would be JavaScript outside magnum's gate. The operator chose
      his own server.
    - A tunnel straight to the daemon: it puts an internet-facing listener inside the process that holds
      the tokens, and it is dead while the Mac sleeps.
    - Go with `modernc.org/sqlite` instead: it is the SQLite module magnum already uses, so there is no new
      dependency. The relay goes through the same gate (tests, vet, lint, govulncheck), and it ships as a
      static image of about 11 MB, built from scratch.
  - **The envelope.** The relay keeps only routing fields: the delivery GUID, the event, the action, the
    installation and repository ids, `owner/name`, `pr_numbers`, the head SHA, the base ref, a check's name
    and conclusion, and `received_at`.
    - It never keeps a body: no titles, comments, user names or URLs. All that rests on the server is
      repository names, numbers and SHAs.
    - An event is a doorbell. The daemon reads what changed from GitHub, as it does today, so a forged or
      replayed event costs at most a read, never an action.
    - A value that is not well formed is left empty. A check name is cleaned of controls and format
      characters and cut to 120 runes.
    - An `issue_comment` names its issue only when the issue is a pull request. Check events name their
      `pull_requests`, which is empty for a fork's, whose head SHA is then the key. A `status` names none.
  - **The auth.**
    - **The webhook.** The relay checks the HMAC-SHA256 of the exact bytes with `hmac.Equal`, under the
      current or the previous secret (a rotation), before anything is parsed. The secrets are read from
      files, never from the environment or argv.
    - **The listing.** It takes a bearer token whose SHA-256 is compared in constant time with the
      accepted hashes (`MAGNUM_RELAY_TOKEN_HASHES`), so the server holds no token.
    - **`/healthz`.** It has no auth and carries no event data. The image's `HEALTHCHECK` runs
      `magnum-relay healthcheck`, since an image built from scratch has no curl.
  - **The journal and the cursor.**
    - `seq` is `AUTOINCREMENT`, so a number is never reused. A cursor is `<epoch>:<seq>`, and the epoch is
      random for each journal: a lost volume brings a new epoch, then a 410 and a resync.
    - Retention deletes a prefix: every event up to the newest one received before the cutoff. It records
      that number as `pruned_through`, so `oldest` only moves forward and names exactly the cursors that
      would miss events. A cursor below `oldest`, one of another epoch, or one ahead of the high water
      answers 410.
    - `oldest` is the cursor just before the oldest kept event, so `after=<oldest>` lists every kept event,
      as `after=` does. Read that way, the contract's two rules agree: a consumer that read up to the last
      pruned event is not told of a gap. Read as the oldest kept event's own cursor, they would not.
    - A listing reads its events and its bounds in one WAL read transaction, so `next` never skips an event
      inserted meanwhile.
  - **Bounds.** A security review of the first version (Codex's) found that requests without a signature
    could send their headers, withhold their bodies and hold every turn for the server's 20 s read
    timeout, so real deliveries got 503. These bounds answer it:
    - **Before a turn.** A request whose `X-Hub-Signature-256`, `X-GitHub-Event` or `X-GitHub-Delivery`
      header is missing or malformed is refused before its body is read or a turn taken. The answer
      says `Connection: close`, and the read deadline passes at once, so net/http reads nothing more of
      the connection.
    - **The body.** A body is read up to 26 MiB (413 above). Four bodies are read at once.
    - **One deadline.** The wait for a turn (at most 2 s, then 503) and the body share one deadline,
      7 s after the headers (`DefaultBodyTimeout`). A body that stalls is cut with 408, which frees its
      turn.
    - **The insert** has 2 s, and it finishes even when the client hangs up. A delivery is therefore
      answered within 9 s of its headers (`WebhookDeadline`), and a shutdown waits that long plus 5 s
      before it closes what is left.
    - **The server.** It has header (5 s), read (9 s), write and idle timeouts. A long poll sets its own
      write deadline.
    - **The listing.** A listing takes `limit` 1 to 500 and `wait` up to 30 s. Whole seconds are
      bounded before they become a Duration, so `wait=18446744074`, which wraps to 0.29 s, answers 400.
      At most 16 polls wait at once, and one more answers 429.
    - **Formats.** A delivery id must match `[A-Za-z0-9-]{1,64}` and an event name `[a-z_]{1,64}`. A
      token is 32 to 512 printable ASCII characters, in `hash-token` and in the listing alike
      (`CheckToken`).
    - **Health.** `/healthz` reads two counters that the insert and the prune keep in `meta` (the
      prune counts them again), never a scan of the events. It answers from a snapshot read again at
      most every 2 s, by one check at a time, so a flood of checks neither loads the journal nor fails
      the container's `HEALTHCHECK`.
  - **Content type.** An App's settings page has no content type. The hook config holds one
    (`content_type`, form by default per the REST docs). So the relay reads a JSON body, and a
    form-encoded `payload` field too. A body that starts as a JSON object is read as JSON, whatever its
    header says.
  - **Permissions.** GitHub's event docs name Issues read for `issue_comment`. The deploy guide lists it
    beside Pull requests, Checks and Commit statuses, which the spec named.
  - **Residuals.**
    - A sender that forges well-formed headers (a signature of the right shape) can still hold the four
      turns, for 7 s per request. GitHub's deliveries then answer 503 meanwhile, and the backstop reads
      them from the deliveries log. The HMAC cannot be checked before the body it covers has arrived.
    - Events from every installation of the App are stored. The daemon filters them by installation and
      repository.
    - `check_run` also arrives for other apps' runs, so CI makes most of the volume.
  - **Rejected:**
    - Storing payloads: private text at rest, and their size.
    - Dropping `check_run` actions or other installations at the relay: the daemon decides, and the relay
      stays a journal.
    - SSE or WebSocket push: no replay, and no fit for a `curl` client.
    - A timestamp cursor: timestamps tie, and commit order can differ from them.
    - An allowlist of GitHub's hook IP ranges: GitHub advises against it, and the HMAC is the guard.
    - A secret read from the environment or argv, which `ps`, `docker inspect` and crash dumps show.

- **The daemon reads the GitHub App's webhook events in shadow mode and compares them with the poll,
  changing nothing** (2026-10-20, spec 99, phase 1 of webhooks; magnum-relay, spec 98, receives the
  deliveries). The operator decided on 2026-10-20 to have GitHub App webhooks through a self-hosted relay,
  after the account's 5,000-point GraphQL hour ran out twice that day while the radar of each watch owner
  costs a point or more every 30 s. The daemon is behind NAT on a Mac that sleeps, so it cannot receive a
  delivery itself: the relay keeps a journal of them (ids and routing only) and the daemon reads it by
  cursor (`[webhooks]`: `mode`, `url`, `token_file`, `owners`, `wait`, `stale_after`).
  - **Events are hints, GitHub reads stay authoritative.** An event says which PR or head changed, never
    what it now is: GitHub does not keep deliveries in order and can send one twice, a broken relay would
    then cost reads and never a decision, and one writer of the GitHub columns stays (the poll). The
    consumer turns each event of a covered owner's watched repository into hints: (repository, PR number)
    for the PR events, (repository, head SHA) for a check run, a check suite (a fork's names no PR) and a
    status.
  - **Shadow first.** Phase 1 acts on nothing. The consumer is a goroutine beside the heavy worker that
    ends with `Run` (never with `--once` or a dry run); it writes no PR, slot or request row, starts no
    round or job, and reads nothing from GitHub. Its rows are three kv keys (`webhooks.cursor` with the
    relay's epoch, `webhooks.health`, `webhooks.hours`) and `webhooks.*` events, none on a PR's subject:
    the CLI reads a PR's latest events by window (a fix's or a whiteboard's wait, `review --dry-run`),
    which `webhooks.missed` events would crowd, so they go on the watch's (`watch:<owner>`). The poll's
    only hook, `webhooksSaw` in `pollRepo`, reads the rows the poll already read before it applies the
    radar, writes nothing (a writer goroutine of the consumer's writes its kv rows and events once told,
    so a slow registry never holds the poll or a page; the last write at the stop is bounded to 5 s), and
    runs under `safely`, so a panic in it is recorded and never the poll's. Whether a later
    phase may let the events stand in for most of a covered owner's radar is decided on these numbers, not
    guessed: TestShadowModeChangesNothingTheDaemonDoes runs the same PRs with webhooks off and in shadow
    mode and finds the registry, the GitHub reads, the rounds and the agents' calls identical.
  - **The comparison.** Each poll of an owner in `owners` lists what it saw change on each PR since the
    comparison last counted it (head, draft, a newer `updatedAt`, a reopen, a new PR, and a close once
    GitHub confirmed it, so a PR the radar's list skipped once counts nothing), against the stored row
    after a restart. A change is announced when a hint for it came within 5 minutes before (or since the
    repository's previous poll, when the poll paused longer, as on a rate pause), or within a minute
    after: a delivery a second or two behind the radar's read is no miss (an estimate: without that
    minute, a change in the last 2 s of a 30 s tick, about one in fifteen, would count as missed). A
    change with neither is missed and leaves one `webhooks.missed` event at debug level (the PR, what
    changed, the last event read for it). A hint no change followed within 5 minutes is early or noise.
    One event announces each PR it names once (a check run of two PRs, a status on a head two PRs share),
    before the poll and after alike; whether it was early or noise is the event's alone. A
    hint is timed by when the consumer read it, and an event the relay received more than 5 minutes
    before the page that lists it (by the relay's own clock: a backlog after a sleep or an outage) is
    counted but hints at nothing. A poll while the stream is unhealthy compares nothing, and neither does
    each repository's first poll after a gap, so an outage or a gap is the health line's and not a miss;
    a PR such a poll saw leave the open list stays uncounted when GitHub confirms its close at a later
    poll (the poll runs its comparison before it confirms closes).
    Totals are kept by the hour for 24 hours; `magnum status` shows their sums on a `webhooks:` line, with
    the stream's health.
  - **The cursor.** A first start, and a gap (410: the relay's journal is another, or no longer holds the
    events after the cursor), put the cursor at the relay's newest event: what came before is what the
    polls already saw. Gaps in a row wait 1 s, then longer, up to 2 minutes, and so does a relay busy with
    long polls (429), which is no failure. A restart reads on from the kept cursor, a kv value counts as
    written only once its write took, and each delivery id counts once.
  - **Why curl.** Little Snitch blocks Go's own HTTP client in a rebuilt, unsigned magnum binary (the
    reason GitHub calls go through gh), and gh reaches only GitHub. curl runs through execx with a fixed
    argv (`curl --disable --config -`): `--disable` keeps a `~/.curlrc` out (one with `verbose` would print
    the header), and the URL, the time bound (the wait and 10 s) and the `Authorization` header (quoted for
    curl's config) go on stdin, so the token never reaches argv, a log or an error. The token is what the
    relay accepts (`relay.CheckToken`: one word of 32 to 512 printable ASCII characters). The token file
    must be a regular file only its owner can open: the consumer reads no other, and `magnum config`
    warns; a missing file is a warning too. The pages are no GitHub call: they spend no GitHub budget, and
    spec 97's meter does not count them.
  - **Rejected:**
    - Acting on the events now: without the numbers, a missed delivery would be a missed review.
    - The App's deliveries log through gh as the source: it lists no PR number and spends the App's REST
      budget per payload read; it stays a candidate backstop for a later phase.
    - Go's net/http to the relay: blocked by the firewall for a rebuilt binary.
    - Timing a hint by the relay's `received_at`: after a sleep the catch-up reads hours-old deliveries for
      the changes the first poll after the wake finds, which would all count as missed; `received_at` only
      leaves the backlog out.
    - Comparing while the stream is unhealthy: an outage's changes would read as the events' misses.
    - Refusing the config over the token file's mode: shadow mode would then keep the daemon from
      starting, and the consumer refuses the file itself.

- **magnum-relay also deploys as a Compose project, `deploy/relay/compose.yaml`** (2026-10-21). The
  operator asked for a compose file to deploy the relay with.
  - **The file.** It builds `deploy/relay/Dockerfile` from the repository root, keeps the journal in the
    named volume `relay-data` (a new named volume takes the image's `/data`, owned by uid 65532) and
    publishes no port: the platform's proxy routes the domain to container port 8080. A deploy without
    `RELAY_TOKEN_HASHES` stops at interpolation with an error that names it.
  - **The secret.** Compose reads `RELAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET` from the platform's `.env` file and mounts it
    as `/run/secrets/webhook_secret` (`secrets:` with `environment:`). The relay still reads the secret
    only from a file, and `docker inspect` shows it in no environment. A local run with Docker Compose
    v5.5 stored a signed delivery (202, then 200 for the repeat), refused a bad signature and a missing
    token (401), kept the journal's epoch across a down and up, and reported healthy as uid 65532.
  - **No previous secret.** Compose refuses to start when a secret's variable is unset, so the file
    holds one secret only. A rotation with Compose changes the relay and then the App, and the
    deliveries between them answer 401: the App's Recent Deliveries can redeliver them, and the poll
    finds their changes in any case.
  - **Rejected:**
    - A bind mount of a file the platform writes: its host path depends on where the platform keeps the
      project and the compose file, and a missing host path is created as a directory.
    - The secret in the relay's environment: rejected in spec 98, and `secrets:` makes it unneeded.
    - The platform's network and proxy labels in the file: the platform adds them to the service a domain
      names.

- **The GitHub meter keeps the lowest live reading, and a call GitHub refuses for its rate limit marks
  the budget spent** (2026-10-21, spec 101, amending spec 97's). The operator pressed `f` on talkable#12054
  at 11:19Z. GitHub refused the fix job's read of the other reviewers' threads ("github review threads
  talkable/talkable#12054: RATE_LIMIT: API rate limit already exceeded for user ID ..."), and the job ran
  without a colleague's thread. The floor of 500 should have held the fix: the poll had paused on 47 and
  44 points at 11:14:02Z and 11:14:03Z (`poll.rate_limited`). The meter's record still said 3,838 points.
  - **Two readings at once.** A call at 11:14:01Z read 3,838 points with reset 11:29:16Z; the radar a
    second later read 44 with reset 11:28:11Z, and GitHub's REST `rate_limit` endpoint gave a third reset.
    The daemon's `zhuravel` shares the operator's token, so these are one budget. The meter, the client's
    last reading and the radar's sum kept the reading with the later reset, so the 44 lost, `githubLow`
    said "not low", and the fix started below the floor.
  - **A refusal no one heard.** GitHub's GraphQL refusal has the error type `RATE_LIMIT`: the daemon's log
    holds 75 such lines and none of type `RATE_LIMITED`, the only type `APIError` matched (besides HTTP
    429 and a 403 that says so). So since spec 97 no live GraphQL refusal matched `ErrRateLimited`, and
    nothing that checks it (the meter now, a held fix whose read GitHub refuses) ever fired.
  - **The reading rule.** `RateLimit.Tighter` decides for the meter's record, the client's last reading
    and the radar's sum:
    - A reading whose reset has passed (at or before now) is ignored.
    - Any live reading replaces a record whose window ended.
    - Of two live readings, the lower remaining wins, whatever their resets. Of equal remaining, the
      later reset wins.
    The status line shows the kept reading, and the floor holds new work until its reset.
  - **A refused call.** `github.Call.RateLimited` says that GitHub refused the call for its rate limit (an
    `*APIError` matching `ErrRateLimited`, GraphQL or REST), and `ErrRateLimited` now matches the type
    `RATE_LIMIT` as well as `RATE_LIMITED`. The meter then sets the identity's budget to 0 of its limit
    (5000 when no call told it one). The 0 holds until the record's reset when that is ahead, else for 5
    minutes, a probe: the next call either tells the real budget or is refused again. The next flush
    writes it, and the floor holds rounds at dispatch, fixes, whiteboards, the retro and curations as
    spec 97 designed ("0/5000, resets HH:MM" on the status line). The poll's own `rateFloor` is unchanged.
  - **Residuals.** The lower reading can belong to a window that resets before the other one; the hold
    then lasts until its own reset, an hour at most. A REST refusal (the core budget, or a secondary
    limit) marks the GraphQL budget too, until the record's reset: every new job reads both. With no reset
    known, each probe that ends and is refused again begins a new run of low budget, with its own event
    and toast, at most one every 5 minutes.
  - **Rejected:**
    - Trusting the later reset: the old rule, which kept the 3,838.
    - A tolerance of 2 minutes between resets, inside which the lower reading wins (the spec's first
      rule): the same login showed two windows at once, so no reset comparison says which one is current.
    - Reading GitHub's `rate_limit` endpoint after every refusal: another call per refusal, and its reset
      disagreed with GraphQL's own the same morning.

- **The reply classifier reads "I did not make this change", "not patching" and a fix sent to a follow-up
  as declines** (2026-10-21, spec 104; amends "A reply "Follow-up in <sha>" is a fix, not a won't-fix").
  Five replies since 10-17 declined or deferred a finding and were `other`: three on talkable#12041 opened
  "I did not make this change" (once after "Correct: …"), which no pattern knew; two on another
  repository's PR accepted the finding ("Confirmed. This is a real gap …", "Thanks — all four are real …
  we are not patching them here. We'll raise them as one templates follow-up") and sent the fix to a
  follow-up, which the deferral pattern missed because it reads a clause's start ("Follow-up …",
  "Deferred to a follow-up") while these name the follow-up at the clause's end, and the first's sat four
  paragraphs down, past the first paragraph, which alone was read. The judge honoured all five, so only the
  threads file's class, the `round.threads` "replies:" line, the evidence tables and the retro's guess
  were wrong. Now `replyDeclines` also takes a clause "I (or we) did not (didn't) make, apply or take this
  (that, the, the suggested) change", alone or before "here", "because", "since" or "in this PR" (so "… yet"
  and "… myself" claim nothing), and "<…> we are (I'm) not patching" or a clause that starts "not
  patching"; and a clause that ends in "as a (one, up to two words) follow-up" (or "follow-up PR", issue,
  ticket, task, change) with no verb saying it was made (pushed, landed, committed, merged, shipped, added,
  made, done, fixed, applied) defers the fix (`replyDefers`), in the first paragraph like the other
  declines, and in a later one only when the first clause acknowledges the finding ("Confirmed", "Thanks")
  and no clause before the deferral says fixed or not a bug (`replyDeferredLater`; a verdict, score or
  other decline past the first paragraph still claims nothing). Ending at the follow-up, the clause names
  no commit, so "follow-up in <sha>" stays `fixed` and "as a follow-up in <sha>" is no deferral. Run over
  the 915 distinct author replies in the stored threads files (excerpts of 600 characters), the change
  moves four from `other` to `won't fix`, the four above, and none of another class; the fifth's deferral
  lies past its excerpt, and its full body moves too. New tests TestAReplyThatDidNotMakeTheChangeIsAWontFix
  and TestAnAcceptedGapDeferredToAFollowUpIsAWontFix. Rejected: "in a follow-up" (the pinned "Good catch,
  added in a follow-up" stays `other`), reading every decline past the first paragraph (the pinned "Noted."
  followed by a paragraph "I score that fix at −8" stays `other`), and a deferral anywhere in a clause
  ("runs as a follow-up step" describes code).

- **A memory pressure level counts only when two samples in a row read it** (2026-10-21, spec 104; amends
  "The daemon records the machine's memory pressure and swap"). `machine.memory_pressure` was recorded at
  every change of a single one-minute sample: 83 events since 10-19, 35 of them warn, in pairs one to five
  minutes apart (10-21: warn 08:49, normal 08:52, warn 08:53, and the same twice more that morning). Now
  `noteMemoryLevel` keeps the level that counts and a pending one: a known sample at another level is
  pending, the next known sample at that level makes it count (one event, with that sample's swap), and a
  sample at the counted level drops it; an unknown sample changes neither. The first known level since a
  start still counts at once (there is nothing to flap from, and a restart records where it starts). The
  critical toast keeps its rule: a run of critical starts at the first critical sample and ends at the next
  normal one, so the toast can come a minute before its error event, and a single critical sample toasts
  with no event. The `memory:` status line still shows the latest sample (kv `machine.memory` is written
  every sample). New test TestAMemoryLevelCountsOnlyWhenTwoSamplesAgree;
  TestEachChangeOfTheMemoryPressureIsOneEvent takes two samples per change. Residual: a level that
  alternates between warn and critical without two equal samples in a row leaves the counted level where it
  was (the toast still goes out).

- **A fix reads the other reviewers' items before it starts, and a read GitHub refuses for the rate limit
  holds it** (2026-10-21, spec 102, amending specs 93, 96 and 97). On 2026-10-21 at 11:19Z `magnum fix` on
  talkable#12054, a review with findings, read the other reviewers' threads at the job's start
  (`writeExternal`); GitHub refused the read for the rate limit, and the job went on with magnum's findings
  alone (`fix.external`, warn), while a colleague's MINOR thread stayed unanswered. The floor looked at the
  budget only in `prepareFix`, before that read, and the meter's record lagged (spec 101): a budget that
  runs out between the two let the job start without the items.
  - **The read before the start.** `prepareFix` reads the items for every cycle (`othersBeforeStart`): a
    new loop on a review with findings, a loop's next cycle, and a review that found nothing (spec 96),
    which still decides on them. It reads after every other refusal and before the pin goes, so a refused
    request reads nothing and a fix held for a pause reads nothing while it waits; the clean review's read
    moved there too (it came before the slot, snooze, cooldown and pause refusals, which now answer first).
    The job writes that read to `external-threads.json` with no second fetch, a request a whiteboard job
    yielded to carries it as before, now for every job, and a dry run reads as well.
  - **The hold.** A read refused for the rate limit (`errors.Is(err, github.ErrRateLimited)`) asks
    `githubLow` again: spec 101's meter marks the identity exhausted on a refused call, so it says low, and
    the job is held as below the floor (`fixJob.budget`, `othersDeferred`, no pin taken,
    `githubBudgetError`): `magnum fix` and autofix become held fixes ("held; the fix of … starts once the
    GitHub budget of zhuravel recovers …"), a next cycle waits in phase reviewing with `fix.waiting`, and
    the held start reads again, so a held job never carries a stale read. The hold depends on that
    sentinel: GitHub's GraphQL refusal carries the error type `RATE_LIMIT` with no HTTP status (the daemon
    log of 2026-10-21), which spec 101 made `ErrRateLimited` match. With the floor off (`budget_floor = 0`)
    `githubLow` never says low, and the job starts as before.
  - **Other failures.** A job with findings whose read fails for another reason starts without it, and
    `writeExternal`'s read at the start is its one retry, its warning unchanged; a review that found nothing
    is refused with the cause, as before. `fixJob.alone` (a new loop on a review that found nothing and left
    nothing open) now marks the job of the other reviewers alone, which `others` marked while only that path
    read.
  - **The loop's end says what was not read.** On talkable#12054 the `fix.external` warning was the only
    trace: no toast, nothing on the board or in `magnum status`, and the loop would have ended "clean after
    1 fix cycle". A cycle whose fixer did not get all the items records it on the loop's row
    (`FixState.OthersUnread`, reset each cycle: "not read (HTTP 502)", "not all read (over 1000 review
    threads)", "not read (their file could not be written)"; a short cause, never an error's text or PR
    text: GitHub's rate limit, a time-out, an HTTP status, a GraphQL error type), and the loop's end carries
    one sentence, "the other reviewers' threads and comments were not read (HTTP 502): `magnum fix
    talkable/talkable#2` reads them again": `fix.replied`, `fix.done` (whose toast reads "clean for magnum's
    findings after 1 fix cycle"), the toast of a loop that ends on replies, every loop-end event's data
    (`others_unread`), `magnum fix --wait` ("clean after 1 fix cycle for magnum's findings; …"), and an
    attention's message, on a second line, so that the reason's cause, calls and remedy, read off its first
    line, stay as they were and the sentence shows in its detail.
  - **Residuals:** a `magnum fix` asked during a drain reads the items to answer its refusals, and the
    restart's start reads them again; the read a job writes is as old as the fixer's start-up.
  - **Rejected:**
    - Reading inside the job and holding it mid-start: the hold would have to unwind a claimed row, the
      reservation and a run.
    - Retrying the read inside the job: it spends the budget the floor keeps, and leaves the items out all
      the same once the budget is gone.
    - A second cycle for the external items after the loop: they would be answered late, and only after a
      loop that ended clean.

- **A held fix waits out its fixer's pause** (2026-10-21, spec 102). On 2026-10-19 talkable#12054's fix,
  asked during a drain, was held (`fix.held` at 23:05Z) and dropped after the restart (`fix.dropped` at
  23:24Z: "…: claude paused (usage_limit) until 14:00"): `startHeldFix` held again only for a new drain and
  for the GitHub floor, and `prepareFix`'s refusal for a paused agent kind was a plain error, so the
  operator had to ask again by hand.
  - That refusal is now a `kindPausedError` naming the kind, its text unchanged: a `magnum fix` or
    an autofix asked during a pause is refused as before. `startHeldFix` keeps a held fix on it, with `why`
    `kind_pause` and the paused kind in `KVPRFixHeld`'s JSON (a new `kind` key; no migration), and the PR
    joins `pauseHeld`. A tick pass after `continueBudgetHeld` (`continuePauseHeld`) starts it once
    `kindPauseReason` is empty for the fix role's kind, through `startHeldFix` and its checks (the head, the
    review, an autofix's own); the restart decides it again (`startHeldFixes`). `magnum fix --wait` says
    "the fix starts when claude's pause ends", and a drop says "while claude was paused".
  - One row holds whichever hold applies now: a pause hold whose start finds the budget low becomes a
    budget hold, and the reverse, so no held fix is dropped for a reason the daemon can wait out.
  - The pass looks at the pause before calling `startHeldFix`, which would only hold the fix again (the
    mutation that drops the check passes the tests): without it a paused fix's row would be taken and
    written back each tick.
  - **Rejected:** holding a `magnum fix` asked during a pause: its answer names the pause and its end, while
    a held fix had been promised to start.

- **`magnum abort` names the hold of the fix it takes back** (2026-10-21, spec 102). `dropHeldFix` said
  "the fix held for the restart is dropped" for every held fix, though the same row holds the GitHub
  budget's holds since spec 97 and the pause's now. Its note is "the fix held <during> is dropped", from
  `heldFix.during` ("during a drain", "while the GitHub budget was low", "while claude was paused"), with
  `why` in the `fix.dropped` event's data. The `KVPRFixHeld` comment and `fix_held.go`'s header describe
  every hold, and `fixJob.started`'s comment names its reader, `dropFixerAnswered`.

- **The webhooks consumer bounds what it takes from the relay, and a sleep or a backlog is no miss**
  (2026-10-21, spec 103). The security lens of an improvement run read spec 99's consumer: the client
  took a page of any length up to execx's output bound (8 MiB) and an event naming any number of PRs,
  the engine kept hints for an hour and last events for a day with no cap on their number, and `next`,
  `high_water` and the epoch reached kv (`webhooks.cursor`) and an event's data at any length. A
  compromised or broken relay, or the proxy that terminates its TLS, could grow the daemon's memory
  without bound and write junk to the registry; shadow mode decides nothing from it, phase 2 will. A
  code-health analyst then reproduced a false miss with a scratch test: a push made while the Mac
  sleeps reaches the relay during the sleep, the page after the wake lists it as a backlog that hints at
  nothing (and did not record it as the PR's last event), and when that page came before the poll the
  stream was healthy, so the poll counted the push as missed with "no event for it in the last 24h".
  The Mac sleeps nightly, so every morning added false misses to the numbers that decide phase 2.
  - **The page.** The client (`internal/webhooks`) refuses a page that lists more events than it asked
    for (the limit, at most 500, or the relay's default of 200), or whose epoch, `next`, `high_water`
    or `oldest` is over 100 bytes or holds a character other than letters, digits and `._:-` (what
    `safe` keeps of a value a message quotes; `ValidCursor`): a malformed answer, refused whole, its
    error naming the count or the field and never the value, so the stream turns unhealthy with the
    cause, said once while it lasts, and the cursor stays the last good one. It cuts an event's PR
    numbers at 100, the relay's own cut (unexported there; a test pins it against `relay.Envelope`).
  - **Memory.** The engine keeps at most 10,000 hints and 10,000 last events (the PRs and heads a missed
    change's event names), letting the oldest go first: the hints in the order they were read, the last
    events by the order they were last read, cut after each page. What goes is counted in the hour's
    totals (`hints_dropped`, `last_events_dropped`, omitted while zero, so `webhooks.hours` keeps its
    format) and `magnum status --json` sums them under `webhooks`; the line stays as it was. The
    delivery ids were already a ring of 10,000.
  - **The kept cursor.** A cursor in kv that the client would refuse (an earlier build kept it from a
    page it took) is dropped at the start: the relay answers such a cursor 400, which would hold the
    stream unhealthy for good, and the first flush would write it again.
  - **A sleep or a backlog holds the comparison, like a gap.** The first poll of each repository after
    a sleep of the Mac (the tick's `afterSleep`; every repository compared before the last tick ended
    before the sleep) compares nothing, and so does a repository's next poll after a page that listed a
    backlog of its events (received more than 5 minutes before the page, by the relay's clock: a sleep,
    an outage of the network, a restart of the daemon). A backlog event still hints at nothing, but it
    is now the last event read for what it names. Each hold closes one gap the other leaves: the sleep's
    covers a poll that comes before the page while `stale_after` is longer than the sleep, and the
    backlog's an outage without a sleep and a restart. The holds count nothing and say nothing: the
    health line is unchanged.
  - **Residual.** The bounds count entries, not bytes: a head SHA or a delivery id kilobytes long still
    fits a page's 8 MiB, so 10,000 such hints or ids hold more memory than real ones (the relay's
    contract keeps both short: 40 hex, a GUID). A held poll also leaves uncounted a real miss in the same
    repository.
  - **Rejected:**
    - Trusting the relay's own limits (100 PRs an event, 500 events a page, 100-byte cursors): the relay
      and the proxy in front of it are not magnum's, and neither is what a broken build of the relay
      sends.
    - Cutting a page over its limit to the events asked for: its `next` cursor is past the events cut,
      which would be lost unread; refusing the page keeps the cursor and says why.
    - Holding on a sleep alone or on a backlog alone: each leaves one order or cause a false miss (above).
    - Timing a backlog event as a hint after a sleep: an event hours old would announce a change it did
      not see, and a hint must come within the window of the poll that sees the change.

- **A failed rake task's reason is the line after "aborted!"** (2026-10-21, spec 105; amends "Verification
  readiness runs before the reviewers"). Since 2026-10-19 17:32Z, 11 talkable rounds' readiness failed all
  three `reset_db` commands (exit 1 within about 6 s) in three pool slots, and each check recorded rake's
  trailer as its last line, "(See full trace by running task with --trace)" or "Tasks: TOP =>
  db:schema:load": the cause, on the line after "rake aborted!", was lost, so neither the readiness file the
  judge reads, the `round.readiness` event nor the machine lines of `magnum status` (the judges' reports)
  said why the schema did not load. `lastLine` now skips that trailer for a failed command and, when the
  output holds a line ending in "aborted!", takes the first non-empty line after the last such line
  (redacted, one line, 200 runes, as before), else the last line that is not the trailer; a passing
  command keeps its last line. The `round.readiness` event adds a failed `reset_db`'s cause in parentheses
  ("reset_db `…`: exit 1 (ActiveRecord::NoDatabaseError: …)"): the pool's own command, whose errors already
  reach the slot's last error and the release's events; prepare and ready output stays in the readiness
  file, and the judge's prompt list still carries the status and magnum's reason only. New test
  TestAFailedRakeCommandsReasonIsTheLineAfterAborted. Rejected: the whole stderr (a backtrace in the file
  and the event).

- **A slot whose schema reset fails in two rounds in a row is broken at its release** (2026-10-21, spec
  105; amends "A slot reloads its databases only when the checkout needs another schema"). The 11 rounds
  above ran in review4 and review13 (since 10-19) and review10 (since 10-20 08:16Z): the release keeps a
  slot's databases (since 10-06), so its "schema reset failed twice → broken" path never ran, readiness
  never escalated, and each later round in the slot failed the same reset, said "the schema its databases
  carry is unknown", and had its judge work around it ("focused DB specs ran successfully") with no word to
  the operator; `magnum status` showed review4 and review13 held with `dirty_schema`. Now the readiness step
  tells the engine when a `reset_db` command failed or ran out of its budget (`ReadinessPlan.ResetFailed`,
  with the first such command's cause; a reset the round's cancel stopped counts nothing), and
  `slots.Manager.ResetFailed` counts the slot's rounds in a row in kv `slot.<id>.reset_failures` (the count
  and the last cause; no migration). A reset that passes clears it (a round's `RecordSchema`, the release's
  reload, `magnum open`'s `EnsureSchema`), as do a repair or an adoption (`reviveSlot`) and a removal. Each
  failure is a `slot.schema_reset_failed` event (a warning from the second on), and the second toasts once:
  "slot review4: the schema reset failed in two rounds (<cause>); it breaks at its release, then `magnum
  slots repair review4`" (a held slot cannot be repaired). The round that found it finishes (its other
  checks ran, its judge is told as before); the slot's next release breaks it in its `schema_check` step
  before any reload (`slots.BreakAfterResetFailures`, 2), from releasing or `dirty_schema` (held, for
  `ReleaseHeld`'s hold) to broken as the release's own break does (`breakSchema`, which both now share),
  with "<slot> schema reset failed in two rounds: <cause>" as its last error and an unpinned slot's PR let
  go; `magnum slots repair` takes it and starts the count again. New tests
  TestASlotWhoseSchemaResetFailsInTwoRoundsIsBrokenForRepair, TestAFailedSchemaResetTellsTheEngineItsCause
  and TestTheSecondRoundWhoseSchemaResetFailsToastsTheRepair. Two rounds, because one failure can be the
  PR's own schema (a migration that does not load), while a second in a row in the same slot, over pushes
  or PRs, points at the slot. Residual: a slot its PR keeps (no eviction, no close) is not released, so its
  rounds keep failing until the PR lets it go or the operator releases it, which the toast says. Rejected:
  an automatic drop-and-recreate of the databases at release (what the keep rule avoids: minutes of MySQL
  writes per release, and a cause outside the databases would fail again), and breaking the slot at the
  first failure (a PR whose own schema does not load would break a healthy slot).

- **A HEAD that is the PR's pushed head is no drift** (2026-10-21, spec 105). On
  talkable/talkable-integration#867 (10-17, requests 323 to 327) a fix ended "needs your call", the operator
  went on in the pane and pushed 3e8c5b6, and the next round's setup failed with "held: head_drift: HEAD is
  3e8c5b6" though 3e8c5b6 was already the PR's head on GitHub: two forced reviews, two releases and an
  unpin, 41 minutes. The guard (`guardHead`) now takes a HEAD that moved off `checked_out_sha` as the
  checkout Magnum expects when it is the PR row's head (what the poll read from GitHub), the tree has no
  changes (untracked files only for a removal's guard, never the rendered local mise file) and none of its
  commits is off the remotes and `refs/magnum/*` (`git rev-list --count HEAD --not --remotes`): it records
  it as `checked_out_sha` with a `slot.head_recorded` event instead of the hold. Any other moved HEAD
  (another commit, a dirty tree, an unpushed commit) holds as before. New test
  TestAHeadThatIsThePRsPushedHeadIsNoDrift. Rejected: asking GitHub for the head at guard time (a read per
  guard, while the PR row is what the round reviews), and taking any pushed HEAD (a person's other branch is
  still theirs).

- **Auto-approval reads nothing while its GitHub budget is spent** (2026-10-21, spec 106; amends spec 97's
  floor). A read of auto-approval that failed kept no fingerprint (`autoSeen`, `autoFollow`), so the next
  tick read again: from 10-19 to 10-21 GitHub refused 127 of them for its rate limit (96 reads of a PR's
  reviews, 31 of a base tip's checks), 15 after the floor went live. Now the pass reads nothing as an
  identity below `[github] budget_floor` (`githubLow`: the identity it approves as for the reviews, the
  watch's poll identity for a base tip's checks) or while the poll is paused for GitHub's rate limit
  (`KVGHPollPausedUntil`, read once per pass), and a read GitHub refused with `github.ErrRateLimited`
  waits for the identity's reset (the meter's, which spec 101's refusal set, else 5 minutes): by PR beside
  the fingerprints (`autoRetry`), by tip for the checks (`baseTipRead.retry`, kept until the later of the
  reset and the ten minutes). A hold is logged once (`auto approval: no GitHub reads until the budget
  recovers`, by identity and its end), a refusal once with when it is read again. A held read refuses
  nothing new: the PR is decided at the first pass after the reset, and the card's CI refusal of a base
  read held is the one a failed read gave. The withdrawal of a standing approval and a post are writes and
  are not held. New tests TestAutoApprovalReadsNothingWhileTheBudgetIsExhausted,
  TestAutoApprovalWaitsForTheGitHubFloorAndThePollsPause, TestAStandingApprovalIsFollowedOnlyOnceTheBudgetRecovers
  and TestARefusedReadOfTheBaseTipsChecksWaitsForTheReset. Rejected: a retry time per identity (a refusal
  marks the identity spent through the meter already, which holds every PR's reads while the floor is on;
  with it off, one read per PR and reset is the cost).

- **A Codex turn that "failed to load workspace requirements" is an overload** (2026-10-21, spec 106). On
  10-19 at 15:24Z the judge's turn on a PR and its nudge ended at once with that error (the rollout's
  `task_complete`, `codex_error_info` "other"), no health pattern matched, and the PR went to needs
  attention; it was forced 22.5 hours later and merged unreviewed 8 minutes after. Four such turns on
  10-14 fell within two minutes: a passing fault. The default `overloaded` patterns (every kind starts from
  them) gain `\bfailed to load workspace requirements\b`, so the round takes the overload path and
  continues. Fixture "codex workspace requirements" in TestClassifyFixtures.

- **A plain `magnum resume` names the agent kinds it leaves paused, and a refusal for a paused kind names
  the command that lifts it** (2026-10-21, spec 106). On 10-20 at 07:25Z `magnum fix` was refused twice
  ("claude paused (usage_limit) until 14:00"), a bare `magnum resume` between the two answered "resumed",
  though it lifts only the daemon's pause, and `--tool claude` came 13 minutes later. Now the plain
  resume's answer adds, for each kind still paused, "; claude is still paused (usage_limit) until 14:00:
  `magnum resume --tool claude` lifts it", and `pausedKind` (with `kindPauseReason`, which `magnum fix`,
  `magnum whiteboard`, `magnum review`'s waiting note, the retro, curation, the skill editor and the gate
  use) ends its reason with "; `magnum resume --tool claude` lifts it". A round's dispatch gate takes the
  reason without it (`kindPause`), since its wait sentence already ends with "`magnum resume --tool …`
  lifts the pause". The settings screen, which adds "still paused: …" to a plain resume's answer, leaves
  out a kind the answer names. New tests TestABareResumeNamesTheToolsStillPaused and
  TestSettingsPlainResumeDoesNotNameAKindTheAnswerNames; TestPauseByKindOmp checks the command. Residual:
  the CLI's offline resume (no daemon) answers as before.

- **A refused config restart says what restarts on the fixed file** (2026-10-21, spec 106; amends "The
  settings screen edits config.toml in place, …, and the daemon restarts on a saved config when idle"). A refusal drops the saved config's mark, but its event
  said "the restart goes on once it loads": with no new build and no skill version waiting, nothing checks
  a file fixed by hand again, and the daemon runs on. The event now says so when only the saved config
  waited: "fix the file (`magnum config` shows why), then `magnum daemon-restart --when-idle` restarts the
  daemon on it, or save it again from the settings screen"; with a build or a skill version waiting it
  keeps "the restart goes on once it loads", which stays true. `settings.RequestRestart`'s comment no
  longer claims a load check it does not make (the daemon's `restartSafe` makes it). The refusal tests
  check both texts.

- **No approval hold in a repository that cannot approve** (2026-10-21, spec 106; amends "An approval rests
  on a whole-PR read"). On one repository whose identity's `no_findings_event` is `COMMENT`, with no
  `[[repo]]` override and no `auto_approve` for it, round 7 posted "No new problems since …. LGTM" with the
  line "A full pass of the whole PR follows before approval.", and round 8, on the same head, was that full
  pass: 24 minutes, three reviewers and two judge passes, a comment with the same body. 6 of the 24
  `round.approval_hold` events since 10-15 were in such repositories. `approvalHoldDue` now holds only
  where a clean review can lead to an approval (`approvalPath`): the judge's no-findings event there is
  `APPROVE` (`pipeline.JudgeEvents`: the `[[repo]]` override, else the posting identity's, `COMMENT` for an
  author the auto-approval lists refuse) or `AutoApproveFor` names an identity. Elsewhere the clean
  re-review posts its comment without the false line and no full pass follows; `full_pass_every` and the
  other full-pass rules still apply. New test TestNoApprovalHoldInARepoThatCannotApprove; the hold tests'
  harness gives the App `no_findings_event = "APPROVE"`.

- **The review skill loses 489 bytes that the code or a prompt already says, may never pass 40,000 bytes,
  and every prompt that links a skill says to read it by itself** (2026-10-21, spec 107). Evidence, from
  102 Codex judge sessions of 2026-10-18 to 10-21: every live judge read `skills/magnum-review/SKILL.md`
  in its first turn (9,068 tokens, 4.9% of the judges' input; the first request's median of 19.5K input
  tokens became 28.6K after the read), and 14 sessions read it 18 more times after a compaction. Codex
  returns at most 10,000 tokens of one tool call's output and drops the middle of a longer one ("original
  token count: 11997 … 1997 tokens truncated"): 5 of 101 judges read the skill in one call with another
  file, lost sections 5 and 6 (the comment form and the re-review mode) and read the gap again with `sed`.
  - The ceiling: at about 4.15 bytes a token (37,676 bytes were 9,068 tokens), a skill of about 40,000
    bytes is the most one call returns whole, with room for a denser text, and only when the call reads
    the skill alone. `TestSkillStaysTight` now also refuses a skill, or a `skillMaxBytes`, over
    `skillCeilingBytes` (40,000), naming Codex's cap and the sections it drops; `skillMaxBytes` stays the
    working cap, which a rule raises, and the ceiling is the bound no raise passes.
  - The read: the initial, rereview, recovery, continue and own-pass judge prompts and `fix.md` (the fix
    skill is 20,763 bytes, and a kind is data: a fixer may run on Codex) say "Read <path> first, by itself,
    unless this session already read that file, …"; `TestJudgePromptsReadTheSkillFirstByItselfAndLoadNoOther`
    and the fix prompt's test pin it.
  - The cuts, from 37,676 bytes to 37,187 (the cap follows; no pin touched), each checked against what
    enforces it: section 0's `readiness` line (117 bytes; the paragraph under the list says what to do with
    the field); the own pass of a full pass, now "With `full_pass: true`, the prompt says what to read."
    (111; only a scheduled full pass sets it, `in.FullPass && in.Kind == KindRecovery` in
    `internal/pipeline/judge.go`, and its own-pass prompt names the full diff, no earlier review, thread or
    reply, and the threads decided in the next prompt); "(do the pass now if missing)" (29; each candidates
    prompt says so when `OwnFindingsMissing`); section 5's local-path line (118; post-review refuses a body
    that names a local path, "name files by their repository path and describe output instead"); section
    1's HEAD check (114; the slot verifies HEAD when it checks the PR out, and `checkTree` restores it after
    each stage, `internal/pipeline/checkout.go`; no judge result of 528 reported a mismatch). The freed
    bytes are for the review rules the operator approves next.
  - Rules applied: `.claude/skills/magnum-improve/rules.txt`'s count-query line read the skill's own
    wording and counted 0, while 4 posted reviews (and own passes in other report directories) wrote the
    query as `SELECT COUNT`, a "Read-only count", "Read-only precondition" or "Count matching
    configurations"; its pattern now takes those phrases, and the line lost its "skill wording". Five lines
    count the fixed phrases of rules approved since: `This is the author's call`, `This PR introduced it:
    on`, `Description: ✗`, `(confirmed: ` and `not run on the review machine`. Over the window from
    2026-10-17T15:15Z (126 report directories, 107 posted reviews) they read 4, 13, 21, 22, 2 and 0.
  - **Rejected:** the optional cut of "Never commit, push, label, merge or edit the PR." (49 bytes): the
    pipeline restores the checkout after a stage, but nothing undoes a label, a merge or an edit on GitHub.

- **The backstop of a delivery the relay missed is the poll, not the App's deliveries log** (2026-10-21,
  spec 109; amends "Webhooks reach magnum through a relay of its own, `magnum-relay`"). The deploy guide said
  that when the journal refuses a write the relay answers 503, "GitHub shows the failed delivery, and the
  daemon's backstop reads it from the App's deliveries log". No code reads that log: spec 99's entry calls
  it a candidate for a later phase (it lists no PR number and spends the App's REST budget per payload
  read), and the guide's own Compose rotation says the poll finds the changes. The guide now says the
  daemon's poll finds the change; `[webhooks]` is in shadow mode, so every change still comes from the poll.
  The earlier entries keep their words: read their "backstop" as the poll until a phase reads the log.

- **The settings screen's help fits its box, names F5, and a line keeps one "was" note** (2026-10-21, spec
  109). The help box is at most 90 cells wide at any screen width, and its `a / x` and `/` entries (90 and
  80 cells of text) ended in "…" at every width; both are shorter now, with a test that no help line is
  cut at 90, 120 and 160 columns. `F5` was bound beside `ctrl+r` and in neither the help nor the README;
  both name it. Each save put its dated note in front of the line's old comment, so a setting saved three
  times read `# 2026-10-23: was "low"; 2026-10-22: was "medium"; 2026-10-21: was "high"; <the reason>`.
  `confedit.withNote` now drops the leading "was" notes of earlier saves (`dropWasNotes`) and puts the new
  one first; the line keeps the newest note and the rest of its comment. A note counts as a save's own
  only when it has the forms the screen writes, up to the next `; ` outside double quotes: `was the
  default`, `was <one TOML value>` and `was <cell> <value or unset>, …` for a level table's cells. A
  comment of the user's that only begins alike (`2026-10-02: was 3, raised after the queue grew`, or
  `2026-10-14: medium -> high`) stays. Residual: a user's dated comment that is nothing but `was <value>`
  is taken for a save's note and replaced. New tests TestANoteReplacesTheEarlierWasNotesOfItsLine,
  TestASecondSaveKeepsTheNewestWasNoteOnly and TestSettingsHelpLinesFitTheirBox. **Rejected:** a marker
  in the note to tell a save's from the user's (it would change a format the README and the saved files
  show).

- **The review skill takes the wording the operator approved on 2026-10-21 and drops three sentences a
  prompt or post-review already says** (2026-10-21, spec 110; the operator approved each item as written in
  the improvement run's batched question, "do as recommended"). Every item changes what PR authors see.
  SKILL.md goes from 37,187 to 37,412 bytes (538 added, 313 cut), and `skillMaxBytes` with it.
  - Cut, each read in place against what enforces it, its pin moved: section 8's "A thread another
    reviewer or the author started is theirs, never answered inline; a reply round with nothing of yours to
    answer ends `replied` with no replies, never `blocked`." (177 bytes; post-review skips a reply in a
    thread its login did not start, `planReplies` in `internal/postreview/replies.go`, and both reply-round
    prompts, `judge-rereview.md` and `judge-recovery.md`, the only rounds that answer without a review,
    carry the sentence verbatim; TestReplyRoundPromptsLeaveOthersThreadsAndEndAnEmptyRoundReplied, renamed,
    checks them and that the skill no longer says it); section 6's gloss of a reply's `class`, now
    "`class` (`fixed`, `not a bug`, `won't fix` or `other`) is a hint." (85; the three prompts that name
    the threads file, the re-review, the recovery and a re-review's own pass, say "Each reply's `class` is
    what its first clause claims: a claim to check, not a verdict.", which
    TestJudgePromptsSayTheReplyClassComesFromTheFirstClause and TestSkillDecidesAReplyByWhatItDoes now
    check); and section 7's "(its database runs take their turn under the lock)" (51; it tells the judge
    nothing to do). The prepass and evidence lines of section 0 stay, as the operator keeps them.
  - A decline that calls a case too rare goes into the notes (section 6, 136 bytes). On talkable#11932 the
    judge posted on 10-16 a P3 that status recovery omits account admins without site roles and wrote only
    a probe recipe into the notes; the author declined it as too rare (net −1). On 10-20, after four
    lifecycle probes, the judge posted its sibling as a P2 "(missed earlier)", and the author answered that
    this edge case was already decided against. After "A reply that states a standing decision of the
    repository goes into the notes (section 2)." the skill now says "So does a decline that calls an actor
    or precondition too rare to support: note what it accepts beside any probe line you wrote for it."
    ("So does" where the approved text read "So is", to agree with "goes into the notes".)
  - A record found by name or slug may not be the feature's own (section 2, 50 bytes). On a site
    repository a person found that a page setup script retemplates any existing page whose slug matches a
    tool's; magnum's review missed it, and the Fix of a finding it posted (look the page up by name only)
    widened the lookup. The structure paragraph's clause is now "a delete, reuse or rewrite of records
    thought unsaved, free or the feature's own (uploads, drafts, unowned rows, a page found by slug)". The
    local eval case `setup-script-takes-over-page-by-slug` measures it; the orchestrator runs the replays.
  - "This is the author's call." only when the options differ for a user (section 5, 62 bytes, less 28).
    13 of 78 findings posted since spec 90 carry the sentence, and at least 4 offer options that change
    nothing a user gets: an own size budget or a recalibrated shared one (talkable#12067's P1), staged
    consumers or a drain (talkable#12061, #12069), a query or a payload change (talkable#12058); each sent
    the fix loop to Needs you. Spec 90's second case now reads "or two plausible fixes differ in what users
    or callers see (never only in rollout, staging or code structure)"; its first case (a fix that restores
    what the PR or a merged related PR removed) and the fixed phrase `This is the author's call.`, which the
    fix skill matches and the local eval case `series-direction-fix-is-a-choice` scores, are unchanged.
    Folding section 5's one-item list ("Reproductions travel with the finding:" over a single bullet) into
    its sentence, "Put the reproduction into the comment as a fenced block …", won 28 bytes back without
    changing a rule.
  - The review body's shape (sections 3, 5 and 7, 72 bytes). Of 154 inline findings posted from 10-17 to
    10-21, 12 titles were instructions ("Pin…", "Collect…", all six of talkable#12069's first round), whose
    body bullets then differed from the inline titles; another reviewer's confirmed finding was marked in
    three forms (a bare URL, `[confirmed](<url>)`, `[existing thread](<url>)`); and two bodies carried a
    collapsed block the body's list does not name (earlier thread decisions before the Checks, a
    reproduction after them). The comment form's title now "states the wrong result, never an instruction"
    (22; the approved line called a title a noun phrase, but the skill's own example title, "Old Reject
    error appears in a new chat", is a clause, so the rule keeps "states the wrong result" and adds what it
    must never be); the marker is "exactly `- P1: <title> (confirmed: <link>)` with a bare URL" (24; the
    form `.claude/skills/magnum-improve/rules.txt` counts); and section 7 adds "No other collapsed block"
    after "nothing after it" (26). Each sentence is short, so each went into the skill, not a prompt. The
    next run measures imperative titles under 3%, one marker form and no unlisted blocks.
  - A probe's package commands run in a scratch package (section 2's databases paragraph, 246 bytes). On an
    infrastructure PR (10-18) an own pass ran an npm install in an empty scratch directory; npm walked up,
    took the home directory for the project and removed 421 packages from its `node_modules` (the
    round.environment line said so), and nothing told the operator. The skill now says "An npm, pnpm or
    yarn install or test for a probe runs in a scratch package (a `package.json` in the directory of
    `result_file`, or `--prefix <that directory>`), never in a directory without one: npm walks up to the
    home directory and changes it."
  - Tests, failing first: the moved pins above, and TestSkillLeavesOnlyAChoiceUsersOrCallersSeeToTheAuthor,
    TestSkillChecksThatARecordFoundBySlugIsTheFeaturesOwn, TestSkillNotesADeclineThatCallsACaseTooRare,
    TestSkillKeepsTheReviewBodysShape and TestSkillRunsAProbesPackageCommandsInAScratchPackage; the pins
    file follows. No prompt changed, so no golden did; the README's "What an author gets" and
    prompts/README.md's reply-round row say the same.

- **The fix skill keeps secrets out of replies** (2026-10-21, spec 110, approved by the operator the same
  day). The fix loop answers other reviewers' threads and comments as the PR's author, bots' included
  (`internal/engine/fix_external.go` trusts `github.IsBot` before the association check), and section 6 of
  the fix skill, where replies are written, had no rule that kept a secret, an environment value or a file
  from outside the checkout out of a reply. It now says "A reply never carries a secret, a token, an
  environment value or a file from outside the checkout." (99 bytes; the fix skill has no size cap and is
  20,862 bytes). New test TestTheFixSkillKeepsSecretsOutOfReplies. **Parked:** an allowlist of the bots
  whose items the fixer answers (the analyst's proposal), not this change.

- **A routine CLI update is recorded at info, without a toast; a change of a CLI mise pins still warns**
  (2026-10-21, spec 115, amending "The daemon records each agent CLI's version and names a launch failure
  shared across PRs", spec 75). From 10-18 to 10-21 the daemon recorded four `kind.version_changed`
  warnings, each with a toast, all Claude Code's daily auto-update (2.1.302 to 2.1.306), and no launch
  failure followed any of them. Codex is pinned by mise (0.162.1, since 0.163.0 broke the judge panes), so a
  change of its version is unexpected; Claude is not, so its changes are routine. Now, when a version
  changes, `cliPin` asks mise once (`mise ls --current --json`, through the runner with the version read's
  15-second timeout; mise is the shim's own binary when the kind's command is one, else the one on the
  daemon's PATH): the tool listed under the kind's name, else the one whose install directory holds the
  binary the kind's command runs (a tool named `npm:@openai/codex`), pins the CLI when the version its
  config requests is the very version mise resolves it to, a leading v aside (`codex = "0.162.1"`). A
  pinned kind's change keeps the warning and the toast, both naming the pin ("mise pins it to 0.162.1",
  the event with the config file and data `pin`, `pin_source`); any other change, a tool mise does not
  list or one it requests as `latest`, `lts` or a prefix, is `kind.version_changed` at info, with no toast.
  A mise that cannot answer (an error, its timeout, output that is not the listing) counts as no pin,
  logged once per cause. The registry's record is the same for both, so `magnum status`'s `clis:` line,
  a parked launch's "; the codex CLI changed at 11:24" (`cliChangeNote`) and a shared failure's line
  (`sayShared`) still name any change of the day. Residual: the 10-16 case itself, mise's `codex =
  "latest"` installing a broken version, is now a routine change with no toast until launches fail, when
  the attention line and the shared failure name it; and mise is asked from the daemon's working directory,
  so a pin only a repository's own mise.toml makes is not seen (the agents start in the slots' checkouts).
  New tests TestARoutineCLIUpdateRecordsInfoAndNoToast (not in mise's config, and requested as latest:
  info, no toast, the parked launch's note and the shared failure still naming the update) and
  TestAChangeOfAPinnedCLIStillWarnsAndToasts (by the kind's name with a binary the pin does not explain,
  and by the install directory with the pin moved: a warning and a toast naming the pin, mise asked once);
  TestACLIVersionChangeIsRecordedOnceAndToasted pins codex. **Rejected:** reading the pin from the
  checkout's mise.toml (the operator's pin is in mise's global config); asking mise at every health check
  (a change is rare, and the answer matters only then); a prefix such as `2.1` as a pin (it moves with each
  install); and a warning when mise cannot answer (each Claude update would toast again whenever mise
  fails, the noise this removes).

- **magnum-relay keeps only the installations `MAGNUM_RELAY_INSTALLATIONS` lists** (2026-10-21, spec 113;
  amends "Webhooks reach magnum through a relay of its own, `magnum-relay`", whose Rejected list holds
  "Dropping `check_run` actions or other installations at the relay"). New evidence: the App is public
  (an unauthenticated GET of the App answers 200), so anyone may install it, and GitHub signs that
  installation's deliveries with the App's secret. The relay kept them for 30 days: the journal's first
  500 rows were 498 of one installation, 1 of another and a ping. The daemon still filters by
  installation and repository, but a stranger's traffic no longer fills the journal, the disk and the
  pages.
  - With the variable set, a signed delivery of an installation it does not list answers 202
    `{"status":"ignored"}` and stores nothing, as does one that names no installation. It is counted in
    the minute's `webhook ignored` line. The installation is the payload's `installation.id`, which the
    envelope already read.
  - The App's `ping` names none and is still stored: only the App's owner sends it, by saving the
    webhook, and the guide checks with it. Any other delivery without an installation is ignored, since
    `github_app_authorization` reaches every App and any user who authorized it can cause one.
  - Empty keeps every installation's deliveries, as before, and `serve` logs a warning at start.
  - **Rejected:** a 4xx (GitHub would list a failed delivery to redeliver); `{"ignored":true}` (the
    other answers say `status`); the `X-GitHub-Hook-Installation-Target-ID` header (on an App's hook it
    names the App, where the hook was made).
  - **Open, the operator's decision, not changed here:** whether the relay's domain stays behind the
    Cloudflare proxy, which terminates TLS and so reads the bearer token, the deliveries and the pages.

- **`/healthz` tells anyone only whether the relay is up; the counters need the token** (2026-10-21, spec
  113; amends the relay entry's "`/healthz`. It has no auth and carries no event data"). The epoch (the
  first half of every cursor), the events kept and when the newest arrived told anyone how busy the
  operator's repositories are. Without an `Authorization` header, or with a token the listing would
  refuse, it answers `{"ok":true}`, or 503 `{"ok":false}` when the journal does not answer. An accepted
  bearer token adds the counters. A wrong token is not answered 401, so a checker with a stale token
  still sees the relay up; it is counted in the minute's `health counters refused` line. The image's
  `HEALTHCHECK` sends no token and reads only `ok`, and the daemon does not read `/healthz`, so its status
  line is unchanged.

- **A health check whose caller hung up no longer fails the checks after it** (2026-10-21, spec 113).
  `refreshHealth` read the journal under the request's context. A check whose caller had gone by then
  stored a failed snapshot, so the checks of the next 2 s answered 503 and each logged `health check
  failed`: a monitor with a short timeout could turn the container unhealthy. The read now runs under
  `context.WithoutCancel` within `healthTimeout`, as the insert outlives a client that hung up. New test
  TestAHungUpHealthCheckDoesNotFailTheNextOne, the analyst's reproduction.

- **The webhook's body buffer grows with the body, not with its Content-Length** (2026-10-21, spec 113).
  `readBody` grew its buffer to the Content-Length, up to 26 MiB, before any of the body came and before
  the signature was checked. Four senders holding the four turns reserved about 104 MiB with headers
  alone. The first reservation is now at most 1 MiB (`firstBodyBuffer`), and the buffer grows as the body
  arrives. A real 25 MB payload still reads whole, with a few copies while it grows. New test
  TestTheBodyBufferGrowsWithTheBodyNotTheContentLength.

- **Refusals are logged as one line a kind a minute, and the container's log is capped** (2026-10-21,
  spec 113). Every request refused before it was authenticated logged its own line, and `compose.yaml`
  set no log limit, so a flood of forged requests could fill the server's disk.
  - Such a refusal, a delivery of another installation and a wrong token on `/healthz` are now counted
    by message, status and class. These are all the relay's own constants, so the kinds stay few.
  - `RunRefusalLog`, which `serve` runs every minute and once more at shutdown, logs one line a kind with
    its `count`. A signed delivery that is not JSON still logs its own line, with its delivery id.
  - `compose.yaml` sets the `json-file` driver to `max-size: 10m` and `max-file: "3"`. The guide gives the
    same for the application built from the Dockerfile: the platform's log setting, else Docker's
    defaults in `daemon.json`.
  - Residual: net/http's own error log (a query holding a semicolon) still writes a line a request; the
    cap bounds it.

- **A test holds the consumer's copy of the relay's types to what the relay serves** (2026-10-21, spec
  113). `internal/webhooks` copies the relay's `Event`, `Page`, `Check` and token bounds, since only its
  tests may import the relay. TestTheConsumerDecodesWhatTheRelayServes stores a pull request's and a check
  run's deliveries in a real relay over a temporary journal, lists them with the token and decodes the
  page with `parsePage`. Every field of the relay's types must be in the consumer's, under the same JSON
  tag and with the same value, and the consumer's page must encode back to the relay's JSON. `MinToken`
  and `MaxToken` must equal the relay's. The two deliveries give every event field a value, which the test
  checks, so a renamed tag cannot hide behind a zero.

- **The automatic approval trusts no workflow the PR adds or edits, keys check runs by workflow file, and
  never lets a status stand for a check run** (2026-10-21, spec 112, a security fix the operator approved;
  amends "The approval's CI gate counts only the checks required_checks names"). The hole: since spec 84
  the CI gate decides by the checks `required_checks` names, and the head's checks were kept one run per
  workflow name and check name, the newest (`rollupContextsJSON.checks` in internal/github, and the gate's
  own count in `requiredCIOf`). talkable/talkable sets `required_checks = ["workflow:CI"]`, auto-approves
  as the operator's login, and GitHub enforces no checks there. So a PR that added a workflow file
  declaring `name: CI` with jobs named like the real ones, which pass after the real ones fail, replaced
  each failed run; a PR that edited the CI workflow controlled it outright; and for a name-glob entry a
  commit status anyone who can write to the repository posts replaced a same-named check run
  (`store.RequiredRuns` took the newest run of each name, a status included).
  - The changed-files gate (`changedFilesRefusal`, internal/engine/autoapprove_gates.go, which now holds
    the agents' files check too and reads the file list once): a head whose file list names any path
    under `.github/workflows/` or `.github/actions/` (at the root, in any case) is refused with "the PR
    changes its own workflows or actions: approve by hand", and a list Magnum has none of for the head, or
    one GitHub cut at 100, with "Magnum cannot tell whether it changes the review agents' instructions or
    hooks, or its own workflows or actions: …". The list is pr_files, which the poller reads with the
    Details: the spec named the round's changed paths too, but a round keeps none (`gitx.ChangedPaths`
    runs inside the round, in the slot, and its result goes only into docs.json, cut at 400), so pr_files
    is the one the gate has when it decides, without a GitHub call. A clean review of a new head that
