    changes a workflow withdraws a standing approval, as any gate does; the operator's `A` is not held.
  - Check runs are keyed by the workflow's file: Details and CommitChecks read `workflow { name
    resourcePath }` (a field of an object read already; GitHub prices connections, not fields), and
    `github.Check.WorkflowFile` is the resourcePath's rest after `/actions/workflows/` ("ci.yml"; a
    read-only query on a public repository on 2026-10-21 answered `/cli/cli/actions/workflows/go.yml` for
    `.github/workflows/go.yml`; `WorkflowRun.file.path` names the full path too, but is a nullable object
    of its own). A commit status is `Status`, kept apart from every check run. `store.CheckResult` gains
    `workflow_file` and `status`, `store.CIStatus` `by_workflow_file`, and `CheckResult.Key` is the check a
    run belongs to (a check run's file, else its workflow's name, and name; a status's context): GitHub's
    dedupe, the gate's count and the base tip's comparison (`failsLikeTheBase`, so a failure of the PR's
    own `CI` no longer passes for the base tip's failure of the base's) all use it. prs.ci_json is JSON,
    so no migration: checks an earlier build stored (`by_workflow_file` unset) are read again by the next
    poll (`fetchDetails`), and until then `requiredCIOf` does not decide and the rollup, which counts every
    check, does.
  - The rule for `workflow:<glob>`: the entry names every check of each workflow whose file name or
    declared name the glob matches. The spec's "the file the base's workflow of that name lives in",
    without reading the base: the CI gate decides only on a head whose whole file list changes no workflow
    (the changed-files gate refuses the rest first, in `autoGateRefusal`'s order, and the standing gate
    and the approval's ignored-checks note run after it), so every workflow file on the head, and the name
    it declares, is the base's as of the merge base. A workflow of the base's name in another file is one
    more workflow the entry names: its runs count beside the base's, never in their place, so the gate is
    stricter for it, not looser.
  - A name glob counts the latest check run of each matching name across workflows (spec 84's choice: a
    check posted through the API lands in another workflow's suite, next to an older run) and, apart, the
    latest commit status of that name.
  - Residuals: under a name glob a run of a workflow the PR adds can still stand for a run of that name
    (the changed-files gate holds such a PR); an action elsewhere that a workflow runs (`uses:
    ./tools/setup`), or a script the CI runs, is the PR's code, which the review reads; a check run an app
    with checks:write posts into a workflow's suite is not told from the workflow's own.
  - New tests, each failing first: in engine TestAPRThatChangesItsWorkflowsIsNotAutoApproved (added,
    edited, a local action, another case, a cut list; a nested `.github` and look-alike directories
    approve; `A` approves the held ones), TestAStandingApprovalIsWithdrawnWhenTheNewHeadChangesAWorkflow,
    TestASameNamedWorkflowAddedByThePRDoesNotPassTheGate (either order of the runs, and the PR's own `CI`
    failing like the base tip's), TestAStatusNeverReplacesACheckRun and
    TestChecksAnEarlierBuildStoredAreReadAgain; in github TestChecksAreKeyedByWorkflowFileWithStatusesApart
    (and the fixtures' resourcePath); in store TestARequiredWorkflowEntryNamesItsFileOrItsDeclaredName,
    TestARequiredNameCountsAStatusApartFromTheCheckRun and
    TestChecksKeyedByWorkflowFileReplaceAnEarlierBuildsRead.
  - **Rejected:** trusting the workflow's name (spec 84's keying: any file may declare any name, a file
    the PR adds included); reading the base's workflow files from GitHub each time (a contents read per
    workflow file and approval, and a YAML parse of each `name:`, for what the changed-files gate already
    guarantees); reading the base tip's checks for every approval to learn which file runs `CI` there (a
    read per tip even for a green head, and a base whose CI runs only on pull requests has no runs to
    tell); dropping the name glob's merge across workflows (it would break the Completion posted through
    the API that spec 84 kept it for).

- **A related PR stacked below this one owns the findings on its lines** (2026-10-21, spec 111, approved by
  the operator the same day). A review of #752 posted a P2 (a rule without a regression test) on a line of
  a background job; #752's head was #751's head plus 41 commits, and the author answered that the line
  came unchanged from #751, which had made the change. related.json listed #751 with that file among 40
  shared paths but nothing said #752 was built on it, so the skill's section 3 rule (a problem in a lower
  layer of a stack is `outside_diff`) never applied; the run before had the mirror case (#751's review,
  "#752 replaces it").
  - The related step (`stackRelated`, internal/pipeline/related.go) now asks the round's checkout, for each
    open related PR whose head it has (`git rev-parse --verify`), `git merge-base --is-ancestor <its head>
    <the head under review>` and the reverse (gitx.IsAncestor; exit 1 is the answer no, logged at Debug):
    an ancestor head gets `"stack": "below"` in related.json and related-all.json, the reverse `"above"`.
    The checkout shares the main clone's objects, so it has every head Magnum fetched for a round of that
    PR and every head in this PR's history: a stack below is always seen, one above when Magnum reviewed
    the PR above at that head. A head never fetched, the same head (git would answer both) and a merged
    PR (merging the base puts its head in this PR's history too) get none; a git failure leaves the PR
    without a stack (a log line), and the checks of one prompt stop after 30 seconds.
  - The judge prompts' `related_prs` line names them (`(#751 stacked below this PR; #753 above it)`), and
    with a PR below, the own pass, initial, rereview and recovery prompts add one line: a finding that sits
    only on lines a PR stacked below this one introduced is that PR's (`outside_diff`, the skill's section
    3), named in the body's related-PR line as the PR it belongs to. The line is built from the round's
    whole related set, not related.json's part of it, so a re-review whose related.json leaves the lower
    PR out (an earlier review named it in its state and paths) still carries it: the stack decides findings
    in every round, while the body names the PR only for such a finding. The continued turn renders only
    the field (the paused turn had the line). The `round.related` event names the PRs below and above
    (`stacked_below`, `stacked_above`). SKILL.md is unchanged: its section 3 rule stands.
  - Tests, failing first: TestARelatedPRWhoseHeadIsAnAncestorIsStackedBelow (below, above, a head never
    fetched, the same head and a merged PR; the files, the prompt and the event) and
    TestAStackedPRNamedBeforeStillGetsItsLineInTheJudgePrompt in pipeline,
    TestJudgePromptsGiveAFindingOnlyOnAStackedBelowPRsLinesToThatPR, TestRelatedStackLineSaysBothDirections
    and five goldens in agents, TestRealIsAncestorAnswersWhetherOneHeadIsInTheOthersHistory and
    TestIsAncestorRefusesAnOptionForARevision in gitx. Mutations checked: no stack, a merged PR checked,
    the same head checked.
  - Rejected: reading the related PRs' base refs from GitHub (a call per PR against the poll's budget, and
    #752's base was the default branch, so its base ref would not have shown the stack); a SKILL.md rule
    (section 3 already has it, the judge only lacked the fact, and the skill is near its byte ceiling);
    marking only the PRs related.json names (a fresh session's re-review would lose the stack); fetching a
    related head the checkout lacks (a network call in the prompt's path, for the "above" case only).

- **A round hands the judge the PR's Jira ticket** (2026-10-21, spec 116, asked for by the operator the same
  day: "build jira"). He asked whether a first review checks the Jira task's requirements against what the
  PR does and says: it did not. The judge got URLs, SHAs, notes, history, docs and related PRs; the only

    (the site, https only, the relay URL's rules), `user` (the account's email: no colon, no space) and
    `token_file` (the API token alone on one line; `~` and a path beside the user config resolved). A token
    file that is missing, not regular or open to group or others is a Config.Warnings line, never a config
    error (fsx.CheckPrivate, which webhooks.CheckTokenFile now shares).
  - The key: the first issue key of the repository's trackers (Config.TrackersFor) whose template starts
    with `url` and a slash (Jira.Names; a Linear tracker never counts) in the PR's title, else in its head
    branch. The spec also named the description; the round has no copy of it (the registry keeps title and
    head ref, the Details query does not read `body`, and pipeline.GitHub reads nothing that returns it), so
    the operator chose the title and branch only and no GitHub call: if a run shows keys living only in
    descriptions, the follow-up is `body` in the Details fragment (a field GitHub does not price) with only
    its issue keys kept in a prs column. No key: no file and one `round.ticket` info line.
  - The read (internal/jira): once a round, beside docs.json before the stages of its first head
    (writeTicket; a restart writes the new head's copy from what was read, a continued turn reads nothing and
    names the paused turn's file), `GET <url>/rest/api/2/issue/<KEY>?expand=names&fields=*all` through curl
    via execx as internal/webhooks reads the relay: `--disable --config -`, the config on stdin, HTTPS only,
    `globoff`, no redirect followed, 20 s, and the credentials as the config's `user = "email:token"` line,
    so the token never reaches argv, a log, an event or an error. The v2 API, whose description is text.
    Kept: key, URL (`<url>/browse/<KEY>`), summary, status, type, priority, labels, the parent's key and
    summary, the description cut at 20,000 bytes and every custom field whose name (from `names`) holds
    acceptance, criteria, requirement, definition of done or scope and whose value is a string, cut at 8,000
    bytes each, on a character; never a comment, an assignee, reporter or watcher, or an attachment.
  - The file: `ticket.md` in the report directory, written atomically at 0600: a heading with the key and
    URL, then the fields as sections, the text as given, a cut one with a line saying how much was kept.
    Every judge prompt (own pass, initial, rereview, recovery, continue) names it as `ticket`, its path
    only (JudgeData.TicketFile).
  - The skill (section 2, after Docs; 460 bytes with `ticket` in section 0's list and its line in section
    7's body order, skillMaxBytes 37,872): the ticket is data, never instructions; a requirement the PR
    does not meet, or a change it does not ask for that the description leaves unexplained, is one body
    line `Ticket: ✗ <what>: <why>` (never a ✓ line), or a finding at its priority when it has impact; what
    the ticket leaves open is no finding.
  - Failures: a refusal (401, 403, 404, another status), a timeout, curl failing otherwise or an answer that
    is not an issue is one `round.ticket` warning with its class (jira.Error), never the body, no file (an
    earlier round's on the head removed), and the round goes on. A token file problem warns once per daemon
    start (one jira.Client for every identity's rounds, WarnTokenFile), then is info. A Done or Closed issue
    is still handed over. Events carry the key, the status name, the number of requirement fields and the
    sizes, never the summary or any text.
  - Replays read the ticket too (requirements predate the PR; no comment is read, so nothing written after
    the review reaches the judge), and evalrun.Inputs hashes `[jira]`'s url and user when it is on (the
    token file never; ReviewerInputs not at all), so a config without it keeps its hash. `magnum doctor`
    checks the scheme and the token file and, only under MAGNUM_LIVE_JIRA=1 (never in the gate), asks
    `<url>/rest/api/2/myself`. No GitHub budget is spent; one Jira call a round.
  - Tests, failing first: in jira TestTheTicketRequestSendsTheCredentialsOnStdinNeverInArgv,
    TestTheTicketKeepsOnlyItsRequirementFields, TestTheTicketCutsLongText,
    TestARefusedOrMalformedAnswerIsAClassOnly, TestTheTokenFileMustBeOwnersOnly and
    TestMyselfChecksTheCredentials; in config TestJiraDefaultsToOff, TestJiraURLIsHTTPSOnly,
    TestJiraTokenFileModeIsAWarningNotAnError and TestJiraOverlayMergesKeyByKey; in pipeline
    TestTheRoundFindsTheIssueKeyInTheTitleThenTheBranch, TestTheTicketFileReachesTheJudgePrompt,
    TestATicketFetchFailureDoesNotFailTheRound and TestARestartWritesTheTicketReadOnceForTheNewHead; in
    agents TestJudgePromptsNameTheTicketFileOnly, TestSkillChecksThePRAgainstItsTicket and five goldens; in
    cli TestDoctorChecksTheJiraTokenFileAndAsksJiraOnlyWhenLive; in evalrun
    TestTheJiraSiteChangesTheInputsButNotTheReviewers. Mutations checked, each failing a test: the
    credentials in argv or in another directive, no requirement-name filter, either cut size, a cut inside a
    character, the branch before the title, a Linear tracker read, a read on every head, a token file
    warning every round, an earlier round's file kept, and a continued turn reading Jira again.
  - Rejected: the Atlassian MCP server (interactive OAuth, nothing an unattended daemon can hold); the judge
    calling Jira itself from the slot (the token would reach the sandbox the PR's code runs in); reading

- **The GitHub meter says how much of each rate-limit window was spent outside magnum's own calls**
  (2026-10-21, spec 117, asked for by the operator the same day: "improve magnum status"). From 16:30 to
  17:13Z the poll identity `zhuravel` (the operator's gh login) went down to 12 GraphQL points, and the
  floor held new work from 17:10. The meter counted 526 points for the whole 16:00 hour (radar 227, ci
  states 227, details 54), so about 4,400 points of that window went to something else on the login, and
  `magnum status` said nothing of it: its github line showed only magnum's spend and the lowest reading.
  The operator logged Herdr.app out of GitHub (its pull request and CI view polls every worktree magnum
  keeps open); from 17:30 to 17:41Z GitHub counted 103 points used and the meter about 100. For an App
  identity the same gap is the agents' own `gh` calls: a pane gets its posting identity's
  `GH_CONFIG_DIR`, so the agents spend the installation's window too, and the meter never hears them.
  - Per window: each identity's record (`github.cost.<identity>`) keeps `windows`, each GraphQL window
    the daemon's calls answered in, keyed by the reset GitHub gave it first (a reading whose reset is
    within 10 seconds of a kept window's is that window's, the nearest one's): its limit, the highest
    `used` any answer in it gave (limit − remaining for an answer without it) and `points`, the sum of
    the daemon's calls' cost answered in it. Outside is used − points, never below 0. Both are
    order-insensitive (a maximum and a sum), so calls in flight may return in any order, and the window's
    used counts what others spent before the daemon's first call in it. A call no rate limit came back
    with (it failed before GraphQL answered, or GitHub refused it) and a REST call add nothing; the
    radar's reading (recordRateLimit) raises its window's used and adds no points, since its calls were
    counted. Windows go 24 hours after their reset, as hours do, and are written and read back with the
    record. The floor is unchanged: it still reads the kept reading.
  - Why by window and not by clock hour: GitHub's budget is a window that starts with the first call
    after a reset and lasts an hour (the day's resets were 13:28:45, 14:29:01, 15:29:07, 16:29:15 and
    17:29:29Z), so an hour's points and a window's used never cover the same calls. And one login can
    show two windows at once (resets 18:29:46 and 18:31:00Z, different remaining, with the daemon's calls
    in both), which a reading per hour would mix. Before relying on the reset as a key, a read-only check
    at 19:11Z made 13 `rateLimit` reads within 15 seconds: they answered two windows, 19:29:51Z (315 used)
    and 19:32:12Z (69 used), each with the same reset and used every time, and used + remaining = limit.
  - Status: when the windows that have not reset hold 100 points or more outside, the identity's line
    ends with `· 4,412 points outside magnum since 16:29` (their sum; the earliest one's start, an hour
    before its reset). `--json` lists every kept window under `windows` (reset_at, limit, used, points,
    outside); the daemon's `told` stays in the record.
  - The notice: the first tick that finds a window that has not reset at a fifth of its own limit or more
    outside (1,000 of 5,000) writes one `github.outside_spend` warning (subject `github:<identity>`, as the
    budget events) and one toast, "GitHub budget of zhuravel: 1,050 points of this window went to calls
    outside magnum (another tool on this login, or the agents' own gh)", the same words in the event, the
    toast's body (its title is "GitHub budget of zhuravel: 1,050 points outside magnum", 80 runes being a
    toast title's most) and the README. The window is marked `told` and the records are written at once,
    so neither a later tick nor a restart says it again; the next window that gets there is told again.
  - Residuals: while calls are in flight a window's used can run ahead of its points by their cost, so
    the line can show a few points too many until they return (the tick, not the call, decides the
    notice). A window whose reset GitHub gives a second off between calls would split its used and its
    points over two keys, each showing outside spend, so the line would count the other tools' spend
    twice and the notice could fire for nothing: at 11:14Z the radar read 47 and then 44 points a second
    apart with resets 11:28:10Z and 11:28:11Z, one window by the look of it, though the 19:11Z check saw
    none move. So a reading whose reset is within 10 seconds of a kept window's belongs to that window
    (the nearest, which keeps its first reset as its key, so its outside spend is counted once), while
    the windows seen at once were 65 to 141 seconds apart (11:28:11Z and 11:29:16Z, 18:29:46Z and
    18:31:00Z, 19:29:51Z and 19:32:12Z) and stay apart. A reset that moved by more than 10 seconds would
    still split its window. The REST core budget is not covered (its headers are not read), and nothing
    says which tool spent the points.
  - Tests, failing first: in engine TestTheMeterKeepsWhatEachWindowSpentOutsideItsCalls,
    TestTwoWindowsOfOneLoginAreKeptApart, TestAResetSecondsOffAKeptWindowsIsThatWindow (1 and 10 seconds
    off either way one window, 11 and 51 seconds two), TestAWindowIsTheSameWhateverOrderItsCallsReturnIn,
    TestACallWithoutARateLimitAddsToNoWindow, TestTheRadarsReadingRaisesUsedWithoutPoints,
    TestAWindowIsPruned24HoursAfterItsReset, TestTheWindowsOutliveARestart,
    TestAWindowsOutsideSpendIsToldOnceAtAFifthOfItsLimit and
    TestTheOutsideNoticeIsAtAFifthOfTheWindowsOwnLimit; in cli
    TestTheGitHubLineSaysWhatWasSpentOutsideMagnum, TestTheGitHubLineSaysNothingOfLessThan100PointsOutside,
    TestTheGitHubLineSumsTheLiveWindows, TestTheGitHubLineLeavesOutAnExpiredWindow and
    TestStatusJSONCarriesTheGitHubWindows; in textx TestThousandsPutsACommaBetweenEachThreeDigits (the
    status line's thousands, now shared with the event). TestARunOfLowBudgetIsAnnouncedOnce's low readings
    now come with the points that spent them, so they hold nothing outside magnum. Mutations checked,
    each failing a test: no points, the last used for the highest, no limit − remaining, the radar's
    points counted, the radar's raise not written, no pruning, pruning at the reset, told ignored, a
    window that reset told, above a fifth only, a fixed 5,000 limit, no write at once, the highest window
    for the sum, the latest start, a window that reset counted, a threshold of 101, no slack, a minute of
    slack, a slack that excludes 10 seconds, and either neighbouring window never matched.
  - Rejected: reading `gh api rate_limit` on a timer (it spends nothing, but it shows one window, and on
    10-21 its reset disagreed with GraphQL's own); counting by clock hour (an hour's points and a
    window's used cover different calls); a hard pause on outside spend (the operator decides what else
    uses the login, and the floor already holds new work when the budget runs low, whoever spent it).
- **`magnum merge-check` is retired** (2026-10-22, amends "`magnum merge-check`: an experiment the operator
  runs, never the daemon" and "Every release of a slot deletes its merge-check refs"). The command ran twice,
  on 2026-10-07, on the two known clashes of 10-05 (#11939 with #11979, #11959 with #11939), and found both;
  it never ran again, so its false-positive rate is unknown, and no later entry decided its future. On
  2026-10-22 the operator approved retiring it. Gone with it: `internal/mergecheck` and
  `internal/cli/merge_check.go`; the slot hold only it used (`slots.HoldFree`, `CheckoutHeld`, `ReleaseHeld`,
  `MergeCheckRef` and `MergeCheckRefs`, and the hold `releaseSteps`, `resetSchema` and `breakSchema` took, so
  a release runs again only from releasing or dirty_schema to free; `guardChecks`, split out for the held
  slot's guard, is part of `guard` again); the gitx helpers only it called (`MergeTree`, `CommitTree`,
  `FetchInto`, `UpdateRef`, `MergeCheckRefPrefix`); and the release's deletion of
  `refs/magnum/merge-check/<slot>/`, which every release has done since 10-08 (a ref still there names a local
  commit nothing reads). The registry holds no slot with the hold reason `merge-check`; one would be handed
  back by `magnum slots unpin` and the daemon's release like any held slot. Kept: hold_reason itself (the
  guard's persisted holds use it), `UpdateRefDelete`, `MergeCommitOid` (the post-merge job reads it) and the
  judge's own `git merge-tree` run on a merged tree, which is the skill's and none of this code. The results
  under the state directory's `merge-check/` are left alone. A revival needs a measured false-positive rate
  first: the command replayed over merges whose outcome is known, clean pairs as well as clashes, not two hits
  on clashes already known.

    TestUnderAnAppPollerARequestForTheOperatorsLoginStartsARound,
    TestUnderAnAppPollerARequestForTheOperatorsLoginSetsTheRequestedFlag,

- **The judge prompts share their common blocks through one partials file** (2026-10-22, spec 04, approved
  by the operator the same day). No judge prompt used `{{define}}` or `{{template}}`. Of the 43 commits
  that touched judge prompts, 27 touched three or more of them. Spec 116 edited five prompts and five
  goldens to add the `ticket:` line. judge-rereview.md and judge-recovery.md shared 13 long lines word for
  word (7,205 bytes), and judge-initial.md and judge-rereview.md shared 2,918 bytes. The prepass,
  evidence-map and stacked-PR paragraphs stood in four prompts. So a rule edit touched three or four
  files, and drift was one missed copy away. `prompts/judge-shared.md` now holds 31 `{{define}}` blocks:
  the paragraphs and the runs of `<magnum>` lines that two or more judge prompts carried word for word.
  The prompts include them with `{{template "<name>" .}}`. The five prompts went from 45,786 to 14,895
  bytes, with 13,304 bytes of blocks beside them.
  - Byte for byte: this is a pure refactor. A script moved each block from the old files, by line range or
    exact text, and asserted its match count. No block was typed again. Every judge golden passes
    unchanged, and none was regenerated. A throwaway check rendered the old and the new prompts with
    150,000 random JudgeData values: each pair was identical, or both refused the data. If all the prompts
    of a paragraph share its condition and leading blank line, its block holds them too. Otherwise the
    block holds the paragraph alone, and each prompt keeps its condition. Whole sentences of 100 bytes or
    more, shared inside lines that differ, are blocks too: the skill link, the blind rules, the earlier
    reviews, the former logins and the threads file. Two composites, `review-rules` and `review-fields`,
    hold the runs that initial, rereview and recovery share whole. They include the blocks that own pass
    and continue also use alone. A prompt keeps the lines only it carries (its mode, phase and per-mode
    fields), so they stay in view.
  - Loading: config.ResolvePrompt gives every judge prompt the file's text in Prompt.Shared
    (config.UsesShared: a `judge-*.md` other than the file itself). The file resolves as a prompt does:
    prompts_dir's file, else the embedded copy, and in the daemon the snapshot's copy. ResolvePrompt
    refuses the file's own name (ErrSharedPrompt), so no role's prompt can name it.
    config.ParseTemplate parses the file first, as its own template, for agents.RenderPrompt and for the
    config check. SnapshotPrompts loads it with any judge prompt. So the start check,
    `daemon.prompts_changed`, the changed count of `magnum status` and the snapshot's Sum count it. The
    eval inputs hash it once per role whose prompts include it, and the reviewers' inputs stay as they
    were. prompts.Names leaves it out. A copy in prompts_dir replaces the embedded file as a whole. A
    prompts_dir without one uses the embedded blocks.
  - The editor glob: the name matches `prompts/judge-*.md`. That is the skill editor's allowed glob
    (learn.EditAllowedGlobs) and the gate's judge-only test (learn.Mode). So the editor can change the
    file, and the gate replays the judge alone for it, with no change to either.

- **An overload that other PRs' rounds share charges no attempt** (2026-10-22, spec 02 of the
  2026-10-22 improvement run, approved by the operator the same day). On 2026-10-20 from 13:01 to 13:27Z a
  provider outage ended 21 rounds as overloaded ("stream disconnected before completion"), 12 of them
  continued judge turns, and six PRs went to needs attention between 13:14 and 13:28: an overload charged
  the PR an attempt, retried after 1 and then 2 minutes, and the third parked it, so an outage longer
  than about 3 minutes parked every PR it touched. At 13:55 the operator forced five of them by hand.
  - The rule: a round that ends overloaded charges nothing when the overload is shared, that is when,
    within the last hour (`overloadShareWindow`, twice `retryMax`), another PR's round
    on the same agent kind ended overloaded (the engine's own `engine.round_result`, which now names the
    kind of the pause or overload a round hit, data `tool`), or another PR's agent of that kind ended with
    the same pane line (`launchLines`, the lines `agents.shared_failure` groups, with the PRs counted once
    each through the same grouping, `onePerPR`). The kind of a pane line is its role's. The PR goes back
    to paused with its attempts untouched and continues after `backoff(n)`, n its shared overloads in a
    row (`pr.<id>.overload_shared`, deleted by any other end of a round of the PR, a lone overload
    included), so the wait doubles from 1 minute up to `retryMax`, 30 minutes, the engine's retry cap.
    Its `last_error` leads with the shared part, which a one-line summary keeps ("overloaded: codex is
    overloaded across 3 PRs (no attempt charged; retry 2 in 2m): judge pane: …"), and one
    `round.overload_shared` info event under the PR names the kind, how many PRs share the overload and
    the wait, never the pane line. A lone overload keeps its charge, its 1- and 2-minute retries and its
    park on the third. The first PR an outage reaches is charged once, since nobody shares its overload
    yet. No kind is paused, and a PR an overload parked is never retried: only the round's own PR moves,
    from the round's states, which keeps the operator's rule of 2026-10-17 that a parked PR waits for his
    `magnum review`. A usage limit and a lost login are charged and paused as before.
  - Why the window is twice the cap: at the 30-minute cap PRs in lockstep (their rounds overloading in the
    same tick with the same duration, so retrying in the same tick again) settle a cap and a round's
    length after their last overloads. The first of them to settle, before the other's round has ended,
    would find the other's last overload just outside a window of 30 minutes, the shared failures' own
    (`sharedFailureWindow`), and be charged, and over a long outage the third such charge would park it.
    Twice the cap keeps the other's last overload inside whatever the rounds' length up to another 30
    minutes. `noteSharedFailures` keeps its 30 minutes: a launch line two PRs share is news only when
    close in time.
  - Tests, failing first: in engine TestAnOverloadSharedAcrossPRsChargesNoAttempt (the 10-20 shape: three
    codex PRs overloading 20 seconds apart, eight times each: only the first overload charged, the others
    waiting 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 minutes, then 30, none parked, one event per uncharged overload naming 2
    and then 3 PRs and never the line, each posting once the provider answers and forgetting its count),
    TestALoneOverloadStillParksOnTheThirdAttempt (which also drops a count of shared overloads),
    TestAnOverloadIsSharedOnlyWithinTheWindowAndOnItsKind (a codex overload 59 minutes before shares, 61
    minutes before does not, nor a claude overload; a codex launch on the same pane line shares, a claude
    one on it or a codex one on another line does not), TestPRsOverloadingInLockstepAtTheCapStayUncharged
    (two PRs whose 2-minute rounds overload in the same tick and settle one after the other, eight cycles:
    both uncharged and retrying together, at 30 minutes from the sixth) and
    TestASharedOverloadNeverRetriesAParkedPR, with the key pinned in
    TestEveryKVKeyTheEngineWritesKeepsItsString. Mutations checked, each failing a test: the PR itself
    counted as sharing, any kind, any pane line, twice the window, a window of the cap (the lockstep pair's
    first settler charged at the seventh cycle), no doubling, no cap, the count never deleted, a lone
    overload keeping it, and the round's result without its kind.
  - Rejected: pausing the kind on a shared overload (spec 75 rejected pausing on a shared failure: the
    operator decides, and a pause hides a short outage behind a wait nobody asked for); retrying the PRs
    an overload already parked (the operator's rule: a parked PR waits for `magnum review`); a longer fixed
    backoff for every overload (a lone overload is the PR's own, and a fixed wait long enough for an
    outage would delay every single blip); the shared failures' 30-minute window (the lockstep gap above).

- **Every role reads the whole notes, in bounded parts of a frozen copy** (2026-10-22, spec 06, approved
  by the operator the same day). The main repository's notes are 96,835 bytes. On 2026-10-20 and 10-21
  Codex roles read the then 89 KB file whole 103 times, and 94 of those reads came back truncated: Codex
  returns at most 10,000 tokens of one tool output by default and drops the middle, where the pitfalls
  and the standing decisions sit. Claude Code's Read refuses a file above about 25,000 tokens, so the
  Claude reviewers had a limit too. A judge's merge read the file the same way, so a truncated read could
  also lose the middle of the file it rewrote. A Codex review of codex-cli 0.162.1's source found the
  layers: a direct `exec_command` returns the smaller of its `max_output_tokens` (10,000 unless the model
  asks for more) and the configured policy, which `tool_output_token_limit` sets; code mode's outer `exec`
  prints 10,000 tokens by default, so several reads printed in one call exceed it; the history keeps a tool
  result within the same policy; no other fixed ceiling applies in these paths but a 1 MiB collection
  bound.
  - Parts of a frozen copy: right before a round's first prompt (after readiness), the pipeline copies the
    live notes into the report directory (`notes-read.md`, agents.FreezeNotes), once per round, kept
    across restarts on newer heads; a blind replay copies its scratch notes the same way. Judges rewrite
    the live file about 20 times a day, so line ranges of the live file would shift between two reads.
    agents.SplitNotes cuts the copy into runs of whole lines of at most 16 KiB (a line counted with its
    newline); only a line longer than that is cut inside it, into 16 KiB pieces (`sed -n 'Np' | cut -b`).
    Every prompt that names the notes renders `.NotesParts` (the copy, its bytes and lines, one `sed -n`
    command per part) with one fixed sentence, "Read the repository notes in these parts, one part per tool
    call. Never print two parts in one call.": the claude reviewer prompts (review, rereview, restart,
    simplify) in their notes paragraph, which now shows only when there is a copy to read; the judge
    prompts as the `notes_parts` field of the partials file's `notes-fields` block; and fix.md, which
    rendered no notes before, from a copy the fix job writes beside its report, with "Read them. Never edit
    the notes." The judge still rewrites the live file under the lock; `notes_reread`, beside `notes_lock`,
    is an awk line (`LC_ALL=C`, so lengths are bytes) that prints the same part commands for the live file
    as it is then, which the judge reads before it merges, since the copy can be older. SKILL.md changed
    in two places, 55 bytes, for sentences the parts contradict: section 2 reads `notes_parts`, else
    `notes`, and the update's step 2 reads `notes` again in the parts `notes_reread` prints (skillMaxBytes
    37,927). The stock `codex review` takes no prompt, so codex-review gets no notes: a documented limit.
  - The ceiling: every Codex process magnum starts passes `-c tool_output_token_limit=65536`, a kind key
    (`tool_output_limit`, 65,536 for codex, 0 = the CLI's own, through `tool_output`, `["-c",
    "tool_output_token_limit={limit}"]`) and not `start`, which the operator's config replaces. Kind.Argv
    puts it after the effort and the subagent cap, before the args that keep configuration out, so it
    reaches every launch and resume (the round's roles, the fixer, the whiteboard writer, the curator, the
    retro, the skill editor and the eval replays all start through agents.StartAgent); codex-review's
    command and codex-review.sh pass `.ToolOutput`, which Manager.ShellLine fills from the tool's kind. A
    person's resume line carries none, as it keeps their MCP servers. 65,536 tokens is about 256 KiB at
    Codex's four bytes a token: room for today's notes and the larger reads a model asks for, never the
    normal reading size.
  - The eval inputs hash the prompt files and the kind's config, so the parts sentence and the key are in

- **Curation organizes the notes and never loses a line** (2026-10-22, amends "Repository notes: triggers,
  history, usage and curation" and "The retro's misses become notes proposals"). The operator asked how to stop
  losing repository notes, now and as they grow. The registry showed where the loss came from: judges insert
  lessons under the lock and delete nothing, but in the main repository he had applied 5 of 20 curation
  proposals, each dropping 54 to 151 lines with nothing like them left, and rejected 11, often for cutting
  durable knowledge ("Too much went: every standing decision and author answer must stay in full", "Keep these
  general pitfalls and QA methods, which no other line carried"). The size trigger drove the cuts: on 10-14 he
  raised `max_bytes` to 48 KiB because curations ran every day and each cut, his notes are now about 95 KiB, and
  as his config sets only `max_bytes` the built-in `["over_limit", "misses"]` still applied. A review of the
  code found three gaps: the validator accounted for every section of the proposal but not of the current
  notes, so a whole old section could vanish without an entry; the prompt pushed toward the limits ("Stay
  within them unless the content truly improves future reviews"); and a notes state was only the notes and the
  harness, so a file beside them would have had no fingerprint, history, apply or restore.
  - The invariant, in `notes.Validate` (`checkPreserved`): every non-empty line of the notes now, trailing
    spaces aside, is in the proposed notes or among the lines the proposal adds to the archive, word for word;
    the archive keeps every line it held, as many times as it held it; every `## ` section of the notes now is
    in `changes.json` with an action and a reason; a proposal with an archive names it in its notes. Exempt:
    the title (a first line starting `# `, which every curation dates anew), a `## ` heading `changes.json`
    accounts for (what became of its section is said there) and a line with a secret or a home directory path
    (the leak rules keep it out of the archive too, and the prompt has such lines removed; the registry keeps
    them). The problems count the lines missing and quote the first three, clipped, to the curator's nudge and
    to the operator's review (an invalid proposal's reason); events still quote no notes text. A rewrapped or
    reworded line is a dropped one: its old words go to the archive, which costs bytes, not validity.
  - The archive is a reserved file of the harness, `ARCHIVE.md` (`notes.ArchiveName`), rather than a new field
    of the state stored beside the notes as `<repo>.archive.md`: as a harness file it is in the state already,
    so the fingerprint, the round's snapshot, every registry version (an entry of notes_version_files, its body
    once in harness_blobs; no migration), `--log`, `--diff`, the three-way merge of a stale proposal, apply and
    restore carry it with no code of their own, and `WriteState` keeps its two-step swap (a third file would
    have needed its own rollback); a forgotten exemption is a miscount, where a forgotten field would have
    dropped the archive on that path. What treats harness files as scripts leaves it out: `Size` (the limits;
    `archive_bytes` and `archive_lines` apart), the judge's `notes_harness` listing, the rounds that count a
    file's uses (so it is never unused), the curator's usage data, the rules that a file be named in the notes
    and have a `changes.json` item, and the harness events and toasts. The archive is history: it may name a
    pull request, while the secret and home-directory rules still hold. Only a curation or a recovery writes
    it: when a judge's round changed it (and no curation applied during the round did), the engine records
    the judge's state (so nothing is lost), then puts back the archive the round found: the body with the hash
    the round's snapshot lists, from the bodies the registry stores for any version of the repository (none
    when the snapshot had no archive), never a newer row such as a waiting proposal's own version; under the
    notes lock, recorded as an import, with a `notes.archive_restored` warning that names the PR and the
    version. When no stored body has that hash (a hand edit not imported yet), the judge's archive stays and
    the warning says it could not be put back.
  - Defaults: `curate = ["misses"]` (no curation starts for size alone; `over_limit` stays a valid choice) and
    `max_bytes = 262144`, which marks notes past it in `magnum notes` as a hint to organize them. The prompt
    lost the sentence that pushed toward the limits and says curation organizes and never loses knowledge:
    merge duplicates naming where each went, retire a line only when proven obsolete or superseded with the
    evidence, keep standing decisions and the authors' answers in full (age, rarity, low use and size are no
    reasons), and put every line taken out or rewritten into the archive word for word with its disposition
    (`→ merged into`, `→ superseded by`, `→ obsolete because`) under `## Retired <date>`.
  - The recovery, `magnum notes <repo> --recover`: an archive of every line a live version held (the history:
    judges', people's, imports and applied curations', never a proposal's own unapplied state) and the notes
    now lack, grouped by the day of the version that last dropped it, the notes text unchanged; a line already
    in the archive is not added again, one with a secret or a home path is left out and counted. It is a
    curation proposal no curator wrote (trigger `recover`, so no migration of the proposals' kinds), reviewed
    like a restore and refused while another proposal waits; the daemon's spacing of curations, the curator's
    rejections and the stale follow-up leave it out. `--json` prints it and records nothing. A dry run against
    a copy of the registry for the main repository: 984 lines from 257 versions over 16 days, 3 left out for a
    home directory path, none with a secret.
  - Tests, failing first: in notes TestAProposalThatMovesALineToTheArchiveIsValid,
    TestAProposalThatDropsALineWithoutArchivingItIsInvalid, TestTheTitleAndALeakingLineNeedNoArchive,
    TestAProposalThatDropsAWholeOldSectionWithoutAnEntryIsInvalid,
    TestAProposalThatRemovesALineFromTheArchiveIsInvalid, TestAProposalNamesItsArchive,
    TestTheArchiveMayNameAPullRequestButNoSecret, TestWithArchiveAndWriteArchive,
    TestRecoverArchivesEveryDroppedLineOnceByTheDayItLeft and TestPrepareScratchCopiesTheArchive; in engine
    TestARepositoryPastMaxBytesGetsNoAutomaticCuration, TestTheArchiveCountsForNoRound,
    TestAJudgesEditOfTheArchiveIsPutBack, TestAJudgesEditOfTheArchiveGoesBackToWhatTheRoundFound (a waiting
    proposal's version, with another archive, the newest row), TestAnArchiveTheRegistryNeverHeldIsNotPutBack
    and TestTheCuratorPromptKeepsEveryLine; in store TestNotesHarnessBlobIsFoundAmongTheRepositorysVersions; in agents
    TestNotesHarnessLeavesTheArchiveOut; in cli TestApplyWritesTheArchiveWithTheNotes,
    TestHistoryDiffAndRestoreCoverTheArchive and TestRecoverArchivesWhatTheHistoryDropped; in config
    TestNotesDefaults and TestNotesCurateReadsAListOrTheEarlierString pin the new defaults.
  - Rejected: a similarity test for kept lines (it passes a line that lost an "unless" or an author's answer,
    which are what the operator's rejections were about); an archive outside the versioned state (no history,
    no restore, no stale merge, and a judge's edit could not be undone); a higher size trigger alone (curations
    would still cut, only less often).
- **A notes proposal is applied by a claim, a write and a record** (2026-10-22, spec 07, amends "A curator
  proposes curated notes" and "Stale notes proposals"). The notes critic (design
  docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-10-notes-critic-and-configurability-design.md, confirmed again by the operator on
  2026-10-22) adds a second decider beside the operator's `magnum notes <repo> --review`. A Codex review of the
  design on that day found a gap. The CLI's apply wrote the files before the compare-and-set of the proposal
  (`notes.WriteState`, then `DecideNotesProposal`). With two deciders, a lost race can leave notes that a rejected
  proposal wrote. The apply is now in the engine (`engine.ApplyNotesProposal`), and the CLI's `y` calls it. It works
  under the notes lock, in this order:
  1. It reads the proposal again. A proposal that no longer waits is refused, and the refusal names who decided it
     and when (`ProposalDecidedError`, from the new `decided_by`).
  2. It reads the notes again. It refuses notes that are not the notes the decider saw (`ErrNotesChanged`). It also
     refuses a target with a fingerprint other than the approved one (`ErrTargetChanged`). The target is the
     proposed state, or the clean merge of a stale proposal.
  3. It runs the preservation check of curation on the target (`notes.CheckPreserved`). No line of the notes now
     can go, and the archive keeps every line. Two rules of `notes.Validate` are not in this check. A section that
     a judge added after the proposal stays in the merge line by line, so `changes.json` does not have to name it.
     A recovery does not change the notes text, so the notes do not have to name the archive. A proposal that fails
     the check (for example, one stored before spec 05) cannot be applied (`NotPreservedError`). It can only be
     rejected or curated again. `--review` shows "CANNOT BE APPLIED" with the lines, and its `y` asks for a new
     curation. That curation supersedes the proposal with the reason, through the new `why` of the request.
  4. It claims the proposal: the state goes from pending to `applying` (`store.ClaimNotesProposal`). The claim
     records the decider, the notes as found (`prior_version_id`) and the fingerprint of the target
     (`target_sha256`).
  5. It writes the notes and the harness, then records the proposal as applied with its version. When the write
     fails, `WriteState` puts the old state back and the apply releases the claim.

  A restore does not get the preservation check. It brings back a version that the operator chose, the critic
  never decides a restore, and the registry keeps the state that the restore replaces.
  - Recovery. A crash between the claim and the record leaves the proposal in `applying`. The daemon start does a
    recovery before it imports the notes. Each curation scan does it again, because the lock of a crashed process
    becomes stale only after ten minutes. The recovery takes the notes lock. It calculates the target again from
    the base, prior and proposed versions, and compares it with the fingerprint of the claim. Then:
    - Notes that hold the target are recorded as applied (`notes.apply_finished`).
    - Notes that hold the prior state show that nothing was written. The claim is released (`notes.apply_reverted`).
    - Notes of one state with the harness of the other show a write that stopped halfway (`WriteState` replaces the
      harness first). The recovery writes the full target and records it.
    - Other notes are recorded as an import, so that the registry keeps them. The claim is released, and the
      proposal is stale against those notes.

    A proposal in `applying` stops a new curation and a recovery, as a pending proposal does.
  - Migration 0027 rebuilds `notes_proposals`, as 0017 did, for the `applying` state. It adds `decided_by`
    (`operator`, `critic` or `magnum`), `prior_version_id` and `target_sha256`. The backfill gives the operator all
    applied and rejected rows, and magnum all expired, invalid and superseded rows. `DecideNotesProposal` takes the
    decider. The CLI gives `operator` for a rejection and `magnum` for an expiry. The engine gives `magnum` for an
    expiry or a supersede. An invalid proposal is magnum's.
  - Tests (written before the code passed them): in engine TestTheOperatorAndTheCriticRaceAndExactlyOneApplies,
    TestARejectionAndAnApplyNeverBothWin, TestAStopBetweenTheClaimAndTheWriteIsRevertedAtTheNextStart,
    TestAStopBetweenTheWriteAndTheRecordIsFinishedAtTheNextStart, TestAWriteStoppedHalfwayIsCompletedAtTheNextStart,
    TestAnApplyCutShortUnderChangedNotesWaitsAgain, TestAProposalThatLosesALineCannotBeAppliedByEitherDecider and
    TestAnApprovalOfAnotherTargetIsRefused. In store TestMigrationV26ToV27AddsApplyingAndBackfillsDeciders and
    TestAClaimIsCompareAndSetAndReleasable. In cli TestReviewOfAProposalThatLosesALineAsksForANewCurationInstead and
    TestTheOperatorsRefusalNamesTheCritic. The CLI test fixtures now put the lines that their proposals drop into
    the archive.
  - Rejected: write first and ignore a lost compare-and-set (the files can then hold a rejected proposal). Store the
    merge as a version at the claim (no history must show that version). The recovery calculates the merge again
    from three recorded versions and compares the fingerprint. Recover only at the daemon start (the lock of a
    crashed CLI is not stale for ten minutes).

- **A pane job whose model hits its own limit goes on on a fallback, and a role names its own fallbacks**
  (2026-10-22, the model-fallback part of spec 07; design docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-10-notes-critic-and-
  configurability-design.md section 4, approved 2026-10-10, the critic re-confirmed by the operator on
  2026-10-22; amends "A per-model limit switches the session's model; an account limit still pauses the
  kind"). A pane job (the curator, the retro's classifier, the skill editor, and the notes critic to come)
  ran its agent over a scratch registry that `Close` deletes: at a model limit it stopped as a Pause, the
  limit was recorded nowhere that outlived the job, and the next job started on the same model and hit the
  same limit. The critic is to run on fable, whose plan share runs out, and must then continue on opus.
  - Per-role lists: `fallback_models` on a `[[role]]`, `[notes] fallback_models` (the curator), `[learn]
    fallback_models` (the classifier) and `[learn] editor_fallback_models` (the editor), each carried into its
    role (`NotesRole`, `LearnRole`, `EditorRole`), empty by default (the kind's list). `agents.fallbacksFor`
    gives the role's list when it has one, else the kind's (never both), and every path that picks a fallback
    asks it: `startModel` (whose guard now considers the role's list), `LaunchModel`, `ensureModel`,
    `FallbackModel` (so a round's reviewer and judge use a `[[role]]` list), `NoteModelLimit`'s `Using`, and
    `ModelLimits` (no role: the kind's). A new role needs only its `Role.FallbackModels`. Each entry is one
    word, listed once, refused under its own key (`role <name>: fallback_models`, `notes.fallback_models`,
    `learn.fallback_models`, `learn.editor_fallback_models`); a shell role takes none. The kind's
    `switch_model = ""` still turns switching off.
  - The limit lives in the live registry: `paneDeps.Store` is the daemon's registry, `setup` seeds the scratch
    one with the kind's active limits and the CLI's default model as a limit message named it
    (`agents.CopyModelLimits`), so a launch skips a model rounds or an earlier job found limited. A
    model-limit reading records the limit live first (`agents.RecordModelLimit`, which `NoteModelLimit` now
    calls for its own writes, with a `kind.model_limited` event there) and then in the scratch registry
    through the scratch manager's `NoteModelLimit` with the live end. `magnum resume --tool` forgets it.
  - A limit hit again within a day of the last one's end (`MaxReset`) lasts twice the last one's span, up to
    24 hours, when its message names no reset time, so a weekly window costs one probe of the model a day; a
    report while the limit lasts is no repeat, a named reset is kept, a cooldown over a day is never shortened.
    The memory is `kind.<kind>.model_limited_at.<model>` ("<first recorded> <end>"), which outlives the limit
    and which `ClearModelLimits` deletes with the limit.
  - The restart stays inside the job (`paneAgent.afterTurn`, which every driver calls after a turn without
    a valid answer): a model limit is no longer a Pause. When the job has not restarted yet and a fresh
    launch would start on a free fallback (`agents.LaunchModel` over the scratch registry), the agent is
    released as `release` does (its open run interrupted and abandoned, parked, else quit and its workspace
    closed) and `ensureAgent` starts it again: a new session row, `StartAgent` with no conversation to
    resume and the scratch limits picking the fallback, so never the parked conversation. It gets the job's
    first prompt (its inputs are files) and the nudge it had left. No fallback left, or a second limit in the
    job, is a Pause of kind `model_limit`, which the callers already turn into a stop without a tool pause (a
    curation uncounted and tried again after `curateRetry`, the retro's PR left due, the editor's run
    stopped): only `usage_limit` and `login_required` pause a kind. A limit naming a model other than the
    one a fresh launch would run starts nothing again.
  - Each result (`ClassifyResult`, `CurateResult`, `EditResult`) carries `Model`, the model of the session
    the answer came from (`paneAgent.currentModel`: the scratch registry's session model, else the role's
    model): the curation proposal's and the skill-edit proposal's `model` column record it (the role's model
    when unknown), the retro's `retro.ok` event names it.
  - A blocked dialog ends a turn: magnum answers only the dialogs it knows, so an unknown one held a turn
    until its timeout. `paneAgent.wait` ends a turn whose session has shown herdr's `blocked` for
    `paneBlockedWait` (2 minutes): it reads the screen, sends escape and abandons the run, and the screen
    read before the escape is what `health` classifies. Claude Code asks before it bills Fable to usage
    credits once the plan's share is used: "Fable limit reached · continuing on Fable 5.1 uses usage
    credits", and, unanswered, "... and the prompt to confirm went unanswered" (third-party guides of
    2026-10; no official page has the wording yet). The claude kind's default `model_limit` patterns gain
    `continuing on (?P<model>fable)\b[\w .-]*\busage credits`; magnum never consents to a bill. When the
    dialog is first seen live, its text goes into docs/spikes.md and the pattern follows it.
  - Spec 119's restarts on a Codex login change mark and park live-registry sessions only
    (`RestartableSessions` over the daemon's store); a pane job's sessions live in its scratch registry, so
    the two never meet.
  - Tests, failing first: in config TestEveryFallbackModelsKeyIsReadIntoItsRoleAndEmptyByDefault and
    TestAFallbackModelsEntryOfTwoWordsIsRefusedUnderItsOwnKey (the model_limit pattern count in
    TestResetModelLimitPatternsSeparateModelFromAccountLimits now 4); in agents
    TestTheFableConsentDialogIsAModelLimitOfFable, TestARoleFallbackListWinsOverTheKindsInEveryPath,
    TestARoleFallbackListNeedsTheKindsSwitchModel, TestCopyModelLimitsSeedsAnotherRegistry,
    TestALimitHitAgainWithinADayDoublesItsCooldownUpTo24Hours and
    TestARepeatedLimitKeepsANamedResetAndDoublesWithoutOne; in pipeline
    TestARolesFallbackListAppliesToARoundsReviewerAndJudge; in engine
    TestAPaneJobOnALimitedModelContinuesOnItsFallbackInsideTheJob,
    TestTheNextPaneJobStartsOnTheFallbackOfALimitRecordedBefore,
    TestAPaneJobWithNoFallbackLeftStopsAndNeverPausesTheKind, TestASecondModelLimitInOnePaneJobStopsIt,
    TestATurnBlockedOnADialogEndsAfterPaneBlockedWait and TestClearModelLimitsForgetsTheRepeatsToo, with the
    key pinned in TestEveryKVKeyTheEngineWritesKeepsItsString.
  - Rejected: Claude Code's `--fallback-model` (it switches on overload and server errors only, never on a
    model or usage limit); pausing the kind once a job's fallback list runs out (a critic's list is short on
    purpose, and the rounds still have sonnet); switching the job's live session with `/model` as rounds do
    (the job's turn ended with no answer, and a fresh session with the same file inputs loses nothing); a
    restart per fallback (one per job bounds a job's cost when a window closes on every model). The design's
    section 5 (policy values moved into the configuration) stays a follow-up.
- **The notes critic decides curation proposals** (2026-10-22, spec 07, amends "A curator proposes curated notes" and
  "The retro's misses become notes proposals"). The operator asked eight times between 2026-10-06 and 10-17 for
  magnum to "process notes for me". On 2026-10-10 he approved the design
  docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-10-notes-critic-and-configurability-design.md. Its implementation stopped after its
  first tasks. On 2026-10-22 he confirmed the critic again. This entry builds section 3 of the design (the critic).
  Section 4 (the model fallback of pane jobs) is the entry before this one. A Codex review of the design on 2026-10-22 gave four
  amendments. The design log rejected an apply without review three times ("the curator deletes scripts", "every
  later round reads the notes", "the operator reviews the merge"). Those reasons were about a proposal applied
  unseen. The critic keeps a review before every apply. It is a second agent on a stronger model than the curator's.
  It has a fresh context and the operator's list of rules as its prompt. The registry records its decision, its
  reason and its record. `[notes] critic = false` is built in.
  - When it runs. With `critic = true`, every tick after `maybeCurate` takes the oldest pending curation proposal
    (never a restore or a recovery). These conditions must all be true:
    - No other learn job runs (`learnMu`), and the daily retro is not due and unrun.
    - Fewer than `critic_per_day` critiques started today.
    - No round of the repository is in its judge stage.
    - No hold, no pause of the critic's CLI, and no `magnum pause` (a proposal from the operator's `--curate` is
      critiqued under a pause).
    - The proposal has fewer than two undecided critiques, and no stop in the last hour.
    - The critic declined fewer than `critic_declines` proposals of the repository in a row.
  - What it reads. Magnum copies the inputs into `<notes>/.critic/<owner>/<repo>/<run>/`: `review.json`,
    `notes.diff`, `archive.diff`, `rejections.json`, the notes now and the proposal with their harness files, and
    `changes.json`. `review.json` is the data of `--review --json`, now `engine.NotesReviewView` from
    `engine.ReviewProposal`, with its diffs in their own files. The prompt (`prompts/notes-critic.md`, `[notes]
    critic_prompt`) gives paths, ids, flags, the limits and the target fingerprint. It gives no notes text. It gives
    every large copy in parts (spec 06's `agents.SplitNotes`). It has the no-loss rules of spec 05: standing decisions
    and the answers of authors stay in full, every removed line is in the archive word for word, and size is no
    reason.
  - What it answers. The critic writes `decision.json`: `apply`, `reject` or `recurate`, the target, a one-line
    reason, and its `losses` and `checked` lists. `notes.ValidateDecision` checks it. An invalid answer gets one
    nudge. A second invalid answer makes the critique undecided, which is an attempt. Apply is valid only for a
    proposal that can be applied (a clean merge, nothing lost). Recurate is valid only for one that cannot. The reason
    gets the leak checks of a revert reason (`learn.ScrubLesson` with the registry's people, magnum's logins and the
    names of the watched repositories). It also gets `notes.ReasonLeaks` (a pull request number, a branch, a probe
    file, a secret, a home path).
  - What the daemon does with the answer:
    - `apply` runs `engine.ApplyNotesProposal` with the critic as the decider (see "A notes proposal is applied by a
      claim, a write and a record").
    - `reject` rejects the proposal with the reason. `recurate` supersedes it with the reason. Both mark the
      repository (`notes.<repo>.recurate`). The next curation scan then starts a curation of trigger `review` under
      the gates of the daemon. It is never the operator's `request` trigger. Its curator reads the reason:
      `usage.json` lists the rejections and the superseded proposals of the operator and the critic, with `by`, and
      `superseded/reason.txt` holds the reason. The stored proposal clears the mark.
    - At `critic_declines` declines in a row, the critic steps back. It marks nothing, and the next proposal of the
      repository waits for the operator.
    - When the operator decided the proposal during the critique, an info event says so. Nothing else happens.
    - When an apply leaves the notes past a limit, the next `over_limit` curation waits a week
      (`notes.<repo>.critic_over`).
    - The decision toast is the only toast of a proposal. The "is ready" toast is not shown with the critic on. The
      expiry of a curation proposal with the critic on shows a toast.
    - Only the operator's rejections dismiss a miss (`decided_by = 'operator'`).
  - The four amendments of the Codex review:
    1. Safe apply, for the operator and the critic: the claim, the write and the record, with a recovery ("A notes
       proposal is applied by a claim, a write and a record").
    2. The decision binds to the target. Magnum gives the fingerprint of the state that an apply writes,
       `decision.json` names it, and an apply of another target is refused.
    3. A changed target is critiqued again. When the notes changed after the critique (`ErrNotesChanged`,
       `ErrTargetChanged`, `ErrStaleConflict`), the critique ends `changed`. That counts as a stop, not as an
       attempt. The next tick critiques the proposal against the new notes. The design applied a clean merge on the
       critic's word. A clean text merge does not prove that the result keeps what the critic approved.
    4. The registry keeps the record of the critic. Migration 0028 adds `notes_critiques`: the proposal, the run, the
       model, the target, the outcome, the decision, the reason, the `checked` and `losses` lists, and the detail of
       magnum. `magnum notes <repo> --decisions [N]` prints it after the run directory is pruned. In the design, that
       record was only in the run directory, which is pruned after 30 days.
  - Recorded state. `KVNotesCritic` marks the critique in flight. Every daemon start deletes it with the other learn
    marks, and ends an open critique row as `stopped` (retried, uncounted). `learnRunning` and `backgroundBusy` name
    the critique, so `magnum stop`, `daemon-restart` and `--drain` treat it as a curation. The events
    `notes.critic_start`, `notes.critic_decided`, `notes.critic_undecided`, `notes.critic_stopped`,
    `notes.critic_changed` and `notes.critic_overtaken` have the subject `notes:<repo>`.
  - Configuration (`[notes]`): `critic` (false), `critic_kind` ("claude"), `critic_model` ("fable"), `critic_effort`
    ("xhigh"), `critic_args`, `critic_prompt` ("notes-critic.md"), `critic_timeout` ("30m"), `critic_fallback_models`
    (["opus"]), `critic_declines` (2) and `critic_per_day` (4). A `critic_kind` without a `critic_model` gets
    `config.DefaultCriticModel`: fable for claude, and the CLI's own model for other kinds. `CriticRole` builds the
    role (`notes-critic`) as `NotesRole` and `EditorRole` do.
  - Tests (written before the code passed them): in engine TestTheCriticAppliesAValidProposalAndRecordsTheDeciderAndTheModel,
    TestAStaleProposalWithACleanMergeIsCritiquedAgainNotApplied, TestACriticRejectionStartsAReviewCurationThatReadsTheReason,
    TestTheCriticRecuratesALossyProposalAndTheCuratorReadsTheReason, TestTheCriticStepsBackAfterDeclinesInARow,
    TestTwoUndecidedAttemptsLeaveAProposalToTheOperatorAcrossARestart,
    TestTheOperatorsDecisionDuringACritiqueIsAnEventAndNothingElse, TestTheRetroDueTodayRunsBeforeAWaitingCritique,
    TestTheCriticsDailyCapHolds, TestACriticApplyLeftOverALimitDelaysTheNextSizeCurationToAWeek and
    TestWithTheCriticOffNothingCritiques. In notes TestPrepareCriticCopiesWhatTheCriticReads,
    TestReadDecisionRefusesUnknownFieldsAndTrailingValues, TestValidateDecisionBindsTheTargetAndTheDecisionToTheProposal
    and TestReasonLeaksNamesAProbeFile. In store TestCritiquesAreRecordedWithTheCriticsRecord and
    TestOnlyTheOperatorsRejectionsDismissAMiss. TestACriticOnFableContinuesOnOpusAtAModelLimit drives the pane critic
    through the fallback of the entry before this one. In cli
    TestDecisionsPrintCheckedLossesAndTheReasonFromTheRegistryAfterTheRunDirectoryIsDeleted,
    TestDecisionsListsTheNewestProposalsAndSaysHowManyMore, TestTheListShowsTheCriticRunningAndWhatItLeftToYou,
    TestTheStatusLineSaysCriticOnARepository, TestTheSummaryNamesTheLastDecision, TestReviewSaysTheCriticIsOnTheProposal,
    TestLogsFollowsTheNotesOfARepository, TestConfigFailsOnACriticPromptThisBuildCannotRender,
    TestDoctorChecksTheCriticsKindWhenTheCriticIsOn and TestARunningCritiqueRefusesAStop. The race, crash, binding and
    preservation tests are in the apply entry.
  - What the operator sees:
    - The decision toast.
    - In `magnum notes`: "critic running (fable, 2m)", "the critic stepped back", and "the critic did not decide it,
      expires in 2d".
    - "critic on <repo>" in `magnum status` and on the dashboard.
    - The last decision in `magnum notes <repo>`. A note in `--review` while the critic works on that proposal.
    - `--decisions [N]` and `magnum logs notes:<owner>/<repo>`.
    - The kind of the critic in `magnum doctor` (with the critic on), and its prompt in `magnum config`.
  - Deferred: section 5 of the design (fourteen policy values moved into the configuration) is the follow-up.
  - Rejected (design section 7): the critic edits the proposal before the apply (a second writer, a second
    validation, no record of who wrote what). Re-curation through the operator's `request` trigger (it runs under
    `magnum pause` and with `curate = []`, and shows the toasts of a requested curation). Claude Code's
    `--fallback-model` (it changes models on an overload only). A pause of the kind after the critic's fallback list
    is used up. A byte cap that the critic enforces. Critiques of restores. The critic chooses sides in a conflicting
    merge. The name "reviewer". Also rejected now: an apply of a clean merge on the critic's word (amendment 3), and
    the `checked` and `losses` lists only in the run directory (amendment 4).
- **Magnum never mistakes its own dismissal for the operator's, and a restart never cuts an approval write**
  (2026-10-23, spec 125 of the 2026-10-17 run, amends "Magnum approves as the operator when its review found nothing
  to fix"). The operator asked why a PR of a watched repository got no automatic approval as him after a clean
  review. The timeline, in UTC:
  1. 17:49:50: round 2 found nothing to fix, and magnum approved the head as the operator.
  2. 19:35:24: round 3 posted blocking problems on a new head. At 19:35:26 magnum began to withdraw the approval.
  3. 19:35:26: in the same second, `magnum daemon-restart --when-idle` restarted the daemon. Its idle check counted
     no running round, but the withdrawal was in flight. The dismissal request ended with "context canceled", and
     magnum planned a retry in 5 minutes. GitHub had received the PUT and dismissed the review.
  4. 19:40:40: the retry got "Validation Failed (HTTP 422)". Magnum read the review as dismissed already, by the
     operator's login in its timeline, and wrote "withdrew approval ... (GitHub lists it as dismissed already: you
     dismissed it)", then `review.auto_approve_stopped`: "magnum no longer approves ... as you: you dismissed it".
  5. 20:41:56: round 4 found nothing again. The App's review approved, but no approval as the operator came: the
     stop held it.

  Magnum had dismissed the review itself. Magnum and the operator both act as the operator's login, so the
  dismissal's actor cannot tell them apart; only magnum's own record of the request can. Now
  (internal/engine/autoapprove_pending.go):
  - A pending record. Before magnum sends an automatic approval or its withdrawal it records the request in kv:
    `pr.<id>.auto_approve_pending` holds the head, `pr.<id>.auto_withdraw_pending` the review id, and no request
    goes without its record. An answer that tells what GitHub did clears it: done, or refused with a 4xx
    (`writeAnswered`), or a retry's 422 that finds the review still standing (a dismissal is for good, so no request
    took). An answer magnum never got (a cancelled context, a timeout, a network failure, a 5xx, after which GitHub
    may have applied the request) leaves it. A row that ends for good (failed after its attempts, its PR closed)
    drops it, so a later dismissal or approval is never taken for it.
  - Its own outcome. A retry that gets 422 and finds the review dismissed while a dismissal of it is pending, and a
    retry or a restart's check (`resumeAutoPost`) that finds an approval of the head by the operator's login while
    an approval of that head is pending, count it as magnum's own success: the normal `review.auto_approval_withdrawn`
    or `review.auto_approved` event and toast, ending "(the first request's answer was lost)", with `answer_lost` in
    its data. Nothing stops auto-approval, and nothing says "you dismissed it" or "you approved it by hand". For
    approvals the marker in the body already told magnum's own; the record makes the approval of the head its own
    whatever its body says (one edited on GitHub). Without a record the current rules stay: a dismissal found is by
    whom the timeline says, and an approval without the marker is the operator's by hand.
  - The restart waits for these writes. An approval or a withdrawal is work in flight from before its record until
    its answer is recorded (`daemon.work`, the entry after this one), so `--when-idle`, `--drain`, the refusal
    without them and the daemon's own idle restart wait for it. A stop that comes anyway (`--now`, a signal) gives a
    write that started `operatorWriteGrace`, 30 s, to finish (`writeContext`: the request and the recording of its
    answer run on a context the stop ends only after the grace), and a stop starts no new write. The bound: gh's
    own timeout for the call is 2 minutes (`execx.DefaultTimeout`), longer than launchd lets a stopping daemon live
    (ExitTimeOut 45 s, then SIGKILL); GitHub itself ends a request it takes more than 10 s on, so 30 s covers gh's
    start, the request and its answer, and equals the shutdown's wait for the rounds, whose goroutines write the
    approvals of the rounds they end. A write the grace runs out on is logged, not failed: the row stays posting or
    dismissing, the record stays, and the next daemon settles it as above.
  - Tests, failing first (mutations of the record, the approval rule, the grace, its bound, the clearing on a known
    answer and the work mark each fail one): TestAWithdrawalWhoseAnswerWasLostIsMagnumsOwnWhenTheRetryFindsTheReviewDismissed
    (the case above; a cancelled context, a timeout and a 502), TestTheOperatorsDismissalAfterAKnownOutcomeStillStopsAutoApproval,
    TestAnApprovalWhoseAnswerWasLostIsMagnumsOwnWithoutItsMarker, TestAnApprovalByHandAfterARefusedPostStillStopsAutoApproval,
    TestAStopDuringAWithdrawalLetsTheRequestFinishWithinTheGrace, TestAWithdrawalPastTheStopsGraceIsCancelledAndSettledByTheNextDaemon,
    TestAnApprovalPastTheStopsGraceIsFoundByTheNextDaemonAsItsOwn and TestARestartWaitsForAnApprovalOrAWithdrawalInFlight
    in engine; TestDaemonRestartWhenIdleWaitsForAHeavyJobAndAnApprovalWrite and TestTheDaemonsWorkInFlightRefusesAStop
    in cli. TestAStopWhilePostingAnAutoApprovalLogsNoWarning's fake now answers when its grace ends.
  - Rejected: telling magnum's dismissal from the operator's by the GitHub actor, which is the same login. The
    auto_approvals row's posting or dismissing state as the record (a request GitHub refused leaves the row
    dismissing too, and the operator's dismissal before the retry would then count as magnum's). A grace as long as
    gh's own 2 minutes (launchd kills the daemon first). Reading the review before each retry instead of sending
    again (the 422 tells the same, one read later).
- **A restart waits for the heavy worker's jobs and the operator's approval writes** (2026-10-23, roadmap item 13
  with spec 125, amends "A restart waits for a running notes curation and the retro"). The restart's guards, the
  engine's `restartBusy` (the daemon's own idle restart for a new build, a landed skill version or a saved config)
  and the CLI's `backgroundWork` (daemon-restart, `--when-idle`, `--drain`, install, uninstall, daemon-stop), counted
  rounds, fix and whiteboard jobs and the learn jobs, but no job on the heavy worker, so an idle restart cancelled a
  slot's provision of 20 to 45 minutes, a release or an eviction half way, and no GitHub write as the operator (the
  entry before this one). Both count them now through one notion of the work in flight no registry row shows
  (internal/engine/work.go): `beginWork` records a piece of work in this process and in the kv mark `daemon.work`
  (`engine.WorkMark`: what, since when), rewritten under one lock whenever it changes, deleted when nothing is in
  flight, and rewritten from the daemon's own state at every start, so a crashed daemon's mark goes. A heavy job
  counts from the time it is queued until it ends ("heavy job provision:talkable/talkable", by its key), so the CLI
  never finds a gap between two queued jobs; the shutdown drops the jobs still queued, which the next daemon queues
  again from the registry. The refusal, the waits and the stop's consequence name them ("2 background job(s) in
  flight: heavy job provision:talkable/talkable (since 15:04), withdrawal of approval 9001 of talkable/talkable#2
  by zhuravel (since 15:04)"). A drain still starts heavy jobs (the reconcile, a pool's provision) and waits for
  those too. Tests: TestARestartWaitsForAHeavyJobQueuedOrRunning (queued, running, ended, dropped at the shutdown,
  a crashed daemon's mark at the start) in engine and TestDaemonRestartWhenIdleWaitsForAHeavyJobAndAnApprovalWrite
  in cli; TestARefusalThatKeepsFailingIsSaidOnce now lets the reconcile its ticks queue run, as the worker does.
  Rejected: counting a heavy job only while it runs (between two jobs the CLI could find nothing in flight), a kv
  mark per kind of work, and holding the heavy worker during a drain (a release a closed PR needs would wait for the
  restart).
- **The judge's own approval passes the approval's gates** (2026-10-23, spec 09 of the 2026-10-22 run). When a
  review finds nothing the judge posts the posting identity's `no_findings_event`, and where that is APPROVE the
  judge approves: a gh identity's default (`magnum init` without an App writes that setup) and a `[[repo]]` override,
  which three repositories of the operator's config set, talkable/talkable, talkable/talkable-proxies and a third,
  private one. The approval as the operator passes the gates of autoapprove_gates.go (a draft, a muted PR, one its
  watch would not review on its own, one that changes its own workflows or actions or what steers the review agents
  or whose file list is cut, CI); the judge's passed none, and `JudgeEvents` dropped it to COMMENT only for a
  post-merge round, a self-authored one, a missing report, the auto-approval author lists and the full-pass hold.
  Measured read-only on 2026-10-22: in talkable/talkable the App's approval does not count toward the ruleset's one
  required approving review (talkable#12056 carries the App's APPROVED review, no human approval, and GitHub's
  reviewDecision is REVIEW_REQUIRED; talkable#12042 shows the App's approval beside CHANGES_REQUESTED; the App has
  `contents: read`, and GitHub counts approvals from accounts with write access), talkable/talkable-proxies has the
  same ruleset, and the third repository, private on a free plan, enforces no review at all. So for the operator the
  App's approval on a PR that changes its own workflows, carries red CI or is a draft was a misleading green signal,
  and for an install whose judge posts as a gh login, or as an App with `contents: write`, a real approval nothing
  checked. Now (internal/engine/approval_gates.go, internal/pipeline/approval_gates.go):
  - A round whose judge would approve a clean review (`judgeApproves`; never a post-merge review, an eval replay, a
    dry run or a round of the operator's own PR, which comment anyway) is held, at its dispatch, to the gates that
    need no review, by the same functions as the approval as the operator (`prStateRefusal`, `watchRefusal`,
    `changedFilesRefusal`, factored out of `autoApproveRefusal` and `autoGateRefusal`, no second copy of a rule):
    `pipeline.RoundInput.NoApproval` carries the refusal in the judge prompt's fixed words ("the PR changes its own
    workflows or actions"; never a path or another word of the PR's), and a continue keeps the paused round's
    (`pr.<id>.no_approval_round`, as the hold's record).
  - The CI gate decides when the judge's prompt is written, through `RoundInput.CIGate`, an engine callback like
    `RestartJudge`, from the registry read the judge's failing-checks.json comes from, so the judge and the gate see
    one CI; a continue's prompt decides it again. Red CI that does not fail the way the base branch's tip fails
    refuses; checks that still run, pass, or fail as the tip's do let the APPROVE through, and a registry that holds
    a newer head's checks than the round's target says `unknown` and lets it through too.
  - A refusal makes the no-findings event COMMENT, whatever the identity. The prompt's `no_findings_event` and its
    `post_review` line's new `--no-findings-event` render from that one value (`agents.PostReviewLine`), so a continue
    that decides again can never leave them disagreeing, and with COMMENT `post-review` refuses a review file whose

  - One `round.approval_refused` info event per head and reason (`pr.<id>.judge_approval_refused`) says why in the

    event carries `ci_gate` (`green`, `running`, `red-like-base`, `red`, `unknown`) whenever the gate was asked, and

    judge's prompt applied (`RoundResult.NoApproval`), the posted review keeps it (`pr.<id>.no_approval_review`,

    listed with the gates' reason in the list's words: "approve by hand: the PR changes its own workflows or
    actions" on the board's card, in the toast and as `needs_me_reason` in `magnum tui --json`. Tests:
    TestAWorkflowChangingPRReviewedCleanNeedsYouWithTheGatesReason in engine,
    TestNeedsMePRsTakesACleanCommentTheGatesAskedForAsAnApproval and two cases of
    TestNeedsMeDecidesWhatTheOperatorsApprovalWouldFix in store, TestTheBoardListsACleanCommentTheGatesAskedForAsNeedingYou

  - Two prerequisites. The base tips' checks the CI gate reads (`baseChecks`) have their own lock, `baseMu`, held for
    no GitHub read, and auto-approval's GitHub budget (`autoRetry`, `autoHeld`, `autoPollPaused`) one of its own,
    `budgetMu`, which the base tip's read asks: before both lived under `autoMu`, which auto-approval holds across its
    writes as the operator (up to gh's 2-minute timeout), and a round's setup and judge prompt must never wait behind

    the tip), while the approval as the operator records `review.auto_approve_ci_base` ("the approval goes ahead")

  - Which moment's CI the gate uses was the spec's open question (its second stop condition), settled by the
    operator on 2026-10-23: when the judge's prompt is written, running checks let through (option C). From the

    CI before it dispatches. Of the 36 approvals posted since 09-15 whose reviewed head was still the PR's head, with

    | CI at dispatch | CI at posting | approvals |
    |---|---|---|
    | green | green | 27 |
    | red | red | 1 |
    | running | green | 5 |
    | running | still running | 3 |

    That sample cannot show CI that ran at dispatch and was red at posting: red CI usually brings a push, which
